meta.textbook: Potter & Perry, Fundamentals of Nursing, 12th ed.; Ignatavicius, Medical Surgical Nursing
meta.notes: Final exam practice questions, built section by section from the lecture PowerPoints taught after Exam 3, with readings as support. Each section has two kinds of questions, marked by tag: "concept" items test the rule itself (most have a short realistic scenario whose answer turns on one rule), covering every concept on every PowerPoint slide; "application" items are regular difficulty NCLEX style clinical judgment questions. Every item has a cjmm step. NGN style items are kept near 15% of each section. All text says "patient", never "client". Bowtie pools and cloze blanks are shuffled so correct choices are spread across positions. Ids are stable: ig33 = Iggy chapter 33, ig18 = Iggy chapter 18, sk-enteral = Enteral Nutrition skill, c = concept, m = application, x = hard application (difficulty: difficult).

optionStrategies.name: Eliminate absolutes
optionStrategies.cue: always, never, all, none, only, every
optionStrategies.note: Absolutes are usually wrong because medicine rarely deals in certainties.

optionStrategies.name: Favor qualifiers
optionStrategies.cue: usually, generally, often, may, approximately, most
optionStrategies.note: Qualifiers make a statement realistic. Not automatically right, but worth a second look against an absolute.

optionStrategies.name: Opposite pair, look closely
optionStrategies.cue: increase vs decrease, before vs after
optionStrategies.note: Often one of the pair is correct. Sometimes both are distractors, so treat it as a flag for attention.

optionStrategies.name: Global or umbrella option
optionStrategies.cue: one option covers two or more others
optionStrategies.note: If one option encompasses the others it is often the most complete answer.

optionStrategies.name: Patient centered option
optionStrategies.cue: asks, involves, or respects the patient
optionStrategies.note: Options that involve the patient beat options that decide for them.

optionStrategies.name: Duplicate facts
optionStrategies.cue: a wrong fact shared by two or more options
optionStrategies.note: One shared wrong fact eliminates several options at once.

optionStrategies.name: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings
optionStrategies.cue: don't worry, it's nothing, most people are fine
optionStrategies.note: Therapeutic communication reflects feelings and invites more.

optionStrategies.name: Odd man wins
optionStrategies.cue: three options share an idea, one stands apart
optionStrategies.note: When most options point one way, the different one is often correct.

optionStrategies.name: Negative polarity
optionStrategies.cue: avoid, except, not, least, contraindicated, requires further teaching
optionStrategies.note: You are hunting the wrong option. Identify polarity before reading the choices.

optionStrategies.name: Priority key word
optionStrategies.cue: priority, immediate, first, best, most, least
optionStrategies.note: More than one option may be true. The key word decides how to choose among them.

optionStrategies.name: Apply the ABCs
optionStrategies.note: In ordering and priority questions, airway, breathing, and circulation come first, then safety, then comfort.

optionStrategies.name: Assessment before intervention
optionStrategies.cue: assess, check, determine versus administer, apply, notify
optionStrategies.note: When the stem asks what comes first and an assessment option is present, assessment usually precedes action.

optionStrategies.name: Treat each option as true or false
optionStrategies.note: Work each option independently. Partial credit means a wrong selection costs you, so only select what the scenario supports.

questions.stem: A patient arrives with a deep forearm laceration that has bled heavily for 20 minutes. The skin is cool and pale and the heart rate is 118/min. Which statements correctly explain what is happening? Select all that apply.

options.text: Platelets are needed to form the first plug at the cut vessel
options.rationale: Platelets are the component that starts clotting by plugging the injured vessel, which is what will limit further loss.

options.text: The body should form clots throughout the circulation to stop the loss
options.rationale: The goal is to clot only where the vessel is hurt. Clots elsewhere would block circulation and impair oxygen delivery, which is the danger of unwanted clots.

options.text: Excessive bleeding has lowered the circulating blood volume
options.rationale: Heavy bleeding removes volume from the vessels; perfusion depends on adequate blood volume.

options.text: Albumin seals the cut vessel wall to stop the bleeding
options.rationale: Albumin holds fluid inside the vessels through osmotic pressure. It does not seal a wound; platelets and fibrin do.

options.text: Lower blood volume compromises perfusion of the tissues
options.rationale: Less volume means less blood flow through tissues and less oxygen delivered, which explains the cool, pale skin and the fast heart rate.

questions.takeaway: Bleeding threatens perfusion by lowering blood volume. Clotting must happen at the injury and nowhere else.
questions.strategy: Hold each statement against the two priority concepts: perfusion needs adequate volume, and clotting should be local to the injury.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Lost volume and reduced tissue perfusion are both true and explain the vital signs.
Platelets plug the vessel; clotting everywhere and albumin sealing the wound are both false.

elimination.verdict: Three statements are true: lowered volume, compromised perfusion and the platelet plug.

questions.objective: Describe major blood components and their functions

questions.stem: A patient on bed rest after hip surgery has a clot in a deep calf vein and asks why a clot is a concern when clotting is helpful. Which explanation is accurate?

options.text: It uses up plasma and lowers the blood volume
options.rationale: Lowered blood volume is the danger of excessive bleeding, not of a clot. A clot does not drain plasma from the circulation.

options.text: It releases plasmin, which weakens the vein wall
options.rationale: Plasmin is the enzyme that breaks down fibrin during fibrinolysis. It does not damage vessel walls and is not the reason a clot is dangerous.

options.text: It destroys the red cells that carry oxygen
options.rationale: A clot traps some cells, but it does not destroy the red cell supply. The harm comes from blocked flow, not from red cell loss.

options.text: It can block blood flow and impair oxygen delivery
options.rationale: Clotting is protective at an injury, but an unwanted or misplaced clot obstructs circulation, so the tissue beyond it loses oxygen.

questions.takeaway: Unwanted or excessive clots obstruct circulation and impair oxygen delivery. Clotting is helpful only where a vessel is injured.
questions.strategy: Ask what a clot does in the wrong place: it blocks the pipe. Pick the option about flow and oxygen.

strategies: Opposite pair, look closely
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Lowered blood volume belongs to bleeding, the opposite problem.
Plasmin dissolves clots and red cells are not destroyed, so both are false.

elimination.verdict: The clot is dangerous because it blocks flow and oxygen delivery.

questions.objective: Describe major blood components and their functions

questions.stem: A patient has a hemoglobin of 7.8 g/dL. The patient becomes short of breath climbing one flight of stairs, and the heart rate rises to 112/min. Which blood component function is reduced?

options.text: Oxygen delivery by red blood cells
options.rationale: Hemoglobin inside red cells carries oxygen from the lungs to the tissues. With less hemoglobin, tissues get less oxygen, so the heart and lungs work harder.

options.text: Immune defense by white blood cells
options.rationale: Low white cells raise infection risk; they do not cause exertional dyspnea and tachycardia.

options.text: Plug formation by platelets
options.rationale: Low platelets cause bruising, petechiae and bleeding, not shortness of breath with activity.

options.text: Fluid retention in vessels by albumin
options.rationale: Albumin keeps fluid inside the vessels; a deficit causes edema, and the cue here is a low hemoglobin.

questions.takeaway: Red blood cells carry oxygen on hemoglobin from the lungs to the tissues and return CO2 for exhalation. Low hemoglobin shows up as dyspnea and a fast heart rate with activity.
questions.strategy: Link the lab value to the component that holds it: hemoglobin lives in red cells, and red cells carry oxygen.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Match the lab to the cell
steps.detail: Hemoglobin is the oxygen carrying protein in red cells.
Dyspnea and tachycardia on exertion mean the tissues are short of oxygen, not of immunity, platelets or albumin.

elimination.verdict: Reduced oxygen delivery by red cells explains the findings.

questions.objective: Describe major blood components and their functions

questions.stem: Which functions are carried out by plasma? Select all that apply.

options.text: Forming the first plug at an injured vessel
options.rationale: That is the platelets' job. Plasma carries the platelets but does not form the plug.

options.text: Transporting nutrients to the tissues
options.rationale: Plasma is the liquid matrix that transports nutrients.

options.text: Carrying hormones through the body
options.rationale: Hormones travel dissolved in plasma or bound to its transport proteins.

options.text: Producing new red and white blood cells
options.rationale: Bone marrow produces red cells, white cells and platelets. Plasma only transports them.

options.text: Transporting blood cells and plasma proteins
options.rationale: Plasma, about 55% of blood, is the liquid that carries the cells and the proteins such as albumin, globulins and clotting proteins.

questions.takeaway: Plasma is the liquid matrix, about 55% of blood, that transports cells, nutrients, hormones and proteins.
questions.strategy: Plasma is a carrier. Keep every option about transport and reject the ones that make, plug or build something.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Duplicate facts

steps.detail: Nutrients, hormones, cells and proteins are all things plasma carries.

steps.action: Reject the jobs of other parts
steps.detail: Plug formation belongs to platelets and cell production to the marrow.

elimination.verdict: Plasma transports nutrients, hormones, cells and proteins.

questions.objective: Describe major blood components and their functions

questions.stem: For each finding, select the blood component whose shortage best explains it.
questions.scenario: A nurse reviews six findings from patients with suspected blood disorders. Each finding reflects a shortage of one blood component.

rows.text: Shortness of breath and fatigue with light activity
rows.rationale: Red cells carry oxygen on hemoglobin; fewer red cells means less oxygen to tissues, so activity causes dyspnea and fatigue.

rows.text: Three infections in the past four months
rows.rationale: White cells recognize pathogens, make antibodies and destroy infected cells; a shortage leaves the patient open to repeated infections.

rows.text: Tiny red pinpoint spots on the lower legs
rows.rationale: Platelets form the first plug at injured vessels. When they are low, the smallest vessels leak first, producing petechiae.

rows.text: Swollen ankles and puffy eyelids
rows.rationale: Albumin keeps fluid inside the vessels by regulating osmotic pressure; when it is low, fluid leaks into the tissues as edema.

rows.text: Gums that bleed after brushing
rows.rationale: Gum bleeding is a small vessel bleed, the classic sign of too few platelets to plug minor injuries.

rows.text: Pale skin and nail beds
rows.rationale: Pallor reflects less hemoglobin in the blood, which means fewer red cells carrying oxygen.

questions.takeaway: Each component has one main job: red cells carry oxygen, white cells defend, platelets plug and albumin holds fluid in the vessels. A shortage shows up as the loss of that job.
questions.strategy: For each finding ask which job has failed: oxygen, defense, plugging or holding fluid in.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Breathlessness and pallor mean oxygen; infections mean defense; spots and gum bleeding mean plugging; swelling means fluid holding.

steps.action: Map the job to the component
steps.detail: Oxygen to red cells, defense to white cells, plugging to platelets, fluid holding to albumin.

elimination.verdict: Red cells for dyspnea and pallor, white cells for infections, platelets for petechiae and gum bleeding, albumin for edema.

questions.objective: Describe major blood components and their functions

questions.stem: A patient with cirrhosis has a serum albumin of 2.1 g/dL. The nurse finds pitting edema in both legs and a swollen abdomen. Which explanation best accounts for the edema?

options.text: Loss of globulin transport of hormones
options.rationale: Globulins serve as antibodies and carry hormones and nutrients. They are not the main protein that holds fluid in the vessels.

options.text: Loss of fibrinogen sealing the vessel walls
options.rationale: Fibrinogen is a clotting protein that becomes fibrin. It does not keep fluid inside intact vessels.

options.text: Loss of albumin's osmotic pull on fluid
options.rationale: Albumin keeps fluid inside the vessels by regulating osmotic pressure. With low albumin, fluid leaks out into the tissues and abdomen.

options.text: Loss of red cells carrying oxygen
options.rationale: Fewer red cells cause fatigue, pallor and dyspnea, not edema.

questions.takeaway: Low albumin lowers the osmotic pressure that holds fluid in the vessels, so fluid leaks out and edema follows.
questions.strategy: Name the mechanism: edema is fluid that left the vessels, and albumin is the protein whose osmotic pressure keeps it in.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Find the protein named in the cues
steps.detail: The low lab value is albumin.
Globulins defend and transport, fibrinogen clots and red cells carry oxygen; only albumin holds fluid in.

elimination.verdict: Low albumin and lost osmotic pressure explain the edema.

questions.objective: Describe major blood components and their functions

questions.stem: A patient with years of heavy alcohol use has yellow sclera and bleeding gums. Platelets are 260,000/mm3 and the prothrombin time (PT) is prolonged. Which organ is most likely failing?

options.text: Bone marrow
options.rationale: The marrow makes platelets, and this platelet count is normal. A marrow problem would lower every cell line.

options.text: Spleen
options.rationale: The spleen filters blood and removes old or damaged cells. It does not make clotting factors.

options.text: Kidney
options.rationale: The kidney makes erythropoietin, which drives red cell production. It does not make clotting factors.

options.text: Liver
options.rationale: The liver makes many plasma proteins and clotting factors. With normal platelets but a prolonged PT and jaundice, the clotting factors are what is missing.

questions.takeaway: The liver makes most plasma proteins and clotting factors. Liver failure means bleeding risk even when the platelet count is normal.
questions.strategy: Separate the two halves of clotting: platelets come from the marrow, clotting factors come from the liver. A normal platelet count points away from the marrow.

strategies: Opposite pair, look closely
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Normal platelets rule out the marrow as the cause of this bleeding.
Neither the spleen nor the kidney makes them; the liver does, and jaundice confirms liver disease.

elimination.verdict: The liver is not making enough clotting factors.

questions.objective: Describe major blood components and their functions

questions.stem: A patient had the spleen removed after a car crash. The nurse teaches the patient to report any fever right away. Which explanation supports this teaching?

options.text: The spleen made most of the white blood cells
options.rationale: In adults, the bone marrow makes the white cells. Removing the spleen does not stop white cell production.

options.text: The spleen filtered blood and helped fight infection
options.rationale: The spleen filters blood, removes aging or damaged cells and takes part in immune defense, so without it infections are harder to control.

options.text: The spleen produced the body's clotting factors
options.rationale: The liver makes clotting factors. Bleeding risk is not why the teaching focuses on fever.

options.text: The spleen stored albumin for fluid balance
options.rationale: The liver makes albumin and the spleen does not store it. Fluid balance is unrelated to fever teaching.

questions.takeaway: The spleen filters blood, removes old or damaged cells and helps defend against infection. Without it, infection risk rises.
questions.strategy: Let the teaching point to the job: fever and vaccines are about infection, so pick the immune role of the spleen and reject the jobs that belong to the marrow and the liver.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: White cell production belongs to the marrow; clotting factors and albumin belong to the liver.
Infection precautions fit the spleen's filtering and immune role.

elimination.verdict: The spleen filtered blood and helped fight infection.

questions.objective: Describe major blood components and their functions

questions.stem: A patient receiving chemotherapy has a treatment that suppresses the bone marrow. Before the next cycle, the nurse reviews the blood work. Which pattern does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Fewer red cells, white cells and platelets
options.rationale: The bone marrow produces all three cell lines, so marrow suppression lowers red cells, white cells and platelets together.

options.text: Fewer clotting factors and less albumin
options.rationale: Clotting factors and albumin come from the liver. That pattern fits liver disease, not marrow suppression.

options.text: More old red cells left in circulation
options.rationale: Removing aging red cells is the spleen's job. Poor filtering points to a spleen problem, not the marrow.

options.text: Fewer white cells with normal other counts
options.rationale: Marrow suppression is not selective; it affects every cell line the marrow makes, not just the white cells.

questions.takeaway: Bone marrow makes red cells, white cells and platelets, so a marrow problem lowers every cell line.
questions.strategy: Ask what the marrow makes, then expect all of it to fall. Reject patterns that belong to the liver or the spleen.

strategies: Global or umbrella option
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Red cells, white cells and platelets.
Clotting factors and albumin are liver products; old cell removal is the spleen's job; a single low line is too narrow.

elimination.verdict: Expect fewer red cells, white cells and platelets.

questions.objective: Describe major blood components and their functions

questions.stem: Which group of plasma proteins provides antibodies for immune defense and carries hormones and nutrients?

options.text: Albumin
options.rationale: Albumin maintains fluid balance by regulating osmotic pressure. It is not the antibody group.

options.text: Globulins
options.rationale: Globulins include the antibodies that defend against infection and the transport proteins that carry hormones and nutrients.

options.text: Fibrinogen
options.rationale: Fibrinogen is a clotting protein that is converted to fibrin. It plays no antibody role.

options.text: Prothrombin
options.rationale: Prothrombin is a clotting protein activated to thrombin during clot formation.

questions.takeaway: Plasma proteins come in three groups: albumin holds fluid in, globulins defend and transport, and clotting proteins (fibrinogen, prothrombin) build the clot.
questions.strategy: Sort the options into the three protein groups; only one group has an immune job.

strategies: Duplicate facts
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Fibrinogen and prothrombin are both clotting proteins, so they lose together.
Albumin controls osmotic pressure; globulins are the antibodies and transporters.

elimination.verdict: Globulins are the antibody and transport proteins.

questions.objective: Describe major blood components and their functions

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes how clotting proteins change during clot formation?

options.text: Fibrin is converted into fibrinogen
options.rationale: This reverses the process. Fibrinogen is the precursor and fibrin is the product.

options.text: Thrombin is activated into prothrombin
options.rationale: This also reverses the order. Prothrombin is the inactive precursor that is activated to thrombin.

options.text: Fibrinogen is converted into fibrin
options.rationale: Fibrinogen is the precursor that is converted to fibrin, the threads that stabilize the clot.

options.text: Plasminogen is converted into fibrin
options.rationale: Plasminogen becomes plasmin, which breaks fibrin down. It is part of clot breakdown, not clot building.

questions.takeaway: Fibrinogen becomes fibrin, and prothrombin becomes thrombin. The precursor carries the extra piece (ogen at the end or pro at the front); the active product has the shorter name.
questions.strategy: Watch the direction of each conversion; the precursor name ends in ogen or starts with pro, and the active product has the shorter name.

strategies: Opposite pair, look closely

steps.detail: Fibrin to fibrinogen and thrombin to prothrombin run backward.
Plasminogen belongs to fibrinolysis and never becomes fibrin.

elimination.verdict: Fibrinogen is converted into fibrin.

questions.objective: Describe major blood components and their functions

questions.stem: A patient is started on a heparin infusion for a clot in the leg. The nurse explains that heparin works partly by inhibiting thrombin. What does thrombin normally do?

options.text: Converts fibrinogen into fibrin
options.rationale: Prothrombin is activated to thrombin, which drives the final clotting steps by converting fibrinogen to fibrin. Blocking thrombin keeps new fibrin from forming.

options.text: Breaks down the fibrin mesh
options.rationale: That is plasmin's role during fibrinolysis. Heparin does not dissolve an existing clot.

options.text: Makes platelets stick to the vessel wall
options.rationale: Platelet adhesion is an early platelet step, not thrombin's main job in the cascade.

options.text: Keeps fluid inside the blood vessels
options.rationale: That is albumin's role through osmotic pressure.

questions.takeaway: Thrombin, made from prothrombin, drives the final clotting steps by turning fibrinogen into fibrin.
questions.strategy: Place thrombin in the sequence: it sits at the end of the cascade, right before fibrin, so its job is to make fibrin.

strategies: Opposite pair, look closely
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Thrombin builds fibrin; plasmin breaks it down.
Adhesion is a platelet step and fluid balance is albumin's job.

elimination.verdict: Thrombin converts fibrinogen into fibrin.

questions.objective: Explain clot formation and breakdown mechanisms

questions.stem: A patient slices a fingertip while chopping vegetables. Bleeding slows over the next few minutes and a firm clot forms. Place the steps of hemostasis in the order they occur.

options.text: Vessel constriction
options.rationale: First. The damaged vessel narrows immediately to reduce blood flow to the injury.

options.text: Clotting factor activation
options.rationale: Fourth. A cascade of clotting factors is activated and converts fibrinogen to fibrin.

options.text: Fibrin formation
options.rationale: Fifth. Fibrin threads weave through the plug and stabilize it into a true clot.

options.text: Platelet aggregation
options.rationale: Third. More platelets clump together into a temporary platelet plug.

options.text: Platelet adhesion
options.rationale: Second. Platelets stick to the exposed vessel wall at the injury.

questions.takeaway: Hemostasis runs constriction, adhesion, aggregation, clotting factor activation, fibrin formation. The vessel acts first, then platelets, then proteins.
questions.strategy: Think vessel, then platelets, then proteins. Platelets must stick before they can clump, and the cascade must run before fibrin exists.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Constriction is immediate and fibrin formation is the final, stabilizing step.
Adhesion comes before aggregation, and both platelet steps come before the clotting factor cascade.

elimination.verdict: Constriction, adhesion, aggregation, clotting factor activation, fibrin formation.

questions.objective: Explain clot formation and breakdown mechanisms

questions.stem: A patient's nosebleed slows after a few minutes of firm pressure, and a temporary plug forms that is not yet a stable clot. Which step of hemostasis formed this plug?

options.text: Vessel constriction
options.rationale: Constriction narrows the vessel to reduce flow, but it does not create a plug.

options.text: Platelet adhesion
options.rationale: Adhesion is platelets sticking to the vessel wall. The plug forms only when more platelets clump together in the next step.

options.text: Platelet aggregation
options.rationale: Platelets clump together into the initial platelet plug. It is temporary until fibrin forms.

options.text: Fibrin formation
options.rationale: Fibrin formation is the last step and is what stabilizes the plug into a true clot, so the plug exists before it.

questions.takeaway: Platelet aggregation forms the temporary platelet plug; fibrin formation turns it into a stable clot.
questions.strategy: Separate temporary from stable: the temporary plug is made of platelets, the stable clot needs fibrin. Then pick the platelet step that actually builds the plug.

strategies: Opposite pair, look closely

steps.detail: Fibrin formation makes the clot stable, which the stem says has not happened yet.
Adhesion attaches platelets; aggregation clumps them into the plug.

elimination.verdict: Platelet aggregation formed the temporary plug.

questions.objective: Explain clot formation and breakdown mechanisms

questions.stem: A patient with hemophilia, an inherited bleeding disorder, has a normal platelet count. A small cut stops bleeding briefly, then oozes again for hours. Which step of hemostasis is failing?

options.text: Blood vessel constriction
options.rationale: The vessel narrows normally; hemophilia does not affect the vessel wall.

options.text: Platelet adhesion
options.rationale: Platelets are normal in number, and the brief stop in bleeding shows they are sticking to the wall.

options.text: Platelet aggregation
options.rationale: The early stop shows a platelet plug formed. The problem comes after the plug.

options.text: Clotting factor activation
options.rationale: A missing clotting factor breaks the cascade, so fibrinogen is not converted to fibrin and the temporary platelet plug never stabilizes.

questions.takeaway: A platelet plug alone is temporary. Without a working clotting factor cascade, no fibrin forms and the wound keeps oozing.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Use the timing: bleeding that stops and then restarts means the platelet steps worked and the protein steps did not.

strategies: Duplicate facts
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Constriction, adhesion and aggregation all worked, which is why the bleeding stopped at first.
The missing factor is used in clotting factor activation, so the cascade fails there.

elimination.verdict: Clotting factor activation is failing.

questions.objective: Explain clot formation and breakdown mechanisms

questions.stem: A patient's hand is crushed in machinery at work. Damaged tissue releases tissue factor into the blood at the injury. Which clotting pathway does this start?

options.text: Intrinsic pathway
options.rationale: The intrinsic pathway starts with factors already present in the blood, and stasis favors it. It is not triggered by tissue factor.

options.text: Extrinsic pathway
options.rationale: The extrinsic pathway starts with tissue factor released from damaged tissue, as in trauma.

options.text: Common pathway
options.rationale: The common pathway is where the intrinsic and extrinsic pathways converge. It is not the starting point.

options.text: Fibrinolytic pathway
options.rationale: Fibrinolysis breaks clots down after healing; it does not start clot formation.

questions.takeaway: Tissue factor from damaged tissue starts the extrinsic pathway; factors already in the blood start the intrinsic pathway; both converge on the common pathway.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Ask where the trigger comes from. Outside the blood, from injured tissue, means extrinsic.

strategies: Opposite pair, look closely

steps.action: Remove what is not a starting point
steps.detail: The common pathway is where the others meet, and fibrinolysis breaks clots down.
Tissue factor comes from outside the blood, so extrinsic wins over intrinsic.

elimination.verdict: Tissue factor starts the extrinsic pathway.

questions.objective: Explain clot formation and breakdown mechanisms

questions.stem: The intrinsic and extrinsic clotting pathways converge on a common pathway. What does the common pathway produce?

options.text: Fibrin, which stabilizes the clot
options.rationale: The common pathway produces fibrin, the threads that weave through the platelet plug and make it a stable clot.

options.text: Plasmin, which degrades the clot
options.rationale: Plasmin comes from plasminogen during fibrinolysis and breaks the clot down. It is not the product of the clotting pathways.

options.text: Fibrinogen, which plugs the vessel
options.rationale: Fibrinogen is the precursor that gets converted, not the end product, and the platelets form the plug.

options.text: Antithrombin, which limits the clot
options.rationale: Antithrombin is a natural anticoagulant that keeps clots from growing too large. It works against the cascade.

questions.takeaway: Both pathways meet in the common pathway, and the common pathway's product is fibrin, which stabilizes the clot.
questions.strategy: Ask what the whole cascade is for: making fibrin. The precursor, the clot dissolver and the clot limiter are all near misses.

strategies: Opposite pair, look closely
Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Remove the substances that oppose clotting
steps.detail: Plasmin breaks clots down and antithrombin limits them.
Fibrinogen goes in; fibrin comes out.

elimination.verdict: The common pathway produces fibrin.

questions.objective: Explain clot formation and breakdown mechanisms

questions.stem: A patient has had two deep vein clots before age 40. Testing shows a deficiency in one of the body's natural anticoagulants. Which substances act as natural anticoagulants? Select all that apply.

options.text: Fibrinogen
options.rationale: Fibrinogen is a clotting protein converted to fibrin; it builds clots.

options.text: Thrombin
options.rationale: Thrombin drives the final clotting steps by converting fibrinogen to fibrin. Antithrombin is the substance that opposes it.

options.text: Antithrombin
options.rationale: Antithrombin is a natural anticoagulant that keeps clots from growing too large or forming where they are not needed.

options.text: Tissue factor
options.rationale: Tissue factor from damaged tissue starts the extrinsic pathway; it promotes clotting.

options.text: Prothrombin
options.rationale: Prothrombin is the precursor activated to thrombin; it promotes clotting.

options.text: Protein C
options.rationale: Protein C is a natural anticoagulant. A deficiency tips the balance toward clotting and raises the risk of venous clots.

questions.takeaway: Antithrombin and protein C are the natural anticoagulants that keep clotting in check. Missing either one raises clot risk.
questions.strategy: Sort each substance by which side of the balance it is on: builds or starts a clot, or limits it. Only the limiters are correct.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Opposite pair, look closely

steps.detail: Fibrinogen, thrombin, prothrombin and tissue factor all promote clotting.
Thrombin builds clots; antithrombin is its opposite and limits them.

elimination.verdict: Antithrombin and protein C are the natural anticoagulants.

questions.objective: Explain clot formation and breakdown mechanisms

questions.stem: A patient treated for a leg clot last week has an elevated D dimer, a fragment released as clot fibrin is broken down. Which substance is actively degrading the fibrin mesh?

options.text: Plasminogen
options.rationale: Plasminogen is the inactive form. It must first be activated into plasmin before it can break down fibrin.

options.text: Plasmin
options.rationale: During fibrinolysis, plasminogen is activated into plasmin, which degrades the fibrin mesh and restores normal blood flow.

options.text: Protein C
options.rationale: Protein C is a natural anticoagulant that limits new clot formation. It does not dissolve an existing clot.

options.text: Antithrombin
options.rationale: Antithrombin limits clot growth by opposing thrombin. It does not break down fibrin already formed.

questions.takeaway: Fibrinolysis activates plasminogen into plasmin, and plasmin cuts the fibrin mesh to restore blood flow.
questions.strategy: Separate preventing a clot from dissolving one, then separate the inactive form from the active one: plasminOGEN is waiting to be GENerated into plasmin.

strategies: Opposite pair, look closely

steps.detail: Protein C and antithrombin stop clots from growing; they do not dissolve formed fibrin.
Only the activated form, plasmin, degrades fibrin.

elimination.verdict: Plasmin is degrading the fibrin mesh.

questions.objective: Explain clot formation and breakdown mechanisms

questions.stem: An 82 year old patient is admitted for a hip fracture. The nurse plans to assess energy, bruising, and how often infections occur. What should the nurse compare these findings with first?

options.text: The usual adult reference ranges
options.rationale: Reference ranges matter for lab values, but changes in an older adult can be subtle and still fall inside a population range. The first comparison is the patient's own baseline.

options.text: The patient's own baseline status
options.rationale: Older adults have less marrow reserve and symptoms are often masked, so a subtle change from this patient's own usual state is the cue. Baseline comes first, then you watch for subtle change, then you evaluate and act.

options.text: Findings expected in most older adults
options.rationale: This invites you to explain changes away as aging. A finding that is common in older adults can still be new for this patient and still need a workup.

options.text: The findings recorded at the last visit only
options.rationale: One prior visit is a single data point, not an established baseline. The comparison is the patient's usual status, built from history and trend.

questions.takeaway: In older adults, compare every hematologic finding with the patient's own baseline, because changes may be subtle.
questions.strategy: When the stem is about an older adult, look for the option that individualizes the comparison rather than one that applies a group norm.

strategies: Patient centered option
Opposite pair, look closely

steps.detail: Reference ranges and findings expected in most older adults both compare the patient with other people.
A single prior visit is narrower than a true baseline, so the patient's own baseline wins.

elimination.verdict: The patient's own baseline is the first comparison.

questions.objective: Recognize hematologic abnormalities from assessments

questions.stem: A 77 year old patient reports two months of growing fatigue and breathlessness on stairs and says, "A little anemia is just part of aging." Which response reflects correct nursing understanding?

options.text: Mild anemia is expected, so no action is needed
options.rationale: This repeats the misconception. Anemia should never be dismissed as a normal part of aging; new fatigue and dyspnea need evaluation.

options.text: Rest more often and the tiredness will improve
options.rationale: Rest may ease the symptom, but it skips the evaluation. The cause of the anemia still has to be found.

options.text: Increase iron rich foods and recheck next year
options.rationale: Diet teaching assumes the cause is iron deficiency and delays a workup for a year. The cause is unknown and the symptoms are new.

options.text: Anemia is not normal aging and needs a workup
options.rationale: A new decline in energy and activity tolerance is a subtle change from baseline. Anemia is never normal aging, and a full workup often finds a treatable cause.

questions.takeaway: Anemia is never a normal part of aging. New fatigue or dyspnea in an older adult is evaluated, not explained away.
questions.strategy: When a statement attributes a new symptom to age, the correct nursing response is the one that keeps the problem open for evaluation.

strategies: Eliminate absolutes
Duplicate facts

steps.detail: "No action is needed" closes the problem, which is exactly the trap.
Resting more and adding iron both treat the symptom or guess the cause without evaluating it.

elimination.verdict: The response that says anemia is not normal aging and needs a workup is correct.

questions.objective: Recognize hematologic abnormalities from assessments

questions.stem: The nurse is taking a health history from a patient with unexplained bruising and fatigue. Which areas belong in a focused hematologic health history? Select all that apply.

options.text: Previous liver or kidney disorders
options.rationale: Prior blood, immune, liver or kidney disorders belong in the history. The liver makes clotting factors and the kidney makes erythropoietin.

options.text: Past bleeding episodes, clots, or transfusions
options.rationale: Past bleeding, clots or transfusions are the best predictor of the next bleeding or clotting problem.

options.text: Dietary habits and alcohol use
options.rationale: Iron, B12 and folic acid build red cells, and alcohol harms the liver and marrow, so diet and alcohol are one of the eight areas.

options.text: Childhood immunization dates
options.rationale: Immunization history is part of a general health history, but it is not one of the eight focused hematologic areas.

options.text: Work, hobbies, and home exposures
options.rationale: Lead, benzene and carbon monoxide harm the blood, so exposures at work, in hobbies and at home are one of the eight areas.

options.text: Family history of bleeding disorders
options.rationale: Hemophilia, sickle cell disease and other blood disorders are inherited, so family history is one of the eight areas.

questions.takeaway: The eight areas are prior disorders, cancer and its treatment, bleeding history, recent infections or surgery, diet and alcohol, family history, current symptoms, and exposures.
questions.strategy: Treat each option as true or false by asking whether it can change blood cell production, clotting, or destruction.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Ask whether the area can explain a blood, bleeding or clotting problem.
Immunization dates do not affect blood cells or clotting; every other option does.

elimination.verdict: Select all except childhood immunization dates.

questions.objective: Recognize hematologic abnormalities from assessments

questions.stem: A patient with recurring nosebleeds hands the nurse a medication list naming only lisinopril. The patient adds, "I also take a few natural things from the health store." Which products should the nurse ask about by name because they can affect bleeding? Select all that apply.

options.text: Fish oil
options.rationale: Fish oil has possible bleeding effects and drug interactions. Patients often leave it off a medication list because they do not think of it as a drug.

options.text: Vitamin E
options.rationale: Vitamin E is one of the supplements with possible bleeding effects or drug interactions.

options.text: Garlic
options.rationale: Garlic supplements have possible bleeding effects or drug interactions.

options.text: Calcium carbonate
options.rationale: Calcium is a common supplement, but it is not one of the supplements linked to bleeding.

options.text: Over the counter ibuprofen
options.rationale: Ibuprofen is an NSAID, which carries a risk of GI bleeding. Patients often omit over the counter drugs from a list.

options.text: A daily multivitamin without iron
options.rationale: A standard multivitamin is not linked to bleeding the way fish oil, vitamin E and garlic are.

questions.takeaway: Ask by name about fish oil, vitamin E, garlic and NSAIDs, because patients often leave supplements and over the counter drugs off the list.
questions.strategy: Sort each product into raises bleeding risk or does not; ignore how natural or harmless it sounds.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Duplicate facts

steps.detail: Fish oil, vitamin E and garlic are the named bleeding supplements.

steps.action: Check the over the counter drug
steps.detail: Ibuprofen is an NSAID with GI bleeding risk, so it is selected too.
Calcium and a plain multivitamin are not bleeding risks.

elimination.verdict: Select fish oil, vitamin E, garlic and ibuprofen.

questions.objective: Recognize hematologic abnormalities from assessments

questions.stem: A patient finished six weeks of chemoradiation for lung cancer one month ago and now reports new fatigue and two recent infections. Which effect of the treatment best explains these findings?

options.text: Suppressed blood cell production in the marrow
options.rationale: Cancer treatment such as chemoradiation suppresses blood cell production. Fewer RBCs explain the fatigue and fewer WBCs explain the infections.

options.text: Increased destruction of cells by the spleen
options.rationale: The spleen removes aging and damaged cells, but chemoradiation acts on the marrow, where cells are made.

options.text: Reduced production of clotting factors by the liver
options.rationale: Low clotting factors cause bleeding, not fatigue and infection. This is the liver's role, not the effect of chemoradiation.

options.text: Blocked platelet function at the site of injury
options.rationale: Blocking platelet function is how antiplatelet drugs work, and it causes bleeding rather than fatigue and infection.

questions.takeaway: Chemotherapy and radiation suppress blood cell production in the marrow, so watch for anemia, infection and bleeding afterward.
questions.strategy: Match the drug class to its effect: cancer treatment hits production, antiplatelets hit platelet function, the liver makes clotting factors.

strategies: Global or umbrella option
Duplicate facts

steps.detail: Fatigue and infections mean two cell lines are low, which points to production, not one organ's function.
Clotting factor loss and blocked platelets both explain bleeding, not this picture.

elimination.verdict: Suppressed production in the marrow explains both findings.

questions.objective: Recognize hematologic abnormalities from assessments

questions.stem: A patient takes clopidogrel daily after a coronary stent. How should the nurse describe the effect of this drug on the patient's blood?

options.text: It reduces vitamin K dependent clotting factors
options.rationale: This is how warfarin works. Clopidogrel acts on platelets, not on clotting factor production.

options.text: It increases the action of antithrombin
options.rationale: This is how heparin and enoxaparin work. Clopidogrel is an antiplatelet drug.

options.text: It reduces platelet function and raises bleeding risk
options.rationale: Antiplatelet drugs such as aspirin and clopidogrel reduce platelet function. Platelets plug less well, so bleeding risk rises.

options.text: It suppresses production of platelets in the marrow
options.rationale: Suppressed production is the effect of chemotherapy and radiation. Clopidogrel leaves platelet numbers alone and changes how they work.

questions.takeaway: Antiplatelet drugs (aspirin, clopidogrel) reduce platelet function; anticoagulants (warfarin, heparin) act on clotting factors.
questions.strategy: Sort each option by which drug class it describes, then pick the one that matches clopidogrel.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Opposite pair, look closely

steps.detail: Vitamin K factors is warfarin, antithrombin is heparin, marrow suppression is cancer treatment.
Reduced platelet function is the only antiplatelet mechanism listed.

elimination.verdict: Clopidogrel reduces platelet function.

questions.objective: Recognize hematologic abnormalities from assessments

questions.stem: A patient with a low platelet count feels lightheaded and reports black, sticky bowel movements for two days. How should the nurse document this stool finding?

options.text: Hematochezia
options.rationale: Hematochezia is bright red or maroon blood passed rectally, usually from a lower GI source. Black, tarry stool is digested blood, which is melena.

options.text: Melena
options.rationale: Melena is black, tarry stool from digested blood, usually from the upper GI tract. With a low platelet count it is a bleeding sign to report.

options.text: Hematemesis
options.rationale: Hematemesis is vomiting blood. The finding here is in the stool.

options.text: Steatorrhea
options.rationale: Steatorrhea is pale, greasy, foul smelling stool from fat malabsorption, not black stool from blood.

questions.takeaway: Melena is black, tarry stool from digested blood; hematuria is blood in the urine. Both are urine and stool bleeding signs.
questions.strategy: Anchor on the body site in the stem, then pick the term for blood found there.

strategies: Opposite pair, look closely
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Hematuria is urine and hematemesis is vomit, so both lose.
Steatorrhea is pale and greasy, not black and tarry.

elimination.verdict: Black, tarry stool is melena.

questions.objective: Recognize hematologic abnormalities from assessments

questions.stem: A patient with leukemia has tiny, flat, pinpoint red spots scattered across both lower legs that do not blanch when pressed. Which term should the nurse use to document this finding?

options.text: Ecchymosis
options.rationale: Ecchymosis is a larger flat bruise, often purple or blue. The size here is pinpoint, which separates the two.

options.text: Purpura
options.rationale: Purpura is also nonblanching bleeding into the skin, but the spots are larger. Pinpoint size means petechiae.

options.text: Spider angioma
options.rationale: A spider angioma is a red vascular lesion that blanches with pressure. These spots do not blanch.

options.text: Petechiae
options.rationale: Petechiae are pinpoint red spots from bleeding in the smallest vessels. Low platelets show first in the small vessels of the skin and gums.

questions.takeaway: Petechiae are pinpoint, nonblanching red spots; ecchymosis is a larger bruise. Both point to a platelet or bleeding problem.
questions.strategy: Use size to separate the two bleeding into the skin terms, then rule out the color changes that are not bleeding.

strategies: Opposite pair, look closely

steps.detail: Jaundice and pallor are skin color changes, not spots of bleeding.
Ecchymosis is large and petechiae are pinpoint; the stem says pinpoint.

elimination.verdict: Pinpoint, nonblanching red spots are petechiae.

questions.objective: Recognize hematologic abnormalities from assessments

questions.stem: The nurse performs a head to toe assessment on a patient being evaluated for a blood disorder. Which findings are abnormal hematologic signs the nurse should report? Select all that apply.

options.text: Enlarged, tender lymph nodes in the neck
options.rationale: Lymphadenopathy, enlargement or tenderness of lymph nodes, is the abnormal lymph node sign.

options.text: Bleeding gums after gentle brushing
options.rationale: Gum bleeding is an abnormal mouth sign and often points to a platelet problem.

options.text: Capillary refill under 3 seconds
options.rationale: Brisk capillary refill is a normal perfusion finding, not a sign of a blood disorder.

options.text: New confusion and dizziness
options.rationale: Dizziness, headache, confusion and altered mental status are the neurologic signs. Poor oxygen delivery or bleeding in the brain can cause them.

options.text: Abdominal fullness with an enlarged spleen
options.rationale: Abdominal fullness with hepatomegaly or splenomegaly is the abdominal sign. The spleen enlarges when it filters or destroys more cells.

options.text: Heart rate of 76/min at rest
options.rationale: A resting rate of 76 is normal. The cardiovascular sign is tachycardia, which appears when the heart works harder to make up for low oxygen delivery.

questions.takeaway: Abnormal hematologic signs by system include lymphadenopathy, gum bleeding, neurologic changes, splenomegaly, tachycardia, pallor, petechiae, hematuria and melena.
questions.strategy: Treat each finding as normal or abnormal on its own; normal values placed next to a body system are the distractors.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Capillary refill under 3 seconds and a heart rate of 76/min are normal findings.
Lymphadenopathy, gum bleeding, confusion and splenomegaly are each on the abnormal list.

elimination.verdict: Select the lymph nodes, gums, confusion and enlarged spleen.

questions.objective: Recognize hematologic abnormalities from assessments

questions.stem: A patient with suspected lymphoma reports left upper abdominal fullness, and the provider notes an enlarged spleen on imaging. What should the nurse do during the abdominal assessment?

options.text: Palpate deeply to estimate the spleen's size
options.rationale: Deep palpation is exactly what to avoid. An enlarged spleen ruptures easily and can hemorrhage.

options.text: Percuss firmly over the left upper quadrant
options.rationale: Firm percussion puts force on the same fragile organ. Gentle handling is the rule with a suspected hematologic problem.

options.text: Avoid palpating the spleen and examine gently
options.rationale: With a suspected hematologic problem, do not palpate the spleen. An enlarged spleen ruptures easily and can bleed heavily, so the exam is gentle.

options.text: Palpate below the left costal margin on deep inspiration
options.rationale: This is the standard spleen palpation technique, which is exactly what is avoided when the spleen is enlarged and fragile.

questions.takeaway: Do not palpate an enlarged spleen; it ruptures easily and can hemorrhage. Examine gently.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: When an organ is enlarged and fragile, choose the option that protects it rather than the one that measures it.

strategies: Duplicate facts
Patient centered option

steps.detail: Deep palpation, firm percussion and massage all put force on the spleen.
Only one option avoids pressure on the organ.

elimination.verdict: Avoid palpating the spleen and examine gently.

questions.objective: Recognize hematologic abnormalities from assessments

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing assessment findings for five patients on a medical unit. For each finding, select the concern it most likely points to.
questions.scenario: The nurse reviews assessment findings for five patients on a medical unit before calling the provider with updates.

rows.text: Pallor, weakness, and dyspnea walking to the bathroom
rows.rationale: Fatigue, pallor, weakness and dyspnea point to anemia: less oxygen is delivered, so the heart and lungs work harder.

rows.text: Third fever and infection in two months
rows.rationale: Fever and recurrent infections point to immune deficiency, because the WBCs that fight infection are low or not working.

rows.text: Petechiae on the shins and bleeding gums
rows.rationale: Petechiae, bruising and gum bleeding point to a platelet disorder. Low platelets show first in the smallest vessels of the skin and gums.

rows.text: Venipuncture site still oozing after 15 minutes
rows.rationale: Prolonged bleeding points to impaired hemostasis, a breakdown in the process that stops bleeding.

rows.text: New swelling and pain in one calf
rows.rationale: New swelling and pain in one limb is a possible venous clot until proven otherwise. Report it and do not massage the limb.

questions.takeaway: Fatigue, pallor and dyspnea mean anemia; recurrent infection means immune deficiency; petechiae and gum bleeding mean a platelet disorder; prolonged bleeding means impaired hemostasis; new limb swelling and pain means a possible clot.
questions.strategy: Ask what each finding says the blood is failing to do: carry oxygen, fight infection, plug small vessels, stop bleeding, or stay fluid.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Oxygen, infection, small vessel plugging, stopping bleeding, or staying fluid.
Small vessel bleeding is platelets; bleeding that will not stop is hemostasis as a whole.

elimination.verdict: Each finding maps to one concern.

questions.objective: Recognize hematologic abnormalities from assessments

questions.stem: A patient with deeply pigmented skin has a hemoglobin of 8.0 g/dL. The nurse wants to confirm whether pallor is present. Where does the nurse best assess?

options.text: Skin of the face and forehead
options.rationale: In deeply pigmented skin, pallor is hard to see on the face. Skin alone is not relied on for pallor.

options.text: Conjunctivae, gums and palms
options.rationale: Pallor shows most reliably in mucous membranes, conjunctivae, gums and palmar creases, in every skin tone. In very dark skin it may look ash gray.

options.text: Skin on the backs of the hands
options.rationale: This is still skin assessment, which can miss pallor in deeply pigmented skin.

options.text: Capillary refill in the toes
options.rationale: Capillary refill checks perfusion timing, not the color change of pallor.

questions.takeaway: Do not rely on skin alone for pallor. Check the conjunctivae, gums, mucous membranes and palmar creases, where pallor shows in every skin tone.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Ask where color changes are visible regardless of skin tone: the mucous membranes and palms.

strategies: Duplicate facts

steps.detail: Face and hands are skin, which can hide pallor in dark skin.
Capillary refill measures time, not color.

elimination.verdict: Conjunctivae, gums and palms.

questions.objective: Recognize hematologic abnormalities from assessments

questions.stem: Which complete blood count value reports the percentage of total blood volume made up of red blood cells?

options.text: Hematocrit
options.rationale: Hematocrit is the percentage of blood volume that is RBCs, for example 42%.

options.text: Hemoglobin
options.rationale: Hemoglobin is the oxygen carrying protein inside RBCs, measured in g/dL, not a percentage of blood volume.

options.text: RBC count
options.rationale: The RBC count is the total number of red cells, reported in millions per microliter, and reflects oxygen carrying capacity.

options.text: Differential
options.rationale: The differential reports the percentages of each WBC type, not red cells.

questions.takeaway: Hematocrit is the percentage of blood that is red cells; hemoglobin is the oxygen carrying protein; the RBC count is the number of red cells.
questions.strategy: Look at the unit the stem describes: a percentage of volume belongs to only one red cell value.

strategies: Opposite pair, look closely

steps.detail: The differential describes white cells.
RBC count is a number, hemoglobin is a protein, hematocrit is a percentage of volume.

elimination.verdict: Hematocrit is the percentage of blood volume that is RBCs.

questions.objective: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes

questions.stem: After chemotherapy, a patient has had a fever for two days, yet the total white blood cell count is normal. Which part of the complete blood count shows neutrophil numbers?

options.text: Platelet count
options.rationale: The platelet count tells you bleeding and clotting risk, not which white cells are present.

options.text: Hematocrit
options.rationale: Hematocrit is the percentage of blood that is red cells.

options.text: Total WBC count
options.rationale: The total count is already known and can look acceptable while one type is low. It does not break white cells down by type.

options.text: WBC differential
options.rationale: The differential reports which WBC types are present, such as neutrophils and lymphocytes. A normal total can hide a low neutrophil count.

questions.takeaway: The differential breaks the WBC count into types. Check it when infection risk matters, because a normal total can hide low neutrophils.
questions.strategy: When the stem says the total looks fine but the concern is one cell type, choose the test that separates the types.

strategies: Opposite pair, look closely
Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Remove the non white cell tests
steps.detail: Platelets and hematocrit do not measure white cells.
The total counts all white cells; the differential names each type.

elimination.verdict: The WBC differential shows the neutrophils.

questions.objective: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes

questions.stem: A patient admitted with a gastrointestinal bleed has hemoglobin values of 14.2 g/dL, 13.1 g/dL and 12.3 g/dL over one day, all flagged within range. How should the nurse interpret these results?

options.text: The steady decline needs to be reported
options.rationale: Reference ranges and trends are used together. A value inside the range that keeps falling in a patient who is bleeding shows ongoing loss and is reported.

options.text: All values are normal, so no action is needed
options.rationale: This uses the reference range alone. One value means less than the direction it is moving.

options.text: Only the admission value is reliable
options.rationale: Each value is valid; the meaning comes from comparing them over time.

options.text: Report only when a value leaves the range
options.rationale: Waiting for the value to leave the range delays the response to a bleed that the trend already shows.

questions.takeaway: Always use reference ranges and trends together. A falling value inside the range can still signal a problem.
questions.strategy: When a stem gives several values over time, the question is about the trend, not any one number.

strategies: Eliminate absolutes
Duplicate facts

steps.detail: "All values are normal" and "report only when a value leaves the range" both ignore the trend.
No reason exists to trust only the first value.

elimination.verdict: Report the steady decline.

questions.objective: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes

questions.stem: Complete the statement about cytopenias.
questions.sentence: A patient whose red cells, white cells and platelets are all low has [[1]], which points to serious marrow suppression. Of the cytopenias, [[2]] carries the highest infection risk, while a patient with [[3]] is watched most closely for bruising, petechiae and bleeding.

options.text: leukopenia
options.rationale: Leukopenia means only the WBC count is low.

options.text: pancytopenia
options.rationale: Pancytopenia means all three cell lines are low. Because the marrow makes all three, it signals serious marrow suppression.

options.text: thrombocytopenia
options.rationale: Thrombocytopenia means only platelets are low.

options.text: anemia
options.rationale: Anemia means only hemoglobin or RBCs are low.

options.text: lymphopenia
options.rationale: Lymphopenia lowers lymphocytes, but neutrophils are the first responders, so neutropenia carries the highest infection risk.

options.text: neutropenia
options.rationale: Neutropenia carries the highest infection vulnerability because neutrophils are the first responders to bacteria.

options.text: leukopenia
options.rationale: Leukopenia raises infection risk, but a low total WBC count is less specific than low neutrophils, which are the first responders.

options.text: anemia
options.rationale: Anemia affects oxygen delivery, not defense against infection.

options.text: polycythemia
options.rationale: Polycythemia is too many red cells, not a cytopenia, and it raises clot risk.

options.text: thrombocytopenia
options.rationale: Thrombocytopenia is a low platelet count, so the danger is bruising, petechiae and bleeding.

options.text: anemia
options.rationale: Anemia causes fatigue, pallor and dyspnea rather than petechiae.

options.text: neutropenia
options.rationale: Neutropenia raises infection risk, not bleeding risk.

questions.takeaway: Match each low count to its danger: red cells and oxygen, white cells and infection (neutrophils most of all), platelets and bleeding. All three low is pancytopenia.
questions.strategy: Fill each blank by matching the cell that is low to the job it does.

strategies: Opposite pair, look closely

steps.detail: All three low is pancytopenia.
Neutropenia beats leukopenia for infection risk.
Bruising and petechiae belong to thrombocytopenia.

elimination.verdict: Pancytopenia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia.

questions.objective: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes

questions.stem: A patient receiving chemotherapy has pancytopenia. Which assessments should the nurse make at every encounter? Select all that apply.

options.text: Rectal temperature to detect early fever
options.rationale: Temperature is checked, but not rectally. The rectal route risks mucosal injury, bleeding and infection with low platelets and low WBCs.

options.text: Energy level and activity tolerance
options.rationale: Low RBCs cause fatigue and poor activity tolerance, so energy is one of the three priority assessments.

options.text: Deep palpation of the spleen
options.rationale: Do not palpate the spleen with a suspected hematologic problem; an enlarged spleen ruptures easily.

options.text: New signs of infection such as fever
options.rationale: Low WBCs, especially low neutrophils, mean infection can develop quickly, so signs of infection are checked every time.

options.text: New bruising, petechiae, or oozing
options.rationale: Low platelets cause bleeding, so new bruising, petechiae and oozing are checked every time.

questions.takeaway: With cytopenias, assess energy, signs of infection and bleeding at every encounter, one for each cell line.
questions.strategy: Pancytopenia means all three lines are low, so pick one assessment for each line and reject anything that adds injury.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Duplicate facts

steps.detail: Energy is red cells, infection is white cells, bleeding is platelets.
Rectal temperatures and spleen palpation both risk injury in this patient.

elimination.verdict: Select energy, infection and bleeding.

questions.objective: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes

questions.stem: Four patients have morning complete blood count results. Which platelet count places the patient at critical risk for spontaneous bleeding?

options.text: Platelets 310,000/mm3
options.rationale: This value is normal. No added bleeding risk exists from the count.

options.text: Platelets 140,000/mm3
options.rationale: This value is slightly low but well above the level where bleeding happens without injury.

options.text: Platelets 18,000/mm3
options.rationale: A platelet count below 20,000 is critical. Bleeding can happen on its own, without injury, including in the brain and GI tract.

options.text: Platelets 65,000/mm3
options.rationale: This value is low. Bleeding may be prolonged after an injury, but spontaneous bleeding is expected below 20,000.

questions.takeaway: Platelets below 20,000 are critical: bleeding can occur spontaneously. Between about 40,000 and 80,000, bleeding is prolonged after injury.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Order the values from highest to lowest and look for the one past the critical threshold, not merely low.

strategies: Priority key word
Opposite pair, look closely

steps.detail: 310,000 and 140,000 do not cause spontaneous bleeding.
65,000 prolongs bleeding after injury; 18,000 bleeds on its own.

elimination.verdict: Platelets 18,000/mm3 is the critical value.

questions.objective: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes

questions.stem: A patient with a new pulmonary embolism is receiving a weight based unfractionated heparin infusion. Which laboratory result does the nurse check before adjusting the infusion rate?

options.text: INR
options.rationale: INR reflects the extrinsic pathway and monitors warfarin. It is the test students pair with the wrong drug.

options.text: aPTT
options.rationale: aPTT reflects the intrinsic pathway and monitors unfractionated heparin; some protocols use anti factor Xa instead. The goal is usually 1.5 to 2.5 times control.

options.text: Platelet count
options.rationale: Platelet counts are monitored during heparin therapy for safety, but they do not guide the rate adjustment.

options.text: D dimer
options.rationale: D dimer shows that a clot is breaking down. It supports the diagnosis but does not measure heparin effect.

questions.takeaway: Unfractionated heparin is monitored with aPTT (or anti factor Xa); warfarin is monitored with PT/INR.
questions.strategy: Pair the drug with its pathway test: heparin goes with aPTT, the test with the extra letters.

strategies: Opposite pair, look closely
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Platelet count and D dimer are useful but do not adjust the infusion.

steps.action: Settle the PT and aPTT pair
steps.detail: INR is warfarin; aPTT is heparin.

elimination.verdict: Check the aPTT.

questions.objective: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes

questions.stem: A patient is scheduled for a packed red cell transfusion. The blood group (ABO) and Rh factor typing shows A positive. What does the nurse know about this result?

options.text: It confirms that the unit is compatible
options.rationale: This is the common trap. Typing identifies the blood group only; it does not test the patient's blood against a specific unit.

options.text: It rules out a transfusion reaction
options.rationale: Single test removes all risk. Compatibility testing lowers the risk of a reaction, and the nurse still monitors during the transfusion.

options.text: It identifies only the patient's blood group
options.rationale: ABO/Rh typing identifies the blood group. The antibody screen and crossmatch confirm compatibility with the specific unit and reduce transfusion reaction risk.

options.text: It replaces the need for an antibody screen
options.rationale: The antibody screen looks for antibodies that typing does not detect. Both are done before the crossmatch.

questions.takeaway: ABO/Rh typing identifies the blood group; the antibody screen and crossmatch confirm compatibility with the unit.
questions.strategy: Ask what each test actually answers: what group the patient is, or whether this unit is safe for this patient.

strategies: Eliminate absolutes
Duplicate facts

steps.detail: "Rules out" a reaction and "replaces" the screen claim more than typing can do.
Typing names the group; crossmatch confirms the unit.

elimination.verdict: Typing identifies the group and crossmatch confirms compatibility.

questions.objective: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes

questions.stem: Before a planned transfusion, the sample is collected, coagulation testing is complete, and blood group (ABO) and Rh factor typing and the antibody screen are done. Which step comes next?

options.text: Begin the transfusion at a slow rate
options.rationale: Starting now skips the crossmatch, the step that confirms this unit is compatible with this patient.

options.text: Repeat the coagulation tests
options.rationale: Coagulation testing is already complete and comes earlier in the workflow.

options.text: Repeat the antibody screen
options.rationale: The antibody screen is already done. Repeating it does not test the specific unit.

options.text: Crossmatch the unit with the patient's blood
options.rationale: The workflow is sample collection, coagulation testing, ABO/Rh typing and antibody screen, crossmatch, then safe transfusion. Crossmatch comes right before the transfusion.

questions.takeaway: Transfusion workflow: sample collection, coagulation testing, ABO/Rh typing and antibody screen, crossmatch, safe transfusion.
questions.strategy: Place the steps already done on the sequence and pick the first one not yet done.

strategies: Duplicate facts
Priority key word

steps.detail: Repeating coagulation tests or the antibody screen redoes finished steps.
Starting the transfusion jumps past the crossmatch.

elimination.verdict: Crossmatch comes next.

questions.objective: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes

questions.stem: How does warfarin prevent clot formation?

options.text: It lowers vitamin K dependent clotting factors
options.rationale: Warfarin reduces production of the vitamin K dependent clotting factors II, VII, IX and X. Because existing factors must be used up first, its effect builds slowly.

options.text: It boosts antithrombin to inhibit thrombin and factor Xa
options.rationale: This is unfractionated heparin, which works quickly by increasing antithrombin action.

options.text: It boosts antithrombin to inhibit mainly factor Xa
options.rationale: This is enoxaparin, a low molecular weight heparin.

options.text: It activates plasminogen to dissolve the fibrin mesh
options.rationale: Activating plasminogen to plasmin is fibrinolysis, the action of fibrinolytic drugs. Warfarin prevents clots; it does not dissolve existing ones.

questions.takeaway: Warfarin lowers production of vitamin K dependent factors II, VII, IX and X; heparins work through antithrombin.
questions.strategy: Separate drugs that slow production of factors from drugs that block factors already in the blood.

strategies: Opposite pair, look closely
Duplicate facts

steps.detail: Both antithrombin choices describe heparins.
Plasminogen activation dissolves clots rather than preventing them.

elimination.verdict: Warfarin reduces vitamin K dependent factors II, VII, IX and X.

questions.objective: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes

questions.stem: A patient with a new deep vein thrombosis starts a heparin infusion and oral warfarin and asks, "Why do I need two blood thinners at once?" Which explanation is accurate?

options.text: Heparin makes warfarin absorb faster from the gut
options.rationale: Heparin does not change warfarin absorption. The two are overlapped because of their different onsets.

options.text: Warfarin protects against bleeding caused by heparin
options.rationale: Both drugs raise bleeding risk. Warfarin does not protect against heparin bleeding.

options.text: Heparin dissolves the clot while warfarin prevents new ones
options.rationale: Heparin prevents clot growth; it does not dissolve an existing clot. Breaking down fibrin is the job of plasmin.

options.text: Warfarin takes several days to reach full effect
options.rationale: Warfarin works slowly by reducing production of clotting factors, so full effect takes several days. Heparin works fast and covers the patient until the INR is therapeutic.

questions.takeaway: Warfarin is slow (several days) and heparin is fast, which is why heparin bridges until warfarin reaches a therapeutic INR.
questions.strategy: Compare onset: when two drugs with the same goal are overlapped, the reason is usually timing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Opposite pair, look closely

steps.detail: Heparin does not speed absorption and does not dissolve clots.
Warfarin adds bleeding risk rather than reducing it.

elimination.verdict: Warfarin takes several days to reach full effect.

questions.objective: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes

questions.stem: A patient recovering from knee replacement surgery receives enoxaparin subcutaneously twice a day. The patient has no kidney disease and no unusual risk factors. What should the nurse plan to monitor?

options.text: Bleeding, platelet count, and kidney function
options.rationale: Enoxaparin usually needs no routine clotting test. The nurse monitors for bleeding, platelet counts and kidney function, which affects how the drug is cleared.

options.text: aPTT before each dose
options.rationale: This is the classic trap. aPTT monitors unfractionated heparin; INR and aPTT do not adequately measure enoxaparin.

options.text: INR every morning
options.rationale: INR monitors warfarin and does not measure enoxaparin's effect.

options.text: Anti factor Xa level before each dose
options.rationale: Anti factor Xa is used for enoxaparin only in selected situations, such as kidney impairment. This patient has no such risk.

questions.takeaway: Enoxaparin usually needs no routine clotting level; monitor bleeding, platelets and kidney function. INR and aPTT do not measure it.
questions.strategy: Ask whether the drug has a routine clotting test at all before choosing which test it is.

strategies: Duplicate facts
Opposite pair, look closely

steps.detail: aPTT and INR measure heparin and warfarin, not enoxaparin.
Anti factor Xa is reserved for special cases this patient does not have.

elimination.verdict: Monitor bleeding, platelet count and kidney function.

questions.objective: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes

questions.stem: A patient taking warfarin for atrial fibrillation tells the nurse, "I stopped eating spinach and broccoli because they cancel out my blood thinner." Which teaching should the nurse provide?

options.text: Avoid all green leafy vegetables while on warfarin
options.rationale: This repeats the misconception. Removing vitamin K foods can push the INR up and raise bleeding risk.

options.text: Eat extra greens on days the INR is high
options.rationale: Changing intake to chase the INR makes it unstable. Dose changes are made by the provider, not through diet.

options.text: Keep vitamin K intake about the same each day
options.rationale: Warfarin reduces vitamin K dependent factors, so a steady vitamin K intake keeps the INR stable. Consistency, not avoidance, is the teaching.

options.text: Take a vitamin K supplement with each dose
options.rationale: A vitamin K supplement directly opposes warfarin and is given only as ordered to reverse its effect.

questions.takeaway: Teach patients on warfarin to keep vitamin K intake consistent rather than avoiding green vegetables.
questions.strategy: When a patient overcorrects, the right teaching is usually the balanced middle option.

strategies: Eliminate absolutes
Opposite pair, look closely

steps.detail: "Avoid all" greens is the trap answer.
Adding greens on high INR days or adding a supplement both change vitamin K intake on purpose.

elimination.verdict: Keep vitamin K intake consistent.

questions.objective: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing anticoagulant therapy for patients on a cardiac unit. Which statements are accurate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Unfractionated heparin works by reducing vitamin K dependent factors
options.rationale: This is warfarin's action. Unfractionated heparin increases antithrombin action and inhibits mainly thrombin and factor Xa.

options.text: Warfarin is given orally and requires many drug interaction checks
options.rationale: Warfarin is an oral tablet with many drug and food interactions, so medication reviews are part of the nursing focus.

options.text: Unfractionated heparin given IV takes effect immediately
options.rationale: IV unfractionated heparin works immediately, which is why it is used when anticoagulation is needed right away.

options.text: An INR can be used to dose enoxaparin
options.rationale: INR and aPTT do not adequately measure enoxaparin. When a level is needed, anti factor Xa is used.

options.text: Enoxaparin inhibits mainly factor Xa
options.rationale: Enoxaparin is a low molecular weight heparin that increases antithrombin action and inhibits mainly factor Xa.

options.text: Patients on heparin need platelet counts monitored
options.rationale: Bleeding and platelet counts are monitored for both unfractionated heparin and enoxaparin.

questions.takeaway: Warfarin: oral, slow, vitamin K factors, INR. Unfractionated heparin: IV or subcutaneous, immediate IV, thrombin and Xa, aPTT, platelets. Enoxaparin: subcutaneous, mainly Xa, no routine test, platelets and kidney function.
questions.strategy: Treat each statement as true or false by checking it against the right column of the comparison: route, onset, action, monitoring.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Opposite pair, look closely

steps.detail: Vitamin K factors belong to warfarin, not heparin.
INR does not measure enoxaparin.

elimination.verdict: Select warfarin interactions, immediate IV heparin, enoxaparin factor Xa, and heparin platelet monitoring.

questions.objective: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing an older adult at a yearly visit. For each finding, indicate whether it fits normal aging or needs further evaluation.
questions.scenario: An 84 year old patient comes for a yearly visit. The nurse compares today's findings with the patient's record from last year.

rows.text: Slow, even thinning of hair on the lower legs over several years
rows.rationale: Gradual, even hair loss on the legs is a normal aging change and is not counted as poor perfusion.

rows.text: Hemoglobin 2 g/dL lower than last year, with new fatigue
rows.rationale: A drop from the patient's own baseline with a new symptom is anemia until proven otherwise. Anemia is never dismissed as normal aging.

rows.text: Bruises on both forearms that the patient cannot explain
rows.rationale: Unexplained bruising is a bleeding tendency to evaluate, not an expected change.

rows.text: Dry skin on the arms and legs
rows.rationale: Dry skin and reduced turgor are common in older adults and are not reliable signs of a blood problem.

rows.text: Three urinary infections since spring, none the year before
rows.rationale: More frequent infections than the patient's baseline can signal falling white cells or weaker immunity and are assessed.

rows.text: Gets winded on the stairs, which was easy 6 months ago
rows.rationale: A loss of activity tolerance compared with the patient's baseline is a subtle change that can point to anemia.

questions.takeaway: Compare every finding with the patient's own baseline. Slow, even changes like leg hair thinning or dry skin fit aging; new fatigue, falling hemoglobin, unexplained bruising, more infections and lost activity tolerance are evaluated.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
