questions.stem: Fifteen minutes into a unit of packed red blood cells, a patient reports chills and low back pain. Temperature rose from 36.9 °C to 38.3 °C. What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Slow the transfusion and recheck vital signs in 15 minutes
options.rationale: Slowing still delivers incompatible cells. Chills, back pain and a fever early in a transfusion suggest a hemolytic reaction, so the transfusion is stopped, not slowed.

options.text: Give acetaminophen and continue the transfusion as ordered
options.rationale: Treating the fever hides the reaction while more incompatible blood is given.

options.text: Stop the transfusion and keep the IV line open
options.rationale: Stopping limits how much incompatible blood enters. Keeping the line open with 0.9% sodium chloride (new tubing) preserves access for treatment; then the provider and blood bank are notified.

options.text: Send a blood sample for a Coombs test before stopping
options.rationale: A Coombs test helps confirm a hemolytic reaction, but testing never comes before stopping the infusion.

questions.takeaway: Signs of a transfusion reaction mean stop the transfusion first, keep the line open with 0.9% sodium chloride, then notify the provider and blood bank. Typing, antibody screen and crossmatch exist to prevent this reaction.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Every option except one keeps the blood running or delays stopping it. In a suspected reaction, the first action removes the cause.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: Chills, back pain and fever 15 minutes in suggest a hemolytic reaction.
Stop the blood; tests and comfort measures come after.

elimination.verdict: Stop the transfusion and keep the line open.

questions.objective: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes

questions.stem: On heparin day 6, a patient's platelets are 98 K/µL, down from 260 K/µL on admission. The activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) is in the ordered range. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Continue the infusion because the aPTT is therapeutic
options.rationale: A therapeutic aPTT shows the dose is right, but it says nothing about platelets. The drop is a separate safety problem.

options.text: Report the platelet drop to the provider promptly
options.rationale: Heparin can lower the platelet count, which is why platelets are monitored during therapy. A fall of more than half from baseline is reported promptly so the provider can decide whether to stop heparin.

options.text: Increase the infusion rate to prevent new clots
options.rationale: Raising the dose ignores the platelet drop and adds bleeding risk.

options.text: Recheck the platelet count again in 1 week
options.rationale: Waiting a week lets a dangerous drop continue.

questions.takeaway: During heparin therapy, the nurse watches the platelet count as well as the aPTT. A large drop from baseline is reported promptly, even when the aPTT is therapeutic.
questions.strategy: Two labs are given. Decide which one is the problem: the aPTT is in range, the platelets have fallen by more than half.

strategies: Opposite pair, look closely

steps.detail: aPTT in range; platelets fell from 260 to 98.
Heparin requires platelet monitoring.

elimination.verdict: Report the platelet drop.

questions.stem: A patient with neutropenia after chemotherapy is going home. Which teaching points does the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Wash hands often and before eating
options.rationale: Hand hygiene is the most important protection when neutrophils, the first responders to bacteria, are low.

options.text: Check temperature daily and report 38 °C or higher right away
options.rationale: Fever may be the only sign of infection when neutrophils are low, and it needs prompt care.

options.text: Avoid people who are sick, and crowds when possible
options.rationale: Limiting exposure lowers the chance of catching an infection the body cannot fight well.

options.text: Use a soft toothbrush and an electric razor
options.rationale: These protect against bleeding from low platelets, a different cytopenia. Nothing here says platelets are low.

options.text: Take temperatures rectally for the most accurate result
options.rationale: Rectal temperatures can injure the mucosa and introduce bacteria; they are avoided in neutropenia.

options.text: Avoid raw or undercooked meat and eggs
options.rationale: Undercooked foods can carry bacteria that a neutropenic patient cannot fight off.

questions.takeaway: Neutropenia carries the highest infection risk: teach hand hygiene, avoiding sick people, safe food handling, and to report a fever right away.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Match each teaching point to the problem this patient has. Infection prevention fits neutropenia; bleeding precautions fit a low platelet count.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Low neutrophils mean infection risk.
Keep infection prevention; set aside bleeding precautions and rectal temperatures.

elimination.verdict: Hand hygiene, temperature checks, avoiding sick people, safe food.

questions.objective: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes

questions.stem: After starting a daily spinach and kale smoothie, a patient on the same warfarin dose has an international normalized ratio (INR) of 1.5, down from 2.6. How does the nurse interpret this?

options.text: New vitamin K intake is reducing warfarin's effect
options.rationale: Warfarin works by reducing the vitamin K dependent clotting factors. A sudden rise in vitamin K from leafy greens lets the liver make more factors, so the INR falls below goal.

options.text: The patient needs to stop eating leafy greens
options.rationale: Leafy greens do not have to be removed; the teaching is to keep vitamin K intake consistent.

options.text: The INR is in the expected range for warfarin
options.rationale: An INR of 1.5 is below the usual goal of 2 to 3, so the patient is less protected from clots.

options.text: The smoothie is raising the risk of bleeding
options.rationale: More vitamin K pushes toward clotting, not bleeding. A falling INR means less anticoagulant effect.

questions.takeaway: A sudden increase in vitamin K lowers warfarin's effect and the INR. Teach consistent vitamin K intake, not avoidance, and report the change to the provider.
questions.strategy: Link the new habit to how warfarin works: more vitamin K means more clotting factors, which means a lower INR.

strategies: Opposite pair, look closely

steps.detail: INR dropped after a new daily source of vitamin K.
Warfarin blocks vitamin K dependent factors; extra vitamin K overrides it.

elimination.verdict: Vitamin K intake is lowering the warfarin effect.

questions.objective: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes

questions.stem: A patient taking warfarin reports black, tarry stools for 2 days and feels lightheaded when standing. The international normalized ratio (INR) is 4.8. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Teach the patient to avoid foods high in vitamin K
options.rationale: Vitamin K foods do not cause a high INR, and teaching does not address active bleeding.

options.text: Hold the warfarin dose and notify the provider
options.rationale: Melena with lightheadedness and an INR above goal is active GI bleeding from too much anticoagulant effect. The dose is held and the provider notified so reversal and a hemoglobin can be ordered.

options.text: Give the scheduled warfarin dose and recheck the INR tomorrow
options.rationale: Giving more anticoagulant to a bleeding patient worsens the bleed.

options.text: Collect a stool sample for occult blood testing
options.rationale: The stool is already black and tarry, which is visible blood. Testing for hidden blood delays action.

questions.takeaway: Melena plus an INR above goal on warfarin means active bleeding: hold the dose and notify the provider. Teaching and further testing come later.
questions.strategy: Find the active problem first. Black stools and lightheadedness show the patient is bleeding now, so the action must stop more anticoagulant and get help.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: Melena, orthostatic symptoms and a high INR are active bleeding.

steps.action: Choose the action that acts on it
steps.detail: Hold the drug and notify; testing and teaching do not.

elimination.verdict: Hold the warfarin and notify the provider.

questions.objective: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes

questions.stem: An 83 year old patient is newly confused 2 days after hip surgery. Temperature is 37.7 °C, crackles are present, and white blood cells are 8,400/mm3. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Report the findings as a possible infection
options.rationale: New confusion with crackles and a temperature rise suggests pneumonia. In older adults the WBC count may not rise with infection, so a normal count does not rule it out.

options.text: Document the confusion as expected after surgery in older adults
options.rationale: New confusion is a change from baseline, often the first sign of infection in an older adult, and is not assumed to be normal.

options.text: Reassure the family that the normal WBC rules out infection
options.rationale: This is the trap: aging blunts the WBC response, so the count can be normal with infection.

options.text: Recheck the temperature in 4 hours before reporting
options.rationale: Waiting delays care when several cues already point to infection.

questions.takeaway: In older adults the WBC count may not rise with infection. New confusion, a temperature rise and focal lung findings are reported even with a normal WBC.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Weigh the cluster of cues against the one normal lab: the WBC is the unreliable piece in an older adult.

strategies: Eliminate absolutes

steps.detail: New confusion, low grade temperature, crackles.
A normal WBC does not rule out infection in an older adult.

elimination.verdict: Report a possible infection.

questions.objective: Recognize hematologic abnormalities from assessments

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the admission note for a patient with fatigue. Highlight the findings that point to vitamin B12 deficiency anemia.
questions.nursesNote: Age 58. Reports increasing fatigue over 3 months. Has followed a strict vegan diet for 12 years and takes no supplements. Tongue is smooth and beefy red. Reports tingling and numbness in both feet. Skin is warm and dry. Hemoglobin 9.6 g/dL. Mean corpuscular volume (MCV) is elevated. Blood pressure 124/78.

segments.text: Has followed a strict vegan diet for 12 years and takes no supplements
segments.rationale: Vitamin B12 comes from animal foods; a long vegan diet without supplements is the cause.

segments.text: Tongue is smooth and beefy red
segments.rationale: A smooth, beefy red tongue is a classic sign of pernicious or B12 deficiency anemia.

segments.text: Reports tingling and numbness in both feet
segments.rationale: B12 deficiency damages nerves, and the damage can become permanent if untreated.

segments.text: Skin is warm and dry
segments.rationale: Dry skin is common and not specific to B12 deficiency.

segments.text: Mean corpuscular volume (MCV) is elevated
segments.rationale: B12 deficiency makes large (macrocytic) red cells, so the MCV is high. Iron deficiency would lower it.

segments.text: Blood pressure 124/78
segments.rationale: A normal blood pressure does not point to any type of anemia.

questions.takeaway: B12 deficiency anemia shows as fatigue with a smooth beefy red tongue, tingling from nerve damage and a high MCV. A vegan diet without supplements is a common cause.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Look for the three things that set B12 apart from other anemias: the diet, the nerve signs and the large cells.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Long vegan diet without supplements.
Tongue, tingling, high MCV.

elimination.verdict: Diet, tongue, tingling and elevated MCV.

questions.objective: Recognize hematologic abnormalities from assessments

questions.stem: The nurse reviews discharge teaching with a patient who had a splenectomy after a car crash. Which patient statement requires further teaching?

options.text: I will call my provider right away if I get a fever
options.rationale: Teaching: after splenectomy, infection can progress quickly, so a fever is reported right away.

options.text: I will stay up to date on my vaccines
options.rationale: Teaching: vaccines lower the higher infection risk that follows splenectomy.

options.text: I will tell new providers that I have no spleen
options.rationale: Teaching: providers need to know so they can treat infections early.

options.text: I can wait out a fever if I feel well
options.rationale: This needs correction. The spleen filters blood and helps fight infection; without it, infection and sepsis can develop fast, so every fever is reported.

questions.takeaway: After splenectomy, infection and sepsis risk rises because the spleen filters blood and helps with immune defense. Teach to report any fever right away and keep vaccines current.
questions.strategy: This is a negative question: find the statement that would put the patient at risk.

strategies: Negative polarity

steps.detail: It filters blood and helps fight infection.
Skipping care for a fever is unsafe.

elimination.verdict: Skipping a visit for a fever needs teaching.

questions.objective: Describe major blood components and their functions

questions.stem: Three weeks after a Johnson & Johnson COVID vaccine, a patient calls the clinic. Which reported findings require immediate follow up? Select all that apply.

options.text: Severe headache that started yesterday
options.rationale: A new severe headache can signal a clot in the brain, a feature of vaccine induced thrombotic thrombocytopenia (VITT).

options.text: Sore arm at the injection site
options.rationale: Arm soreness is an expected local effect in the first days after a vaccine, not a sign of clotting or low platelets.

options.text: Swelling and pain in one calf
options.rationale: Leg pain and swelling suggest a deep vein clot, one half of the VITT picture.

options.text: New bruises without any injury
options.rationale: Unexplained bruising points to low platelets, the other half of VITT.

options.text: Mild fatigue the day after the shot
options.rationale: Short lived fatigue right after vaccination is expected. The window that matters for VITT is 4 to 42 days later.

options.text: Shortness of breath when walking
options.rationale: New shortness of breath can signal a pulmonary embolism from a vaccine related clot.

questions.takeaway: VITT is clotting plus low platelets 4 to 42 days after an adenovirus vector COVID vaccine. Report severe headache, leg swelling, shortness of breath and unexplained bruising or bleeding right away.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Sort each finding by timing and meaning: expected effects come in the first days; clot signs and bleeding signs weeks later are reported.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Three weeks falls inside the 4 to 42 day window.
Clot signs and bleeding signs are reported; early local effects are expected.

elimination.verdict: Headache, calf swelling, unexplained bruises and shortness of breath.

questions.objective: Recognize hematologic abnormalities from assessments

questions.stem: The occupational health nurse is reviewing the note for a refinery worker with fatigue. Highlight the findings that require follow up.
questions.nursesNote: Works 12 years at a refinery cleaning fuel storage tanks. Reports fatigue for 2 months. Smokes half a pack of cigarettes daily. Bruises appear on the arms without injury. Has had 3 sinus infections since spring. Wears hearing protection at work. Blood pressure 122/76 mm Hg. Hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL. Platelets 88 K/µL.

segments.text: Works 12 years at a refinery cleaning fuel storage tanks
segments.rationale: Long exposure to gasoline vapors at a refinery is a benzene exposure, which disrupts blood cell production in the marrow.

segments.text: Smokes half a pack of cigarettes daily
segments.rationale: Cigarette smoke is another benzene source, adding to the work exposure.

segments.text: Bruises appear on the arms without injury
segments.rationale: Unexplained bruising points to low platelets, which fits marrow disruption.

segments.text: Has had 3 sinus infections since spring
segments.rationale: Frequent infections suggest low white cells, another cell line the marrow is failing to make.

segments.text: Wears hearing protection at work
segments.rationale: Hearing protection addresses noise, not a blood related exposure.

segments.text: Blood pressure 122/76 mm Hg
segments.rationale: This blood pressure does not point to a hematologic problem.

segments.text: Platelets 88 K/µL
segments.rationale: A low platelet count confirms that the bruising has a cause and adds to the picture of marrow suppression.

questions.takeaway: Benzene from gasoline, industrial emissions and cigarette smoke disrupts the marrow. Low counts in more than one cell line in an exposed worker are followed up, along with the exposures themselves.
questions.strategy: Highlight both the exposures and the findings that show the marrow is affected; leave out details unrelated to blood.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Refinery tank work and cigarette smoke are benzene sources.
Bruising, infections and low platelets.

elimination.verdict: The two exposures plus bruising, infections and low platelets.

questions.objective: Identify environmental exposures affecting blood health

questions.stem: A patient with type O positive blood is ordered one unit of red blood cells. At the bedside check, the unit is labeled A positive. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Hang the unit slowly and stay for 15 minutes
options.rationale: Staying the first 15 minutes is correct for a compatible unit, but this unit is incompatible. Slow infusion still risks a hemolytic reaction.

options.text: Ask the patient whether they have had transfusions before
options.rationale: A transfusion history matters for antibodies, but it does not change the fact that this unit does not match.

options.text: Return the unit to the blood bank unused
options.rationale: An O patient has antibodies against A cells. A mismatched unit is never given; it goes back to the blood bank so the right unit can be issued.

options.text: Give it because both are Rh positive
options.rationale: Rh matching alone is not enough. ABO must also be compatible, and an O patient cannot receive A cells.

questions.takeaway: ABO/Rh typing, antibody screen and crossmatch exist to prevent a transfusion reaction. If the unit does not match at the bedside check, it is not given.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Check both parts of the type: Rh matches, but ABO does not, and either mismatch stops the transfusion.

strategies: Duplicate facts

steps.detail: O patient, A unit: ABO mismatch.
Never hang it; return it.

elimination.verdict: Do not hang it; return it to the blood bank.

questions.objective: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes

questions.stem: The nurse is observing a nursing student assess a patient with suspected leukemia. For each student action, indicate whether it is appropriate or requires the nurse to intervene.
questions.scenario: A patient with suspected leukemia has left upper abdominal fullness, petechiae on both legs and a platelet count of 34 K/µL.

rows.text: Inspects the skin and gums for bleeding
rows.rationale: Inspection for petechiae, bruising and gum bleeding is a key part of assessing a patient with low platelets.

rows.text: Palpates deeply under the left ribs to feel the spleen
rows.rationale: An enlarged spleen ruptures easily. The nurse does not palpate it when a hematologic problem is suspected; the provider assesses it.

rows.text: Uses a firm, tight blood pressure cuff on the same arm repeatedly
rows.rationale: Repeated, prolonged cuff pressure can cause bruising and petechiae with a low platelet count; handle the patient gently.

rows.text: Asks about bleeding after brushing teeth
rows.rationale: Gum bleeding is a platelet related finding worth asking about.

rows.text: Palpates lymph nodes gently and notes size
rows.rationale: Gentle lymph node palpation is part of the hematologic assessment; document size, tenderness and whether the node moves.

rows.text: Applies brief pressure, then moves on after a blood draw
rows.rationale: With a known or suspected bleeding problem, pressure is held until the bleeding stops, which can take several minutes.

questions.takeaway: With a suspected hematologic problem, examine gently, do not palpate the spleen, and hold pressure on puncture sites until bleeding stops.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: For each action ask: could it cause bleeding or rupture in a patient with low platelets and an enlarged spleen?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Low platelets and a possibly enlarged spleen.
Inspection, gentle palpation and history are safe; deep spleen palpation, repeated tight cuffs and brief pressure are not.

elimination.verdict: Three appropriate, three require intervention.

questions.stem: The nurse teaches a patient scheduled for a bone scan with an IV radioactive tracer. Which statements indicate understanding? Select all that apply.

options.text: “I will need to lie still for about an hour during the scan.”
options.rationale: The scan itself takes about an hour of lying still on the table, so the teaching was understood.

options.text: “I should keep away from my family for a week afterward.”
options.rationale: The tracer dose is small and short lived. No isolation from family is needed after a bone scan.

options.text: “I will drink extra water after the scan.”
options.rationale: Extra fluids help flush the tracer out through the urine.

options.text: “The tracer will be given to me as a pill.”
options.rationale: The tracer is usually injected IV, then the scan is done after it collects in bone.

options.text: “Airport screening may detect the tracer for a few days.”
options.rationale: Small amounts of tracer can set off airport radiation detectors for several days, so the patient may carry a note.

questions.takeaway: A bone scan uses a small IV dose of radioactive tracer: lie still about an hour, drink water afterward, and expect that airport screening may detect it for several days. No isolation is needed.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Judge each statement as true or false about a diagnostic tracer, which is a small dose that leaves through the urine.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: IV tracer, not a pill.
A small tracer dose needs no isolation.
Lying still, fluids, airport screening.

elimination.verdict: Lie still about an hour, drink water, airport screening may detect it.

questions.objective: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a patient with advanced liver cirrhosis. Which findings does the nurse expect because of the liver's role in blood health? Select all that apply.

options.text: Platelet count above normal
options.rationale: Platelets are often low in cirrhosis, because an enlarged spleen traps them. A high count is not expected.

options.text: Easy bruising on the arms
options.rationale: The liver makes most clotting factors. With fewer factors, small bumps bruise easily.

options.text: Shortened time for blood to clot
options.rationale: Fewer clotting factors make clotting slower, not faster.

options.text: Prolonged international normalized ratio
options.rationale: The INR rises when the liver cannot make enough clotting factors, even without warfarin.

options.text: Gums that bleed when brushing teeth
options.rationale: Low clotting factors cause oozing from small mucosal injuries like brushing.

questions.takeaway: The liver makes many plasma proteins and clotting factors. In liver failure, expect bruising, mucosal bleeding and a prolonged INR.
questions.strategy: Start from what the liver makes: clotting factors. Every correct finding is a result of having too few of them.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: It makes clotting factors.
Slower clotting: bruising, bleeding gums, high INR.
Faster clotting and high platelets do not fit.

elimination.verdict: Bruising, a prolonged INR and bleeding gums.

questions.objective: Describe major blood components and their functions

questions.stem: A patient with a new leg clot started on heparin asks, “Will this dissolve my clot?” Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: “Heparin keeps the clot from growing while your body breaks it down.”
options.rationale: Heparin is an anticoagulant: it stops new fibrin from forming. The body's own fibrinolytic system, through plasmin, dissolves the existing clot over time.

options.text: “Yes, heparin dissolves the clot within the first few hours.”
options.rationale: Heparin does not break down fibrin. Dissolving a clot quickly takes a fibrinolytic drug such as alteplase.

options.text: “Heparin thins the blood so the clot passes through your veins.”
options.rationale: Heparin does not thin the blood or move the clot. A clot that travels is an embolism, which is a danger, not a goal.

options.text: “No, the clot will stay the same size for the rest of your life.”
options.rationale: The body's fibrinolytic system breaks clots down over weeks, so the clot usually shrinks.

questions.takeaway: Anticoagulants such as heparin stop new clot formation; they do not dissolve an existing clot. Fibrinolysis, through plasmin, breaks the clot down.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Separate the two halves of hemostasis: formation and breakdown. Heparin acts on formation only, so any option claiming it dissolves or moves the clot is wrong.

strategies: Eliminate absolutes
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Heparin is an anticoagulant, not a fibrinolytic.
Plasmin, from the body's fibrinolytic system.
“The rest of your life” is never accurate here.

elimination.verdict: Heparin stops growth; the body breaks the clot down.

questions.objective: Explain clot formation and breakdown mechanisms

questions.stem: A patient with severe anemia has hemoglobin 6.8 g/dL. Which finding requires immediate follow up?

options.text: Pale inner eyelids and nail beds
options.rationale: Pallor is expected with this hemoglobin. It confirms the anemia but is not a new danger.

options.text: Chest pressure while walking to the bathroom
options.rationale: Chest pressure on exertion means the heart is not getting enough oxygen. Low hemoglobin can cause myocardial ischemia, so this needs immediate follow up.

options.text: Fatigue after showering in the morning
options.rationale: Fatigue is expected with low oxygen carrying capacity. It is planned for, not escalated.

options.text: Cool hands and feeling cold in the room
options.rationale: Feeling cold is a common, expected finding with anemia.

questions.takeaway: With severe anemia, pallor, fatigue and cold intolerance are expected; chest pain or pressure means the heart is short of oxygen and is escalated right away.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Every option fits anemia, so ask which one threatens an organ. Chest pressure signals the heart is starved of oxygen.

strategies: Priority key word
Apply the ABCs

steps.detail: Pallor, fatigue and feeling cold all fit anemia.
Chest pressure on exertion means cardiac ischemia.

elimination.verdict: Chest pressure while walking.

questions.objective: Recognize hematologic abnormalities from assessments

questions.stem: A patient has new anemia with a low white blood cell count. Which history findings suggest an environmental exposure that can harm blood health? Select all that apply.

options.text: Drinks filtered tap water at home
options.rationale: Filtered water is not a known source of a blood harming exposure.

options.text: Sanded old paint while restoring a 1940s house
options.rationale: Old paint often contains lead, which blocks heme production and can cause anemia.

options.text: Uses a fitness tracker every day
options.rationale: A fitness tracker is not an exposure that affects the blood.

options.text: Works at a refinery handling gasoline products
options.rationale: Gasoline contains benzene, which damages the bone marrow and can lower blood cell counts.

options.text: Smokes one pack of cigarettes a day
options.rationale: Cigarette smoke contains benzene, a marrow toxin.

questions.takeaway: Ask about home, work and hobby exposures: lead from old paint impairs hemoglobin production, and benzene from gasoline, industry and cigarette smoke harms the marrow.
questions.strategy: Match each history detail to a known blood toxin: lead or benzene. Anything that is not a source of either is not the answer.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Disturbing old paint, soil, dust.
Gasoline, industrial work, cigarette smoke.
Filtered water and a fitness tracker carry no exposure.

elimination.verdict: Old paint, refinery work and smoking.

questions.objective: Identify environmental exposures affecting blood health

questions.stem: Two hours after a posterior iliac crest bone marrow biopsy, a patient with platelets of 54 K/µL rates site pain 5 of 10 and asks for ibuprofen. A 2 cm spot on the dressing is unchanged from the last check. Blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg and heart rate 84/min. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Give the prescribed ibuprofen, since the bleeding is controlled
options.rationale: Ibuprofen is an NSAID that impairs platelet function. With platelets already low, it raises the risk of new bleeding at the site even if the spot is stable now.

options.text: Remove the dressing to look directly at the puncture site
options.rationale: Removing the pressure dressing this early can restart bleeding. An unchanged spot is assessed through the dressing.

options.text: Give the prescribed acetaminophen and apply an ice pack
options.rationale: Acetaminophen relieves pain without affecting platelets, and ice reduces bleeding and swelling at the site. The stable spot and normal vital signs show no active bleeding.

options.text: Notify the provider about the drainage on the dressing
options.rationale: A small spot that has not grown, with normal vital signs, is expected after a biopsy. Calling about it delays the pain relief the patient needs now.

questions.takeaway: After a bone marrow biopsy in a patient with low platelets, avoid NSAIDs and aspirin, keep the pressure dressing on, use ice and a non platelet drug for pain, and watch for a growing stain.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Two cues decide it: the low platelet count rules out the NSAID, and the unchanged spot with normal vital signs means there is nothing new to report.

strategies: Duplicate facts
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 54 K/µL: avoid anything that weakens platelets.
Unchanged spot, normal vital signs: expected, not active bleeding.
Acetaminophen plus ice.

elimination.verdict: Acetaminophen and ice; no NSAID, no dressing removal.

questions.objective: Understand nursing care before and after bone marrow tests

questions.stem: A patient is on day 6 of subcutaneous enoxaparin after a hip replacement. Which result does the nurse report to the provider?

options.text: Activated partial thromboplastin time 31 seconds
options.rationale: Enoxaparin is not monitored with the aPTT, so a normal aPTT is expected and says nothing about the drug's effect.

options.text: Hemoglobin 11.8 g/dL, down from 12.1 g/dL
options.rationale: A drop of 0.3 g/dL after hip surgery is small and expected from postoperative blood loss and fluids. It does not suggest new bleeding.

options.text: International normalized ratio 1.0
options.rationale: The INR measures warfarin effect. Enoxaparin does not change it, so a normal INR is expected.

options.text: Platelets 105 K/µL, down from 240 K/µL
options.rationale: A platelet count that falls by more than half 5 to 10 days into heparin or enoxaparin suggests heparin induced thrombocytopenia, which needs prompt report.

questions.takeaway: INR and aPTT do not measure enoxaparin. What is monitored is bleeding, kidney function and the platelet count; a fall of more than half 5 to 10 days in is reported.
questions.strategy: Ask which test actually tracks enoxaparin safety. The two clotting times are normal because the drug does not affect them; the platelet trend is the danger signal.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Duplicate facts

steps.detail: INR is for warfarin, aPTT for unfractionated heparin.
Hemoglobin barely moved; platelets fell by more than half.
Day 6 fits heparin induced thrombocytopenia.

elimination.verdict: The platelet drop from 240 to 105 K/µL.

questions.objective: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes

questions.stem: A patient rescued from a house fire has a headache and is slow to answer questions. Pulse oximetry reads 99% on room air. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Apply 100% oxygen by nonrebreather mask
options.rationale: Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin, and the pulse oximeter reads carboxyhemoglobin as oxygenated, so 99% is falsely reassuring. Headache and confusion after smoke exposure call for high flow oxygen right away.

options.text: Draw an arterial blood gas with carboxyhemoglobin
options.rationale: A carboxyhemoglobin level confirms the poisoning, but it is drawn after oxygen is started. Waiting for the result delays treatment.

options.text: Recheck the oxygen saturation on another finger
options.rationale: Rechecking at another site gives the same falsely normal value. The problem is the device, not the finger.

options.text: Give acetaminophen for the headache as prescribed
options.rationale: The headache comes from poor oxygen delivery to the brain. Treating the symptom leaves the cause untreated.

questions.takeaway: In suspected carbon monoxide poisoning, a normal pulse oximetry value is not reassuring. Start 100% oxygen by nonrebreather first, then confirm with a carboxyhemoglobin level.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Weigh the cue against the number: smoke exposure plus headache and confusion outranks a 99% value the device cannot get right.

strategies: Apply the ABCs
Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: Pulse oximetry cannot tell carboxyhemoglobin from oxygenated hemoglobin.
The cause is clear and harmful; treat first, confirm second.

elimination.verdict: High flow oxygen by nonrebreather now.

questions.objective: Recognize carbon monoxide poisoning and nursing priorities

questions.stem: For each worker, indicate the environmental exposure the nurse most suspects.
questions.scenario: The occupational health nurse reviews six workers with new blood or oxygen related complaints.

rows.text: Forklift driver in a closed propane warehouse with headaches that ease on weekends
rows.rationale: Fuel burning engines indoors produce carbon monoxide. Symptoms that improve away from the site point to an exposure at work.

rows.text: Painter scraping old paint off a 1930s bridge with fatigue and anemia
rows.rationale: Old paint is a major lead source. Lead blocks heme production, which causes anemia.

rows.text: Refinery worker with bruising, frequent infections and low counts of all blood cells
rows.rationale: Benzene damages the bone marrow itself, so every cell line can fall: bleeding, infection and anemia.

rows.text: Home renovator sanding window frames in an older house, with abdominal pain and anemia
rows.rationale: Sanding releases lead dust. Abdominal pain with anemia is a classic lead picture.

rows.text: Mechanic who runs engines in a closed garage, now with headache and nausea
rows.rationale: Running engines in a closed space builds up carbon monoxide, which binds hemoglobin and starves tissues of oxygen.

rows.text: Gas station attendant with fatigue and a falling platelet count over a year
rows.rationale: Gasoline vapor contains benzene, a marrow toxin. A slow fall in counts fits long term exposure.

questions.takeaway: Lead comes from old paint, dust and soil and causes anemia by blocking heme production. Benzene from gasoline and industry harms the marrow, lowering all counts. Carbon monoxide from burning fuel in closed spaces binds hemoglobin.
questions.strategy: Match the source first, then confirm with the blood effect: anemia alone fits lead, all cell lines low fits benzene, headache that clears away from the site fits carbon monoxide.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Old paint = lead; gasoline or refinery = benzene; engines or fuel indoors = carbon monoxide.
Anemia, low counts in every line, or headache with nausea.

elimination.verdict: Propane forklift and closed garage: carbon monoxide; bridge paint and sanding: lead; refinery and gas station: benzene.

questions.objective: Identify environmental exposures affecting blood health

questions.stem: A patient on a continuous heparin infusion has an activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) of 118 seconds; the target range is 60 to 80 seconds. The patient has new oozing at an old IV site and the gums bleed with brushing. Blood pressure is 124/76 mm Hg and heart rate 88/min. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Stop the heparin infusion
options.rationale: The aPTT is far above the target and new bleeding has started. Stopping the drug removes the cause, and heparin's short half life means its effect begins to fade within hours.

options.text: Give protamine sulfate as the heparin antidote
options.rationale: Protamine reverses heparin, but it needs a provider order and is usually saved for serious bleeding. Stopping the infusion comes first and may be enough.

options.text: Recheck the aPTT in 1 hour to confirm the result
options.rationale: Confirming the value while the drug keeps running lets the bleeding worsen. The bleeding already confirms the result.

options.text: Apply firm pressure to the oozing IV site
options.rationale: Pressure helps the site, but the infusion is still delivering the drug that causes bleeding everywhere. Treat the cause first.

questions.takeaway: An aPTT far above target with new bleeding means stop the heparin first, then notify the provider, who may order protamine. Pressure and rechecks come after.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Every option is reasonable, so ask which one stops the harm at its source. The vital signs are normal, so this is not yet a resuscitation; removing the drug is.

strategies: Priority key word
Assessment before intervention

steps.action: Read the lab against the target
steps.detail: 118 seconds is well above 60 to 80.
Oozing and bleeding gums are new.
Stopping heparin comes before the antidote, a recheck or local pressure.

elimination.verdict: Stop the heparin infusion.

questions.objective: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes

questions.stem: A patient with iron deficiency anemia started oral ferrous sulfate 2 weeks ago. Hemoglobin is 7.6 g/dL. At a clinic visit, the patient reports four concerns. Which finding requires immediate follow up?

options.text: Heart rate 118/min at rest and dizziness when standing
options.rationale: A fast resting heart rate with dizziness on standing shows the body can no longer compensate for the low hemoglobin. This patient may need a transfusion and an evaluation for ongoing blood loss.

options.text: Stools that have turned dark green to black
options.rationale: Oral iron commonly darkens stools. Without a tarry texture, lightheadedness or a falling hemoglobin, this is expected.

options.text: A strong craving to chew ice throughout the day
options.rationale: Craving ice, called pica, is a typical sign of iron deficiency. It confirms the diagnosis but is not dangerous.

options.text: Tiredness after climbing one flight of stairs
options.rationale: Fatigue with exertion is expected at this hemoglobin. It is planned for with rest periods, not escalated.

questions.takeaway: In anemia, pallor, fatigue, pica and dark stools on oral iron are expected. A fast resting heart rate with orthostatic dizziness means compensation is failing and needs follow up now.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Three options are classic findings of iron deficiency or its treatment. The decision is which one shows the body is decompensating; a trap is the dark stool, which is expected on iron.

strategies: Priority key word
Apply the ABCs

steps.detail: Dark stools are expected on oral iron.
Pica and exertional fatigue fit iron deficiency.
Resting tachycardia with dizziness.

elimination.verdict: Heart rate 118/min at rest with dizziness.

questions.objective: Recognize hematologic abnormalities from assessments

questions.stem: A patient receiving chemotherapy has a temperature of 37.6 °C. White blood cells are 2,000/mm3 with 20% neutrophils and 5% bands. The patient asks whether visitors can come. Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: “Your infection fighting cells are very low, so visitors who are sick must stay away.”
options.rationale: The absolute neutrophil count is 2,000 × (0.20 + 0.05) = 500/mm3, which is severe neutropenia. Visitors are allowed, but anyone with signs of illness should not visit, and everyone performs hand hygiene.

options.text: “Your white count is only mildly low, so normal visiting is fine.”
options.rationale: The total count hides the danger. Only neutrophils and bands fight bacteria, and they total 500/mm3, which is severe.

options.text: “No visitors are allowed until your white count returns to normal.”
options.rationale: Banning all visitors is not required and harms the patient's support. Screening visitors for illness and hand hygiene are the protective steps.

options.text: “Visitors can come as long as they wear a mask and you have no fever today.”
options.rationale: The neutrophil count, not the temperature, sets the risk. A patient with severe neutropenia may not mount a fever, and masks alone do not replace excluding ill visitors.

questions.takeaway: Absolute neutrophil count = white cells × (percent neutrophils + percent bands). Below 500/mm3 is severe: screen visitors for illness, enforce hand hygiene and treat any fever as an emergency.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Do the math before judging: the white count alone looks only mildly low. Then pick the response that protects the patient without needless isolation.

strategies: Eliminate absolutes
Duplicate facts

steps.detail: 500/mm3 or less is severe neutropenia.
Keep ill visitors away; no total ban.

elimination.verdict: Visitors who are sick must stay away.

chapters.title: Concepts of Care for Patients With Cancer

questions.stem: Which statement best describes how a normal cell becomes a cancer cell?

options.text: It speeds up programmed cell death in nearby tissue
options.rationale: Cancer cells evade programmed cell death; they do not cause it in neighbors.

options.text: It stops dividing and grows larger than surrounding cells
options.rationale: Cancer cells keep dividing; they do not stop. Size alone does not define a cancer cell.

options.text: It is replaced by a foreign cell carried in the blood
options.rationale: Cancer cells come from the patient's own normal cells, not from outside cells.

options.text: It loses the cellular regulation that controls growth and division
options.rationale: Every cancer cell was once a normal cell. Cancer begins when the genetic and physiologic controls on growth, replication, differentiation and function are lost.

questions.takeaway: All cancer cells were once normal cells that lost cellular regulation, the processes that control growth, replication, differentiation and function.
questions.strategy: Look for the option about losing control, the core idea of cancer.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Cancer = loss of cellular regulation.

elimination.verdict: Loss of cellular regulation.

questions.objective: Explain how cancer develops, invades nearby tissue, and spreads

questions.stem: Which statement about a benign tumor is accurate?

options.text: It invades nearby tissue but never spreads far
options.rationale: Invasion is a feature of malignant cells. A benign tumor stays localized.

options.text: It stays localized but can press on nearby structures
options.rationale: Benign tumors do not invade or metastasize, yet their size can still harm by pressing on nearby organs, vessels or nerves.

options.text: It cannot cause any harm because it is not cancer
options.rationale: Benign does not mean harmless. A benign tumor pressing on the brain or an airway can be dangerous.

options.text: It spreads through lymph vessels but not through blood
options.rationale: Benign tumors do not spread by any route.

questions.takeaway: A benign tumor remains localized and does not invade or spread, but it can cause harm by pressing on nearby structures.
questions.strategy: Separate where the tumor stays from whether it can still do harm.

strategies: Eliminate absolutes

steps.detail: "Cannot cause any harm" is too absolute.
Invasion and spread belong to cancer.

elimination.verdict: Localized, but can press on structures.

questions.objective: Explain how cancer develops, invades nearby tissue, and spreads

questions.stem: For each feature, indicate whether it describes a normal cell, a benign tumor cell or a malignant cell.
questions.scenario: The nurse is reviewing cell features.

rows.text: Divides only to build or replace tissue and undergoes programmed cell death
rows.rationale: Normal cells regulate division and undergo programmed cell death (apoptosis).

rows.text: Grows in the wrong place or at the wrong time but stays localized
rows.rationale: Benign tumor cells are normal looking cells growing where or when they should not, without invading.

rows.text: Evades growth controls and grows into surrounding tissue
rows.rationale: Evading growth controls and invading tissue are the defining features of cancer.

rows.text: Breaks away and forms new tumors in distant organs
rows.rationale: Metastasis happens only with malignant cells.

rows.text: Looks very different from its tissue of origin
rows.rationale: Cancer cells vary in how closely they resemble their tissue of origin, and many look very different.

questions.takeaway: Normal cells regulate division and die on schedule; benign cells stay put; malignant cells evade growth controls, invade and spread.
questions.strategy: Ask of each feature: is it controlled, misplaced but contained, or uncontrolled and invasive?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Controlled = normal; contained = benign; invades or spreads = malignant.

elimination.verdict: One normal, one benign, three malignant.

questions.objective: Explain how cancer develops, invades nearby tissue, and spreads

questions.stem: During carcinogenesis, which stage produces increasingly aggressive populations of cancer cells?

options.text: Initiation
options.rationale: Initiation is the first genetic damage that alters cell regulation; the cells are not yet aggressive.

options.text: Promotion
options.rationale: Promotion favors multiplication of the altered cells but does not by itself make them more aggressive.

options.text: Progression
options.rationale: Progression is when the tumor keeps mutating and its cells become more and more aggressive.

options.text: Apoptosis
options.rationale: Apoptosis is programmed cell death, a normal process cancer cells evade, not a stage of carcinogenesis.

questions.takeaway: Initiation damages DNA, promotion multiplies the altered cells, progression makes them increasingly aggressive, and angiogenesis feeds the growing tumor.
questions.strategy: Match the stage name to what happens; progress means getting worse.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Initiation, promotion, progression.

elimination.verdict: Progression.

questions.objective: Explain how cancer develops, invades nearby tissue, and spreads

questions.stem: Which process allows a growing tumor to obtain its own blood supply?

options.text: Promotion
options.rationale: Promotion is multiplication of altered cells, not blood vessel growth.

options.text: Initiation
options.rationale: Initiation is the first DNA damage; the tumor does not yet need a blood supply.

options.text: Differentiation
options.rationale: Differentiation is how specialized a cell is, not vessel growth.

options.text: Angiogenesis
options.rationale: Angiogenesis is the growth of new blood vessels that supply a tumor so it can keep growing.

questions.takeaway: Angiogenesis supplies a growing tumor with blood vessels; without it, a tumor cannot grow beyond a tiny size.
questions.strategy: Angio means vessel, genesis means making.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Angio = vessel, genesis = creation.

elimination.verdict: Angiogenesis.

questions.objective: Explain how cancer develops, invades nearby tissue, and spreads

questions.stem: What is the difference between invasion and metastasis?

options.text: Invasion is spread through blood; metastasis is spread through lymph
options.rationale: Both blood and lymph are routes of metastasis. Invasion is local growth into neighboring tissue.

options.text: Invasion is growth into nearby tissue; metastasis is spread to distant sites
options.rationale: Invasion means cancer cells grow into tissue next to the tumor. Metastasis means cells travel through blood or lymph and form tumors far away.

options.text: Invasion happens with benign tumors; metastasis happens with malignant tumors
options.rationale: Benign tumors do neither. Both invasion and metastasis are malignant features.

options.text: Invasion is the original tumor; metastasis is a new type of cancer
options.rationale: A metastatic tumor is the same cancer in a new site, not a new type of cancer.

questions.takeaway: Invasion is local growth into nearby tissue; metastasis is spread through blood or lymph vessels to form tumors at distant sites.
questions.strategy: Think distance: next door is invasion, far away is metastasis.

strategies: Opposite pair, look closely

steps.detail: Near versus far.

elimination.verdict: Invasion is local; metastasis is distant.

questions.objective: Explain how cancer develops, invades nearby tissue, and spreads

questions.stem: A patient with breast cancer has a new tumor in the spine. How is the spinal tumor classified?

options.text: Primary bone cancer
options.rationale: The spinal tumor came from breast cells, so it is not a bone cancer.

options.text: A second, unrelated cancer
options.rationale: Metastatic tumors are the same cancer that spread, not a new unrelated one.

options.text: Metastatic breast cancer
options.rationale: Tumors are named for the tissue they arose from. Breast cancer cells that settle in bone are still breast cancer, so this is metastatic breast cancer.

options.text: Benign spinal tumor
options.rationale: A tumor formed by spreading cancer cells is malignant.

questions.takeaway: A primary tumor is named for its parent tissue. When it spreads, the new (secondary) tumor keeps that name: breast cancer in bone is metastatic breast cancer.
questions.strategy: Name the tumor for where the cells came from, not where they landed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Breast.

elimination.verdict: Metastatic breast cancer.

questions.objective: Explain how cancer develops, invades nearby tissue, and spreads

questions.stem: Which statements about metastasis are accurate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Cancer cells can travel through blood vessels
options.rationale: Blood vessels are one route of metastasis.

options.text: Cancer cells can travel through lymphatic vessels
options.rationale: Lymphatic vessels are the other main route.

options.text: Every cell that breaks away forms a new tumor
options.rationale: Only the cells that survive and grow at the distant site form metastatic tumors; most do not.

options.text: A secondary tumor forms when cells set up a remote colony
options.rationale: Secondary (metastatic) tumors form when cells break off and establish colonies elsewhere.

options.text: Benign tumors metastasize slowly over many years
options.rationale: Benign tumors never metastasize.

questions.takeaway: Metastasis happens through blood or lymph; the cells that survive and grow at distant sites form secondary tumors.
questions.strategy: Check each statement against what malignant cells can and cannot do.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Eliminate absolutes

steps.detail: "Every cell" is too absolute.
Benign tumors never spread.

elimination.verdict: Blood, lymph, remote colonies.

questions.objective: Explain how cancer develops, invades nearby tissue, and spreads

questions.stem: A malignant tumor arises from epithelial tissue. Which classification applies?

options.text: Sarcoma
options.rationale: Sarcomas arise from connective tissue such as bone, cartilage, fat and muscle.

options.text: Lymphoma
options.rationale: Lymphomas arise from lymphoid tissue.

options.text: Leukemia
options.rationale: Leukemias arise from blood forming tissue in the marrow.

options.text: Carcinoma
options.rationale: Carcinomas are malignant tumors of epithelial or glandular tissue, the covering and lining tissues.

questions.takeaway: Cancers are classified by tissue of origin: carcinoma (epithelial), sarcoma (connective), leukemia (blood forming), lymphoma (lymphoid).
questions.strategy: Carcinoma covers; sarcoma supports.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

elimination.verdict: Carcinoma.

questions.objective: Differentiate tumor grade from cancer stage

questions.stem: What does the grade of a tumor describe?

options.rationale: Spread describes stage, not grade.

options.text: How abnormal the cells look and how well differentiated they are
options.rationale: Grade is judged under the microscope: the less the cells resemble the parent tissue, the higher the grade.

options.text: Which lymph nodes contain cancer
options.rationale: Lymph node involvement is part of staging (the N in TNM).

options.text: Which treatment the patient prefers
options.rationale: Patient goals guide treatment choice but are not part of grading.

elimination.verdict: Cell appearance and differentiation.

options.rationale: Staging is done at diagnosis so it can guide treatment.

options.text: tumor grade
options.rationale: Grade is a separate system based on cell appearance.

options.text: primary tumor
options.rationale: T stands for the primary tumor: its size and depth.

options.text: tissue type
options.rationale: Tissue type is classification, not part of TNM.

questions.stem: A pathology report describes a tumor as poorly differentiated. Compared with a well differentiated tumor, what does this mean?

options.text: It has spread to more lymph nodes
options.rationale: Lymph node spread is stage, not differentiation.

options.text: It is a benign tumor
options.rationale: Differentiation describes malignant cells too; poor differentiation points to a more aggressive cancer, not a benign one.

options.text: It is higher grade and usually more aggressive
options.rationale: Poorly differentiated cells look little like the parent tissue, which means a higher grade and usually faster, more aggressive growth.

options.text: It is lower grade and grows more slowly
options.rationale: That describes a well differentiated tumor.

questions.takeaway: The less differentiated the cells, the higher the grade and the more aggressive the cancer tends to be.

Less differentiated = higher grade.

questions.stem: Which are examples of physical carcinogenesis? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: Radiation, including ultraviolet light, is a physical carcinogen.

options.text: Chronic irritation of a tissue
options.rationale: Long term irritation is listed as a physical cause of cancer.

options.text: Human papillomavirus infection
options.rationale: HPV is an oncovirus, a viral cause.

options.text: Radon gas in a basement
options.rationale: Radon gives off ionizing radiation, a physical carcinogen.

options.text: Cigarette smoke
options.rationale: Tobacco smoke is a chemical carcinogen.

questions.stem: Why does cancer risk increase with age?

options.text: Cells stop dividing after age 65, so damaged cells are never replaced
options.rationale: Cells keep dividing; aging does not stop cell division.

options.text: Immune defenses decline while DNA changes and exposures build up
options.rationale: With age the immune system is less able to destroy abnormal cells, and DNA damage and carcinogen exposure accumulate over time.

options.text: Older adults inherit new gene mutations
options.rationale: Inherited mutations are present from birth; they are not acquired with age.

options.text: Screening tests create cancers in older adults
options.rationale: Screening detects cancer; it does not cause it.

questions.takeaway: Age raises risk because immune defenses decline while DNA changes and carcinogen exposure build up over time.

questions.stem: For each action, indicate whether it is primary or secondary prevention.

options.text: Give the prescribed calcium tablets with meals
options.rationale: Calcium is not the treatment for tumor lysis; the priority is fluids and lowering uric acid.

options.text: Restrict fluids to 1 L per day
options.rationale: Fluid restriction is for SIADH; this patient needs more fluid, not less.

options.text: Give the prescribed uric acid lowering drug
options.rationale: Allopurinol or rasburicase lowers uric acid and protects the kidneys.

options.text: Encourage foods high in potassium
options.rationale: Potassium is already dangerously high.

options.text: Give the prescribed IV hydration
options.rationale: IV fluids flush potassium, phosphate and uric acid through the kidneys.

options.text: Hypercalcemia
options.rationale: Hypercalcemia causes constipation and polyuria, and does not explain high potassium and phosphate.

options.text: SIADH
options.rationale: SIADH causes low sodium from water retention, not high potassium and uric acid.

options.text: Spinal cord compression
options.rationale: Cord compression causes back pain and nerve deficits, not these lab changes.

options.text: Tumor lysis syndrome
options.rationale: Rapid breakdown of a bulky, treatment sensitive tumor releases potassium, phosphate and uric acid.

options.text: Urine output
options.rationale: Falling urine output signals kidney injury from uric acid crystals.

options.text: Blood glucose
options.rationale: Glucose is not affected by tumor lysis.

options.text: Pupil size
options.rationale: Pupils are not a priority parameter for this problem.

options.text: Oxygen saturation
options.rationale: Oxygenation is not the main risk here.

options.text: Cardiac rhythm
options.rationale: High potassium can cause dangerous dysrhythmias.

questions.takeaway: Tumor lysis syndrome follows treatment of bulky, fast growing cancers: potassium, phosphate and uric acid rise. Give IV hydration and uric acid lowering therapy; monitor rhythm, urine output, electrolytes and daily weight.

questions.stem: A patient with colon cancer who has not started treatment now has right upper abdominal pain and rising liver enzymes. What is the most likely explanation?

options.rationale: The patient has not started treatment, so this cannot be a treatment effect.

options.text: A new, unrelated primary cancer in the liver
options.rationale: A second primary cancer is possible but far less likely than spread from the known colon cancer.

options.text: Cancer cells spread through the blood to the liver
options.rationale: Blood from the colon drains to the liver first, so colon cancer commonly metastasizes there. Cells break off, travel in the blood and seed a new tumor.

options.text: Normal tissue reacting to the stress of a diagnosis
options.rationale: Emotional stress does not raise liver enzymes or cause organ pain.

questions.takeaway: Metastasis happens when cancer cells break away, travel through blood or lymph, and grow in a distant organ. Colon cancer commonly spreads to the liver.

questions.stem: A patient with no symptoms asks which activities are cancer screening. Which activities does the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Getting the HPV vaccine
options.rationale: The vaccine prevents infection with a virus that causes cancer. That is risk reduction, not screening.

options.text: A yearly fecal immunochemical stool test
options.rationale: This looks for hidden blood from colon cancer in a person without symptoms, which is screening.

options.text: Wearing sunscreen outdoors
options.rationale: Sunscreen lowers the chance of skin cancer starting. That is risk reduction.

options.text: A yearly low dose chest CT after years of heavy smoking
options.rationale: Low dose CT finds lung cancer early in a high risk person without symptoms, which is screening.

options.text: A biopsy of a mole that changed color
options.rationale: A biopsy works up a finding that already exists. That is diagnostic evaluation, not screening.

options.text: A monthly skin check for new or changing moles
options.rationale: A routine skin check looks for skin cancer early in a person without symptoms, which is screening.

questions.takeaway: Screening finds cancer early in people without symptoms. Risk reduction stops cancer from starting, and diagnostic evaluation works up a finding.
questions.strategy: For each option ask: does it prevent cancer, look for it in a well person, or work up a finding? Only the middle group is screening.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Vaccine and sunscreen lower risk.
A biopsy of a changed mole works up a finding.
Stool test, low dose CT, skin checks.

elimination.verdict: Stool test, low dose CT and skin checks.
