questions.stem: A patient with a small breast tumor, T1 N0 M0, grade 3, asks why chemotherapy is recommended when the tumor is so small. Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: “Grade 3 cells look very abnormal and tend to grow and spread faster.”
options.rationale: Grade describes how abnormal the cells look. Poorly differentiated, grade 3 cells are aggressive, so treatment may be advised even when the stage is early.

options.text: “A small tumor always needs chemotherapy before surgery.”
options.rationale: Tumor size alone does not require chemotherapy, and the absolute “always” is inaccurate.

options.text: “Grade 3 means the cancer is already in three lymph nodes.”
options.rationale: Grade is not about lymph nodes. N0 means no nodes are involved.

options.text: “Your cancer has already spread, so the size of the tumor no longer matters at all.”
options.rationale: M0 means no distant spread was found. The stage is early.

questions.takeaway: Stage (TNM) tells how far the cancer has spread; grade tells how abnormal and aggressive the cells are. A high grade can change treatment even at an early stage.
questions.strategy: The TNM part is reassuring, so the reason for chemotherapy must come from the grade. Reject options that confuse grade with nodes or spread.

strategies: Eliminate absolutes
Opposite pair, look closely

steps.detail: T1 N0 M0: small, no nodes, no distant spread.
Grade 3: very abnormal, aggressive cells.
Aggressive cells justify systemic treatment.

elimination.verdict: Grade 3 cells are aggressive.

questions.objective: Differentiate tumor grade from cancer stage

questions.stem: After surgery removed a colon tumor with clear margins, a patient asks, “Why do I need chemotherapy if the cancer is gone?” Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: “Chemotherapy will shrink the tumor before your surgery.”
options.rationale: Chemotherapy before surgery to shrink a tumor is neoadjuvant. This patient's surgery is already done.

options.text: “Chemotherapy is only to keep you comfortable now.”
options.rationale: Comfort focused treatment is palliative. This chemotherapy aims to prevent the cancer from coming back.

options.text: “It kills cancer cells that may remain but are too small to detect.”
options.rationale: This is adjuvant chemotherapy: given after the main treatment to destroy hidden cells and lower the chance of recurrence.

options.text: “Clear margins mean the surgeon was not able to remove all of the cancer cells.”
options.rationale: Clear margins mean no cancer was seen at the edges of the removed tissue, which is the goal of surgery.

questions.takeaway: Adjuvant therapy follows surgery to kill undetected cells and prevent recurrence. Neoadjuvant therapy comes before surgery to shrink the tumor.
questions.strategy: Timing decides the name: the surgery is done, so the treatment is adjuvant, and its job is to catch what cannot be seen.

strategies: Opposite pair, look closely
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: After surgery is adjuvant; before is neoadjuvant.
Kill hidden cells, prevent recurrence.
Clear margins are good news.

elimination.verdict: It kills cells too small to detect.

questions.objective: Compare the goals and common types of cancer treatment

questions.stem: A patient is told a lump on the back is a lipoma, a benign tumor, and asks, “Can it spread to other organs?” Which response is accurate?

options.text: “It stays in one place, but it can press on nearby structures.”
options.rationale: Benign cells grow in the wrong place or at the wrong time but stay localized. They do not invade or metastasize, yet a growing mass can still press on nerves or organs.

options.text: “It can spread, but much more slowly than a cancer.”
options.rationale: Benign tumors do not spread at all. Slow spread is not a feature of a benign tumor.

options.text: “It cannot spread, so it will never cause any problems.”
options.rationale: Benign tumors can still cause problems by pressure or by their size, so “never” is wrong.

options.text: “It will turn into a cancer over time if it is not removed soon.”
options.rationale: A benign tumor is a separate kind of growth. It does not routinely become malignant.

questions.takeaway: Benign tumors stay localized and do not invade or spread, but they can press on nearby structures. Malignant cells invade and metastasize.
questions.strategy: Separate spread from harm: benign means no spread, not no harm. Reject the option that claims spread and the one with an absolute.

strategies: Eliminate absolutes
Opposite pair, look closely

steps.detail: Localized, no invasion, no metastasis.
Size alone can cause symptoms.
Absolutes are rarely right here.

elimination.verdict: It stays in one place but can press on nearby structures.

questions.objective: Explain how cancer develops, invades nearby tissue, and spreads

questions.stem: A patient starting bevacizumab, a drug that blocks angiogenesis, asks how it fights the tumor. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: “It kills every fast dividing cell in your body.”
options.rationale: That describes traditional chemotherapy. Bevacizumab acts on blood vessel growth, not on all dividing cells.

options.text: “It helps your immune system recognize the cancer.”
options.rationale: That describes immunotherapy. Bevacizumab does not act on the immune system.

options.text: “It blocks the new blood vessels the tumor needs to grow.”
options.rationale: Tumors larger than a few millimeters must grow their own blood supply, a process called angiogenesis. Blocking it starves the tumor of oxygen and nutrients.

options.text: “It repairs the damaged genes inside each of the cancer cells in your body.”
options.rationale: Current drug repairs the gene changes in cancer cells. This is a common misconception.

questions.takeaway: Angiogenesis lets a tumor build its own blood supply so it can keep growing and spread. Drugs that block it slow tumor growth.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Name the process in the stem, angiogenesis, then match each option to the therapy it really describes.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: New blood vessel growth.
All dividing cells = chemotherapy; immune system = immunotherapy.

elimination.verdict: It blocks the new blood vessels the tumor needs.

questions.objective: Explain how cancer develops, invades nearby tissue, and spreads

questions.stem: A patient treated for colon cancer 2 years ago has a lung nodule showing colon cancer cells and asks, “So now I have lung cancer too?” Which response is accurate?

options.text: “It is colon cancer that has spread to the lung.”
options.rationale: A tumor is named for the tissue it started in. Colon cells that traveled through blood or lymph and formed a new colony in the lung are metastatic colon cancer.

options.text: “Yes, the lung tumor is a new and separate cancer.”
options.rationale: A new primary lung cancer would be made of lung cells. The biopsy shows colon cells, so this is spread.

options.text: “It is a benign growth caused by the earlier treatment.”
options.rationale: The biopsy shows cancer cells, so the growth is malignant, not benign.

options.text: “The colon cancer turned into lung cancer as it spread.”
options.rationale: Cancer cells keep their tissue of origin when they spread. They do not change into lung cancer.

questions.takeaway: Metastatic tumors keep the name of the primary cancer: colon cells in the lung are metastatic colon cancer, not lung cancer.
questions.strategy: Let the biopsy decide. The cell type tells you where the cancer started, wherever it is found.

strategies: Opposite pair, look closely
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Colon cancer cells.
Metastases keep the primary's name.

elimination.verdict: Colon cancer that spread to the lung.

questions.objective: Explain how cancer develops, invades nearby tissue, and spreads

questions.stem: For each diagnosis, indicate how the tumor is classified.
questions.scenario: The nurse reviews the diagnoses of six patients on an oncology unit.

rows.text: Adenocarcinoma of the colon
rows.rationale: Carcinomas arise from epithelial tissue; “adeno” means glandular epithelium.

rows.text: Osteosarcoma of the femur
rows.rationale: Sarcomas arise from connective tissue such as bone; “osteo” means bone.

rows.text: Lipoma on the shoulder
rows.rationale: The ending “oma” without carcinoma or sarcoma usually names a benign tumor; “lipo” means fat.

rows.text: Liposarcoma of the thigh
rows.rationale: A malignant tumor of fat, which is connective tissue, is a sarcoma.

rows.text: Squamous cell carcinoma of the skin
rows.rationale: Skin surface cells are epithelial, so this malignant tumor is a carcinoma.

rows.text: Osteoma of the skull
rows.rationale: Osteoma is a benign bone tumor; the malignant version is osteosarcoma.

questions.takeaway: Tumor names combine tissue and behavior: “oma” alone is usually benign, carcinoma is malignant epithelial tissue, and sarcoma is malignant connective tissue such as bone, fat or muscle.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Read the ending first: plain “oma” is benign, “carcinoma” is epithelial, “sarcoma” is connective tissue. Then use the prefix to confirm the tissue.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: oma, carcinoma or sarcoma.
adeno = gland, osteo = bone, lipo = fat.

elimination.verdict: Lipoma and osteoma benign; adenocarcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma are carcinomas; osteosarcoma and liposarcoma are sarcomas.

questions.objective: Differentiate tumor grade from cancer stage

questions.stem: A patient newly diagnosed with lung cancer asks why a PET scan and more tests are needed before treatment starts. Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: “The scans confirm whether the tumor is cancer.”
options.rationale: The biopsy already confirmed cancer. Further scans look for how far it has spread.

options.text: “The tests show how abnormal your cancer cells look.”
options.rationale: How abnormal the cells look is the grade, which comes from the biopsy sample, not from scans.

options.text: “The tests show how far it has spread, which guides treatment.”
options.rationale: Staging uses the TNM findings, tumor size, lymph nodes and distant spread, to describe the extent of disease. The stage guides which treatments will help.

options.text: “The tests are done so the team can plan your exact radiation dose.”
options.rationale: Radiation planning may come later, but the purpose of these tests is staging, which decides whether radiation is even used.

questions.takeaway: Staging (TNM: tumor, nodes, metastasis) describes how far the cancer has spread and guides treatment. Grade describes the cells and comes from the tissue sample.
questions.strategy: Ask what a scan can see: size and location. That is staging, not diagnosis (already done) or grade (needs a microscope).

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Global or umbrella option

steps.detail: Biopsy already done.
Grade needs cells under a microscope.
Stage the extent, then pick treatment.

elimination.verdict: They show how far it has spread to guide treatment.

questions.objective: Differentiate tumor grade from cancer stage

questions.stem: The nurse teaches a community group about lowering cancer risk. Which statements indicate understanding? Select all that apply.

options.text: “Using a tanning bed twice a month is safe.”
options.rationale: Ultraviolet radiation from tanning beds is a physical carcinogen at any frequency.

options.text: “Quitting smoking is the biggest step I can take.”
options.rationale: Tobacco is linked to about 30% of cancers, the largest single preventable cause.

options.text: “I will test my basement for radon gas.”
options.rationale: Radon is a radioactive gas that seeps from soil and is a leading cause of lung cancer after smoking.

options.text: “Switching from cigarettes to cigars removes the risk.”
options.rationale: Cigars still expose the mouth, throat and lungs to tobacco carcinogens.

options.text: “I will wear sunscreen and avoid the midday sun.”
options.rationale: Limiting ultraviolet exposure reduces skin cancer risk.

questions.takeaway: Primary prevention removes carcinogens: stop all tobacco, test for radon, and limit ultraviolet exposure from the sun and tanning beds.
questions.strategy: Each correct statement removes or limits a known carcinogen. Each wrong one only changes the form or amount of the same exposure.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Find the carcinogen in each option
steps.detail: Tobacco, radon, ultraviolet light.
Switching tobacco forms or tanning less still leaves the exposure.

elimination.verdict: Quitting smoking, testing for radon, sunscreen.

questions.objective: Distinguish cancer risk reduction, screening, and diagnostic evaluation

questions.stem: A 72 year old patient with no family history of cancer asks why colon cancer screening is still recommended. Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: “Age itself is the strongest risk factor for most cancers.”
options.rationale: With age, DNA changes and exposures build up while immune defenses decline, so cancer risk rises even without a family history.

options.text: “Screening is only needed when cancer runs in families.”
options.rationale: Most cancers occur in people with no family history. Average risk adults are screened too.

options.text: “After 70, screening is no longer useful for anyone.”
options.rationale: Screening decisions after 75 are individualized, but at 72 screening is still recommended for a person in good health.

options.text: “Your risk is low, so screening is just a precaution.”
options.rationale: This understates the risk. Age is a major risk factor, so the patient's risk is not low.

questions.takeaway: Cancer risk rises with age because DNA damage accumulates and immune surveillance declines. Most cancers occur in people without a family history.
questions.strategy: The patient's age is the deciding cue. Reject options that make family history the only reason to screen.

strategies: Eliminate absolutes
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Age 72.
Most cancers are not inherited.

elimination.verdict: Age is the strongest risk factor.

questions.objective: Distinguish cancer risk reduction, screening, and diagnostic evaluation

questions.stem: The nurse is taking a health history from a patient at a primary care visit. Highlight the findings that suggest an inherited cancer risk.
questions.nursesNote: Patient is 34 years old and walks 30 minutes daily. A parent was diagnosed with colon cancer at age 41. A grandparent had prostate cancer at age 84. A sibling and two cousins on the same side of the family had colon or uterine cancer. Patient quit smoking 5 years ago. A cousin was treated for a rare adrenal tumor. Patient drinks one glass of wine a week.

segments.text: walks 30 minutes daily
segments.rationale: Regular activity lowers risk and is not a genetic clue.

segments.text: A parent was diagnosed with colon cancer at age 41
segments.rationale: Cancer at an unusually young age is a key clue to an inherited syndrome.

segments.text: A grandparent had prostate cancer at age 84
segments.rationale: Prostate cancer at an advanced age is common and does not suggest an inherited pattern.

segments.text: A sibling and two cousins on the same side of the family had colon or uterine cancer
segments.rationale: Several close relatives on one side with related cancers suggests an inherited pattern, such as Lynch syndrome.

segments.text: quit smoking 5 years ago
segments.rationale: Past smoking affects risk, but it is an exposure, not an inherited clue.

segments.text: A cousin was treated for a rare adrenal tumor
segments.rationale: A rare cancer in the family is a clue to an inherited syndrome.

questions.takeaway: Clues to inherited cancer risk are cancer at a young age, several close relatives with the same or related cancers, and rare cancers in the family. These prompt referral for genetic counseling.
questions.strategy: Separate inherited clues from lifestyle and from common, late cancers. Age at diagnosis and clustering on one side of the family are what count.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Colon cancer at 41.
Several relatives on one side.
Rare adrenal tumor.

steps.action: Set aside lifestyle and common late cancers
steps.detail: Exercise, past smoking, prostate cancer at 84.

elimination.verdict: Parent at 41, the cluster on one side, and the rare adrenal tumor.

questions.objective: Distinguish cancer risk reduction, screening, and diagnostic evaluation

questions.stem: A patient whose sibling has a BRCA2 mutation asks the nurse, “Should I get tested?” Which response is best?

options.text: “Yes, you should get tested as soon as possible.”
options.rationale: Advising testing without counseling skips the discussion of what results mean for the patient and family. The decision is the patient's after counseling.

options.text: “A genetic counselor can review the risks and benefits with you first.”
options.rationale: Genetic counseling belongs before and after testing. The nurse gives risk information and refers, and the patient decides.

options.text: “No, only people who already have cancer are tested.”
options.rationale: People without cancer who have a family mutation are often offered testing. This statement is wrong.

options.text: “Your result will tell you for certain whether or not you will get cancer.”
options.rationale: A positive result shows higher risk, not certainty. This misstates what testing can tell.

questions.takeaway: The nurse provides risk information, not a diagnosis or a decision. A genetic counselor should be involved before and after testing.
questions.strategy: Look for the option that keeps the decision with the patient and brings in the right expert at the right time.

strategies: Patient centered option
Eliminate absolutes

steps.detail: Risk information and referral.
Before and after testing.

elimination.verdict: Refer to a genetic counselor first.

questions.objective: Distinguish cancer risk reduction, screening, and diagnostic evaluation

questions.stem: After genetic counseling, a patient learns of a harmful BRCA1 gene change. Which statement indicates the patient understands the result?

options.text: “My risk is higher, but I may never get cancer.”
options.rationale: A harmful gene change raises risk; it does not guarantee cancer. Screening and risk reduction options can lower the chance further.

options.text: “This means I already have cancer somewhere.”
options.rationale: A gene result is not a diagnosis. It describes inherited risk.

options.text: “My children will definitely inherit this change.”
options.rationale: Each child has about a 50% chance of inheriting it, not a certainty.

options.text: “Since this is genetic, there is nothing at all that can lower my risk.”
options.rationale: Closer screening, medicines and surgery can lower risk for gene carriers.

questions.takeaway: A harmful gene change means higher risk, not certain cancer. Options to lower risk include closer screening, medicines and preventive surgery.
questions.strategy: The correct statement holds two ideas at once: higher risk and not certain. Each wrong option turns risk into certainty or hopelessness.

strategies: Eliminate absolutes
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A gene result is not cancer.
“Definitely” and “nothing” are wrong.

elimination.verdict: Higher risk, but cancer may never develop.

questions.objective: Distinguish cancer risk reduction, screening, and diagnostic evaluation

questions.stem: At a clinic visit, a patient mentions several changes. Which findings does the nurse recommend be evaluated for cancer? Select all that apply.

options.text: Muscle soreness for 3 days after starting a new workout
options.rationale: Soreness after new exercise has an obvious cause and resolves on its own.

options.text: Hoarseness that has lasted 6 weeks
options.rationale: A nagging cough or hoarseness is one of the seven warning signs of cancer.

options.text: A sore on the lip that has not healed in 5 weeks
options.rationale: A sore that does not heal is a warning sign.

options.text: A cough with a cold that started 4 days ago
options.rationale: A short cough with a cold is expected; persistence is what makes it a warning sign.

options.text: A mole that has changed shape and color
options.rationale: An obvious change in a wart or mole is a warning sign of skin cancer.

questions.takeaway: The seven warning signs (CAUTION): change in bowel or bladder habits, a sore that does not heal, unusual bleeding or discharge, a thickening or lump, indigestion or trouble swallowing, an obvious change in a wart or mole, and a nagging cough or hoarseness.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two features make a finding a warning sign: it persists without an obvious cause, and it matches one of the CAUTION signs.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Weeks, not days.
A workout or a cold explains the others.

elimination.verdict: Hoarseness, a sore that will not heal, and a changing mole.

questions.objective: Distinguish cancer risk reduction, screening, and diagnostic evaluation

questions.stem: A patient reports blood mixed in the stool for 3 weeks and asks for a home stool test kit. Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: “The kit is a good first step to look for hidden blood.”
options.rationale: Stool tests screen people without symptoms. Visible bleeding is already a symptom, so screening adds nothing.

options.text: “Repeat the test yearly if this one comes back normal.”
options.rationale: Yearly stool testing is a screening plan. A normal result would not explain the bleeding the patient already has.

options.text: “The provider needs to see you for a diagnostic exam, such as a colonoscopy.”
options.rationale: Symptoms call for a diagnostic evaluation, not screening. A colonoscopy can find and biopsy the source.

options.text: “Bleeding like this is usually from hemorrhoids, so just watch it for another month or two.”
options.rationale: Assuming a benign cause delays diagnosis. Rectal bleeding for 3 weeks needs evaluation.

questions.takeaway: Screening is for people without symptoms. A symptom such as rectal bleeding calls for a diagnostic evaluation.
questions.strategy: First ask: does the patient have a symptom? If yes, every screening option is the wrong tool.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Visible blood for 3 weeks.
Diagnostic evaluation, not screening.

elimination.verdict: A diagnostic exam such as a colonoscopy.

questions.objective: Distinguish cancer risk reduction, screening, and diagnostic evaluation

questions.stem: A patient with breast cancer asks why the treatment plan differs from a friend's plan for the same cancer. Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: “Plans depend on stage, tumor markers, your health and your goals.”
options.rationale: Treatment is chosen from the type and stage of cancer, tumor biomarkers, overall health and the patient's own goals, so two people with the same cancer can get different plans.

options.text: “Your provider prefers a different approach than your friend's.”
options.rationale: Plans follow evidence based factors, not provider preference.

options.text: “The plan is based on the size of the tumor only.”
options.rationale: Size is one part of staging, but nodes, spread, biomarkers, health and goals also matter.

options.text: “Your friend's cancer was probably more advanced than yours.”
options.rationale: This guesses about another patient and ignores the other factors in choosing treatment.

questions.takeaway: Treatment choice depends on the type and stage of cancer, tumor biomarkers, overall health and the patient's goals.
questions.strategy: Pick the global option that names all the factors; the others reduce treatment choice to one factor or to a guess.

strategies: Global or umbrella option

steps.detail: Type, stage, biomarkers, health, goals.
Size only, or provider preference.

elimination.verdict: Stage, tumor markers, health and goals.

questions.objective: Compare the goals and common types of cancer treatment

questions.stem: A patient with cancer found in the liver, lungs and bones asks why surgery is not being offered. Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: “Surgery is used only after chemotherapy has failed.”
options.rationale: Surgery is often the first treatment for localized cancer. It is not reserved for after chemotherapy.

options.text: “Cancer in several organs needs treatment that reaches the whole body.”
options.rationale: Surgery and external beam radiation are local: they treat one site. Spread to several organs calls for systemic therapy, such as chemotherapy or immunotherapy, that travels through the blood.

options.text: “Surgery would remove the cancer but is too risky for you.”
options.rationale: Even a safe surgery could not remove cancer in three organ systems. The reason is the spread, not the risk.

options.text: “Radiation to each organ works better than surgery.”
options.rationale: Radiation is also local. Treating each site does not reach cells throughout the body.

questions.takeaway: Local treatments (surgery, external beam radiation) treat one site; systemic treatments (chemotherapy, immunotherapy, hormonal and targeted therapy) reach the whole body and are used for widespread cancer.
questions.strategy: Classify each option as local or systemic. Cancer in several organs needs systemic therapy.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Liver, lungs and bones.
Surgery and radiation are local.
Widespread disease needs systemic therapy.

elimination.verdict: Treatment that reaches the whole body.

questions.objective: Compare the goals and common types of cancer treatment

questions.stem: For each plan, indicate the goal of the surgery.
questions.scenario: The nurse reviews the surgical plans of six patients with cancer or cancer risk.

rows.text: Removing as much of a large abdominal tumor as possible when it cannot all be removed
rows.rationale: Debulking removes part of a tumor that cannot be fully removed so other treatments work better.

rows.text: Removing the colon of a patient with familial adenomatous polyposis and no cancer yet
rows.rationale: Prophylactic surgery removes tissue at very high risk before cancer develops.

rows.text: Removing a tissue sample from a new breast lump
rows.rationale: A biopsy obtains tissue to confirm whether a mass is cancer and what type.

rows.text: Removing an early lung tumor with clear margins and no spread
rows.rationale: Removing all of a localized tumor aims to cure.

rows.text: Bypassing a bowel blocked by widespread cancer to relieve vomiting
rows.rationale: Palliative surgery relieves symptoms and improves comfort without aiming to cure.

rows.text: Removing a thyroid gland in a patient with an inherited RET gene change and no cancer
rows.rationale: A preventive removal in a person with a high risk gene change and no cancer is prophylactic.

questions.takeaway: Prophylactic surgery prevents cancer in high risk tissue; diagnostic surgery gets tissue; curative surgery removes all localized cancer; debulking removes part of a tumor; palliative surgery relieves symptoms.
questions.strategy: Ask two questions for each plan: is there cancer yet, and is the aim to prevent, confirm, cure, reduce or relieve?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Prophylactic.
Diagnostic.
Curative.
Debulking.
Palliative.

elimination.verdict: Colon and thyroid prophylactic, biopsy diagnostic, early lung curative, large abdominal debulking, bowel bypass palliative.

questions.objective: Compare the goals and common types of cancer treatment

questions.stem: A patient asks why radiation is scheduled 5 days a week for 6 weeks instead of one large dose. Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: “Small daily doses let normal tissue recover between treatments.”
options.rationale: Dividing the dose, called fractionation, kills more cancer cells over time while normal tissue repairs between sessions, so side effects are fewer.

options.text: “One large dose would make you radioactive afterward.”
options.rationale: External beam radiation never makes the patient radioactive, whatever the dose.

options.text: “The machine can only deliver a small dose each day.”
options.rationale: The schedule is set by biology, not by machine limits.

options.text: “Daily treatment gives your cancer less time to spread.”
options.rationale: The daily schedule exists to protect normal tissue, not to outpace spread.

questions.takeaway: Radiation is fractionated into small daily doses so cancer cells are killed while normal tissue recovers between treatments.
questions.strategy: The reason must explain why small doses beat one large dose: the protection of normal tissue.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Fractionation.
Normal tissue recovery.
External beam does not make anyone radioactive.

elimination.verdict: Small daily doses let normal tissue recover.

questions.objective: Compare the goals and common types of cancer treatment

questions.stem: The nurse is assigned four patients receiving cancer treatment. Which patient requires radiation safety precautions?

options.text: A patient receiving external beam radiation to the chest
options.rationale: External beam radiation comes from a machine outside the body, so the patient never gives off radiation.

options.text: A patient who finished IV chemotherapy 6 hours ago
options.rationale: This patient needs hazardous drug precautions for body fluids, not radiation precautions.

options.text: A patient with a sealed radioactive implant in place
options.rationale: Brachytherapy places the source inside the body, so the patient emits radiation while it is in place. Time, distance and shielding apply.

options.text: A patient who had a CT scan with contrast today
options.rationale: A CT scan uses x rays only during the scan, and contrast is not radioactive.

questions.takeaway: Only internal radiation (brachytherapy) makes the patient a radiation source. External beam radiation does not; chemotherapy needs hazardous drug precautions instead.
questions.strategy: Ask where the radiation source is. Only a source inside the body requires radiation precautions; watch for the chemotherapy patient, who needs a different kind of precaution.

strategies: Opposite pair, look closely
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Inside the body only with an implant.
Body fluid precautions are for chemotherapy.

elimination.verdict: The patient with a sealed implant.

questions.objective: Compare the goals and common types of cancer treatment

questions.stem: A patient starting immunotherapy asks why the nurse expects less hair loss than with the chemotherapy a relative received. Which explanation is accurate?

options.text: “Immunotherapy helps your immune system attack the cancer cells.”
options.rationale: Chemotherapy kills all fast dividing cells, including hair follicles. Immunotherapy works by helping the immune system find and attack cancer, so hair loss is uncommon.

options.text: “Immunotherapy is a weaker form of chemotherapy.”
options.rationale: Immunotherapy is a different class of treatment, not a weaker chemotherapy.

options.text: “Immunotherapy is given at a much lower dose.”
options.rationale: Dose is not the reason. The mechanism of action differs.

options.text: “Immunotherapy only kills the fast dividing cells in tumors.”
options.rationale: Killing fast dividing cells describes chemotherapy, which cannot tell tumor cells from hair follicles.

questions.takeaway: Chemotherapy kills fast dividing cells, healthy or not; immunotherapy helps the immune system attack cancer. Side effects follow the mechanism.
questions.strategy: Explain side effects through mechanism. Hair loss comes from killing dividing cells, which immunotherapy does not do.

strategies: Opposite pair, look closely

steps.detail: All fast dividing cells.
The immune response against cancer.

elimination.verdict: It helps the immune system attack cancer.

questions.objective: Compare the goals and common types of cancer treatment

questions.stem: A patient receiving chemotherapy every 21 days asks, “Why can't I get it every week to finish sooner?” Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: “Weekly doses would not reach the tumor.”
options.rationale: Every dose reaches the tumor through the blood. The gap is about healthy cells.

options.text: “The rest period lets your healthy cells recover.”
options.rationale: Chemotherapy is given in cycles so the bone marrow and other healthy tissues can recover before the next dose.

options.text: “The cancer needs time to grow so the drug works better.”
options.rationale: Cycles are not timed to let the cancer grow; they are timed for normal tissue recovery.

options.text: “Your body needs time to clear the drug from your blood.”
options.rationale: Most drugs clear within days. The 21 days are for blood counts to recover from the nadir.

questions.takeaway: Chemotherapy is given in cycles so healthy cells, especially the bone marrow, can recover between doses.
questions.strategy: The schedule protects normal tissue. Choose the option about healthy cells, not about the drug or the tumor.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Recovery of healthy cells.
Counts fall then recover before the next dose.

elimination.verdict: The rest period lets healthy cells recover.

questions.objective: Compare the goals and common types of cancer treatment

questions.stem: A patient's breast tumor tested positive for HER2. The patient asks why that test mattered before starting trastuzumab. Which response is accurate?

options.text: “The drug only works when the tumor has that target.”
options.rationale: Trastuzumab is a monoclonal antibody, a targeted therapy that attaches to the HER2 protein. Without the target, it has nothing to act on.

options.text: “The test shows how much of the chemotherapy your body can handle.”
options.rationale: Tolerance is judged by health and blood counts, not by HER2 status.

options.text: “A positive test means the cancer has spread.”
options.rationale: HER2 is a tumor marker, not a measure of spread. Staging shows spread.

options.text: “The test decides how many cycles you will need.”
options.rationale: The number of cycles comes from the treatment plan, not from the target test.

questions.takeaway: Targeted therapies and monoclonal antibodies attach to or block a specific target the cancer has, so the tumor is tested for that target first.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Connect the drug to its target. A targeted drug needs the target, which is why biomarker testing comes first.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Monoclonal antibody, targeted therapy.

steps.action: Name the purpose of the test
steps.detail: Confirm the target is present.

elimination.verdict: The drug works only when the tumor has the target.
