questions.stem: The nurse is preparing to give a patient's first dose of IV chemotherapy. Which information does the nurse verify before the dose is prepared?

options.text: The patient's current height and weight
options.rationale: Many chemotherapy doses are based on body surface area, which is calculated from height and weight. An outdated weight gives a wrong dose.

options.text: The patient's blood type and Rh factor
options.rationale: Blood type is needed for transfusion, not for chemotherapy dosing.

options.text: The patient's preferred pain medicine
options.rationale: Pain control matters, but it does not affect the chemotherapy dose.

options.text: The patient's most recent chest x ray
options.rationale: A chest x ray is not used to calculate chemotherapy doses.

questions.takeaway: Many chemotherapy doses are calculated from body surface area, so a current, measured height and weight are verified before preparation.
questions.strategy: Ask what the dose depends on. Body surface area comes from height and weight.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Body surface area.
Height and weight.

elimination.verdict: Current height and weight.

questions.objective: Compare the goals and common types of cancer treatment

questions.stem: A patient with leukemia that has spread to the cerebrospinal fluid will receive intrathecal methotrexate. The patient asks why it is not given IV. Which response is accurate?

options.text: “IV drugs work too fast to be safe for you.”
options.rationale: Speed is not the reason. The issue is whether the drug reaches the cerebrospinal fluid.

options.text: “Intrathecal dosing avoids all side effects.”
options.rationale: Intrathecal chemotherapy still has side effects, such as headache and infection risk at the site.

options.text: “Most IV drugs do not reach the fluid around your brain.”
options.rationale: The blood brain barrier keeps most IV drugs out of the cerebrospinal fluid. Intrathecal dosing delivers the drug directly into it.

options.text: “Intrathecal dosing is used when your veins are too fragile for any IV.”
options.rationale: Fragile veins call for a central line, not an intrathecal route.

questions.takeaway: Intrathecal chemotherapy is given into the cerebrospinal fluid because the blood brain barrier blocks most IV drugs from reaching it.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Name the route, then ask what problem it solves: getting the drug past the blood brain barrier.

strategies: Eliminate absolutes
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Into the cerebrospinal fluid.
Blood brain barrier.
No route avoids all side effects.

elimination.verdict: Most IV drugs do not reach the fluid around the brain.

questions.objective: Compare the goals and common types of cancer treatment

questions.stem: Three weeks into radiation to the head and neck, a patient reports a sore, dry mouth and trouble swallowing. Which actions does the nurse include in the plan? Select all that apply.

options.text: Rinse often with a salt and baking soda solution
options.rationale: Bland rinses clean the mouth and soothe mucositis without irritating it.

options.text: Use an alcohol based mouthwash after meals
options.rationale: Alcohol dries and burns inflamed tissue, making mucositis worse.

options.text: Offer soft, moist foods such as yogurt and mashed potatoes
options.rationale: Soft, moist foods are easier to swallow and less painful on inflamed tissue.

options.text: Sip water often throughout the day
options.rationale: Frequent sips relieve dry mouth from salivary gland damage.

options.text: Use lemon glycerin swabs to moisten the lips and mouth
options.rationale: Lemon glycerin swabs dry and irritate the mouth and are avoided in mucositis.

options.text: Weigh the patient at each visit
options.rationale: Painful swallowing reduces intake, so weight is tracked to catch malnutrition early.

questions.takeaway: Head and neck radiation causes mucositis, dry mouth and trouble swallowing. Use bland rinses, frequent sips, soft moist foods and weight checks; avoid alcohol rinses and lemon glycerin.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Every correct action soothes the mouth, moistens it, eases swallowing or watches nutrition. The wrong ones dry or irritate inflamed tissue.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Mucositis, dry mouth, trouble swallowing.
Alcohol rinses and lemon glycerin.
Bland rinses, sips, soft foods, weights.

elimination.verdict: Salt and baking soda rinses, soft moist foods, sips of water, weights.

questions.objective: Identify common treatment side effects and appropriate nursing interventions

questions.stem: Nurses on different shifts describe a patient's chemotherapy diarrhea as “bad,” “moderate” and “a lot.” Which action best makes the documentation consistent?

options.text: Grade the diarrhea with the CTCAE scale each shift
options.rationale: The Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) grade side effects from 1 to 5 using defined criteria, so every nurse describes the same severity the same way.

options.text: Ask the patient to rate the diarrhea from 0 to 10
options.rationale: A 0 to 10 rating is subjective and is not the standard tool for grading treatment side effects.

options.text: Write a detailed narrative note on each shift
options.rationale: Narratives still vary between nurses. A standardized scale is what removes the inconsistency.

options.text: Record only the number of stools each day
options.rationale: Stool count is part of grading, but alone it misses other criteria such as the effect on daily activities.

questions.takeaway: The CTCAE is a standardized scale for grading and documenting treatment side effects, so changes can be compared over time and between nurses.
questions.strategy: The problem is inconsistent wording, so the fix is a shared scale.

strategies: Global or umbrella option

steps.detail: Vague, different words for severity.
CTCAE grading.

elimination.verdict: Grade it with the CTCAE scale.

questions.objective: Identify common treatment side effects and appropriate nursing interventions

questions.stem: Before the third chemotherapy cycle, a patient begins vomiting in the parking lot on seeing the clinic. Which intervention best addresses this problem?

options.text: Give the prescribed antiemetic only after chemotherapy starts
options.rationale: This is anticipatory nausea, which starts before treatment. Waiting until chemotherapy starts misses it.

options.text: Delay the cycle until the vomiting stops on its own
options.rationale: Delaying treatment does not treat a learned response and can harm the cancer plan.

options.text: Teach guided imagery and relaxation to use before visits
options.rationale: Anticipatory nausea is a conditioned response. Relaxation, guided imagery and distraction, along with prescribed antianxiety medicine before visits, help prevent it.

options.text: Encourage a large meal before each appointment
options.rationale: A large meal tends to worsen nausea. Small, bland meals are preferred.

questions.takeaway: Anticipatory nausea is triggered by cues linked to past treatment. Prevent it with relaxation, guided imagery, distraction and prescribed antianxiety medicine before treatment, and by controlling nausea well in every cycle.
questions.strategy: Name the type from the timing: before treatment, triggered by a cue. Then choose the intervention that targets a learned response.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Anticipatory: begins before treatment.
Relaxation and guided imagery.

elimination.verdict: Teach guided imagery and relaxation.

questions.objective: Identify common treatment side effects and appropriate nursing interventions

questions.stem: A patient is scheduled for highly emetogenic chemotherapy at 1000. Complete the sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence: The nurse gives the prescribed ondansetron [[1]] because antiemetics work best when [[2]].

options.text: at the first sign of nausea
options.rationale: Waiting for nausea lets vomiting become established, and it is much harder to stop.

options.text: after the infusion is complete
options.rationale: By then the chemotherapy has already triggered the vomiting pathway.

options.text: only if the patient vomits twice
options.rationale: Using vomiting as the trigger is too late and leads to poorly controlled symptoms.

options.text: at 0930, before the infusion starts
options.rationale: Antiemetics are given 30 to 60 minutes before chemotherapy so they are working when the drug arrives.

options.text: the stomach is completely empty
options.rationale: An empty stomach is not required, and light meals may help.

options.text: combined with a full liquid diet
options.rationale: Diet does not change how the drug works.

options.text: given to prevent symptoms rather than treat them
options.rationale: Prevention is the goal in chemotherapy induced nausea and vomiting; scheduled dosing keeps blood levels steady.

options.text: given in the largest possible dose
options.rationale: Doses are fixed by the prescription; timing, not a larger dose, is the key.

questions.takeaway: Antiemetics for chemotherapy are given before treatment begins and on schedule afterward, to prevent nausea and vomiting rather than chase it.
questions.strategy: Prevention beats rescue: the drug must be in the body before the chemotherapy is.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Before the infusion.
Prevent rather than treat.

elimination.verdict: At 0930, before the infusion, because prevention works best.

questions.objective: Identify common treatment side effects and appropriate nursing interventions

questions.stem: Four patients receiving chemotherapy call the clinic. Which patient does the nurse call back first?

options.text: A 45 year old patient with nausea who is keeping down fluids and soup
options.rationale: Nausea with adequate fluid intake can be managed with the antiemetic plan.

options.text: A 60 year old patient with hair loss who feels embarrassed
options.rationale: Body image distress is real and is addressed, but it is not physiologically urgent.

options.text: A 52 year old patient with a metallic taste in the mouth
options.rationale: Taste changes affect appetite but are not urgent.

options.text: An 84 year old patient who vomited 6 times overnight and is dizzy
options.rationale: Older adults have less body water reserve and become dehydrated quickly. Repeated vomiting with dizziness suggests dehydration that needs prompt treatment.

questions.takeaway: Persistent chemotherapy induced vomiting is especially dangerous in older adults, who dehydrate faster and are prone to falls and kidney injury.
questions.strategy: Age matters here because it changes how fast fluid loss becomes dangerous. Combine the vomiting with the dizziness and the age.

strategies: Priority key word
Apply the ABCs

steps.detail: Vomiting 6 times with dizziness.
Older adults dehydrate faster.

elimination.verdict: The 84 year old patient who is vomiting and dizzy.

questions.objective: Identify common treatment side effects and appropriate nursing interventions

questions.stem: A patient is receiving a short IV push of fluorouracil, a drug known to cause mouth sores. Which action during the infusion helps prevent mucositis?

options.text: Rinse the mouth with hydrogen peroxide
options.rationale: Peroxide damages healing tissue and is not used to prevent mucositis.

options.text: Have the patient hold ice chips in the mouth
options.rationale: Ice chips during the infusion constrict mouth blood vessels so less drug reaches the lining. This oral cryotherapy is used with selected drugs such as fluorouracil.

options.text: Have the patient drink hot tea to stay warm
options.rationale: Warmth increases blood flow to the mouth, which is the opposite of the goal.

options.text: Brush the teeth firmly during the infusion
options.rationale: Firm brushing injures the lining. A soft brush is used gently between treatments.

questions.takeaway: Ice chips during selected chemotherapy infusions, such as fluorouracil, help prevent mucositis by limiting blood flow to the mouth. Cold is avoided with oxaliplatin, which causes cold sensitivity.
questions.strategy: Think about the mechanism: less blood flow to the mouth means less drug in the lining.

strategies: Opposite pair, look closely

steps.detail: Cold narrows blood vessels.
Warmth increases flow.

elimination.verdict: Ice chips during the infusion.

questions.objective: Identify common treatment side effects and appropriate nursing interventions

questions.stem: A patient who finished chemotherapy last week asks about the hair that fell out. Which statement indicates understanding?

options.text: “My hair may start growing back in about a month.”
options.rationale: Regrowth often begins about 3 to 4 weeks after chemotherapy ends, and the new hair may differ in color or texture.

options.text: “My hair will grow back exactly the same color and texture as it was before.”
options.rationale: New hair can be a different color or texture, so “exactly” is not accurate.

options.text: “My hair loss from chemotherapy is permanent.”
options.rationale: Chemotherapy hair loss is usually temporary.

options.text: “I can skip covering my scalp outdoors.”
options.rationale: The bare scalp burns easily, so a hat or sunscreen is needed outdoors.

questions.takeaway: Chemotherapy hair loss is usually temporary; regrowth may begin about a month after treatment ends, sometimes with a new color or texture. Protect the scalp from sun and cold.
questions.strategy: Look for the statement that gets both the timing and the uncertainty right, and reject absolutes.

strategies: Eliminate absolutes

steps.detail: About a month after treatment ends.
“Exactly” and “permanent” are wrong.

elimination.verdict: Regrowth may start in about a month.

questions.objective: Identify common treatment side effects and appropriate nursing interventions

questions.stem: A patient receiving chemotherapy has missed two doses of an oral medicine because of trouble remembering. Which actions does the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Tell the patient to double the next dose
options.rationale: Doubling a missed dose is unsafe and not part of managing memory changes.

options.text: Provide a written medicine schedule
options.rationale: Written instructions give the patient something to check later, which is the most helpful step for chemotherapy related memory changes.

options.text: Suggest stopping chemotherapy until memory improves
options.rationale: Memory changes are managed with supports; stopping treatment is the provider's decision and not the first step.

options.text: Set phone alarms for each dose time
options.rationale: Reminders reduce reliance on memory.

options.text: Advise avoiding books and puzzles to rest the brain
options.rationale: Mental activity is encouraged; avoiding it does not help.

questions.takeaway: For chemotherapy related memory changes, use written instructions, reminders and routines so the patient does not depend on memory alone.
questions.strategy: Each correct action supports memory from outside the brain. Each wrong action is unsafe or unhelpful.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Written schedules and alarms.
Doubling a dose.

elimination.verdict: Written schedule and phone alarms.

questions.objective: Identify common treatment side effects and appropriate nursing interventions

questions.stem: A patient receiving chemotherapy has hemoglobin 8.6 g/dL and reports being exhausted after showering. Which intervention does the nurse include?

options.text: Encourage a full bath and shampoo every morning
options.rationale: A full routine at once uses more energy than the patient has. Activities are spaced out instead.

options.text: Plan rest periods between daily activities
options.rationale: Anemia lowers oxygen delivery, so energy is limited. Spacing activities with rest periods conserves energy.

options.text: Teach use of an electric razor and soft toothbrush
options.rationale: These protect against bleeding from low platelets, not fatigue from anemia.

options.text: Have the patient avoid crowds and sick contacts
options.rationale: This protects against infection from neutropenia, not fatigue from anemia.

questions.takeaway: Match the intervention to the low cell: anemia means fatigue, so conserve energy; low platelets means bleeding precautions; neutropenia means infection precautions.
questions.strategy: Name the low cell first, then pick the intervention for that cell. Two distractors are correct for a different cell.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Red cells: anemia.
Fatigue, so conserve energy.
Razor for platelets, crowds for neutrophils.

elimination.verdict: Plan rest periods between activities.

questions.objective: Identify common treatment side effects and appropriate nursing interventions

questions.stem: A nurse floated from a medical unit without chemotherapy training is assigned a patient due for IV chemotherapy. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Give it after reviewing the drug guide carefully
options.rationale: Reviewing a drug guide does not replace specialized training and demonstrated competency.

options.text: Have another nurse watch while the dose is given
options.rationale: Supervision by any nurse does not make the floated nurse qualified to give chemotherapy.

options.text: Ask the charge nurse for a chemotherapy trained nurse
options.rationale: Only RNs who have completed specialized training and shown competency may give chemotherapy. The floated nurse can still provide the rest of the care.

options.text: Delay the dose until the next shift
options.rationale: Delaying treatment is unnecessary when a qualified nurse can give it now.

questions.takeaway: Chemotherapy is given only by RNs who completed specialized training and showed competency. An untrained nurse gets a qualified nurse to give it.
questions.strategy: This is about scope, not knowledge: training plus demonstrated competency is required.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Trained, competent RNs.
Get a qualified nurse now.

elimination.verdict: Ask the charge nurse for a chemotherapy trained nurse.

questions.objective: Apply safety precautions when caring for patients receiving cancer treatment

questions.stem: The nurse teaches a caregiver of a patient who received IV chemotherapy today and is going home. Which instructions does the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Wear gloves when handling vomit, urine or stool
options.rationale: Chemotherapy is excreted in body fluids for about 48 hours, so gloves protect the caregiver.

options.text: Flush the toilet twice with the lid closed
options.rationale: Double flushing with the lid down limits splashing of drug in the urine and stool.

options.text: Wash soiled linens separately from other laundry
options.rationale: Separate washing keeps drug residue off the household's other clothes.

options.text: Wash hands with soap and water after removing gloves
options.rationale: Hand hygiene removes any drug that reached the skin.

options.text: Share the toilet without any precautions after 2 hours
options.rationale: Drug stays in body fluids for about 48 hours, not 2 hours.

options.text: Place soiled pads in a sealed plastic bag before discarding
options.rationale: Sealing contaminated items keeps the drug contained.

questions.takeaway: For about 48 hours after chemotherapy, body fluids contain the drug: wear gloves, flush twice with the lid closed, wash linens separately, bag soiled items and wash hands.
questions.strategy: Every correct instruction contains the drug in body fluids. The one wrong instruction gets the time frame wrong.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: About 48 hours.
Gloves, double flush, separate laundry, sealed bags, hand hygiene.

elimination.verdict: All except sharing the toilet after 2 hours.

questions.objective: Apply safety precautions when caring for patients receiving cancer treatment

questions.stem: The nurse teaches a caregiver about the patient's oral capecitabine tablets. Which caregiver statement requires further teaching?

options.text: “I will wear gloves if I need to touch the tablets.”
options.rationale: Gloves protect the caregiver, because oral chemotherapy is hazardous too.

options.text: “I will crush the tablets in applesauce if they are hard to swallow.”
options.rationale: Crushing hazardous tablets releases drug dust and can change the dose. If swallowing is a problem, the nurse contacts the pharmacist or provider about another form.

options.text: “I will store the tablets in their own container away from other family medicines.”
options.rationale: Separate storage prevents mix ups and exposure.

options.text: “I will wash my hands after giving the dose.”
options.rationale: Hand hygiene after handling is correct.

questions.takeaway: Oral chemotherapy is hazardous: handle it with gloves, store it separately, and never crush or split it. Swallowing problems go to the pharmacist or provider.
questions.strategy: Look for the statement that exposes someone to the drug or changes the dose.

strategies: Negative polarity

steps.action: Read the question as a negative
steps.detail: Find the wrong statement.
Crushing makes hazardous dust.

elimination.verdict: Crushing the tablets.

questions.objective: Apply safety precautions when caring for patients receiving cancer treatment

questions.stem: For each action, indicate whether it is appropriate or requires the nurse to intervene.
questions.scenario: A patient has a sealed radioactive implant in place. The nurse observes visitors and staff in the room.

rows.text: A visitor sits in a chair 6 feet from the bed
rows.rationale: Distance lowers exposure; visitors stay at least 6 feet away.

rows.text: A visitor brings a 10 year old child to the bedside
rows.rationale: Children are not allowed to visit while the implant is in place because they are more sensitive to radiation.

rows.text: A staff member wears a radiation dosimeter badge
rows.rationale: The badge tracks each person's cumulative exposure.

rows.text: A nursing assistant picks up a dislodged implant with gloved hands
rows.rationale: A dislodged source is never handled with hands. It is picked up with long forceps and placed in the lead container.

rows.text: The nurse clusters care to limit time in the room
rows.rationale: Less time near the source means less exposure.

rows.text: A visitor plans to stay for the whole afternoon
rows.rationale: Visits are limited in length, often to 30 minutes a day, to limit time near the source.

questions.takeaway: Time, distance and shielding: limit time, keep distance, use shielding, badge every staff member, keep children away, and pick up a dislodged source only with long forceps into the lead container.
questions.strategy: Test each action against time, distance and shielding. Anything that adds time, removes distance or handles the source directly requires intervention.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Clustered care is right; a whole afternoon is not.
6 feet is right; a child at the bedside is not.
Forceps and the lead container, never hands.

elimination.verdict: Chair at 6 feet, badge and clustered care are appropriate; the child, the dislodged implant and the long visit require intervention.

questions.objective: Apply safety precautions when caring for patients receiving cancer treatment

questions.stem: The nurse reviews the note for a patient with neutropenia after chemotherapy. Highlight the findings that suggest the infection is progressing to sepsis.
questions.nursesNote: Day 10 after chemotherapy. Temperature 38.4 °C. Blood pressure 86/50 mm Hg, down from 118/72 mm Hg this morning. Newly confused about the date. Hair thinning on the scalp. Urine output 60 mL over the last 4 hours. Reports mild nausea after lunch. Skin is warm.

segments.text: Temperature 38.4 °C
segments.rationale: Fever signals infection, which is already known. It does not by itself show progression to sepsis.

segments.text: Blood pressure 86/50 mm Hg, down from 118/72 mm Hg this morning
segments.rationale: Falling blood pressure shows poor perfusion, a sign of sepsis.

segments.text: Newly confused about the date
segments.rationale: New confusion signals reduced brain perfusion in sepsis.

segments.text: Hair thinning on the scalp
segments.rationale: Hair loss is an expected chemotherapy effect.

segments.text: Urine output 60 mL over the last 4 hours
segments.rationale: Output of 15 mL/hr is below 30 mL/hr and shows poor kidney perfusion.

segments.text: Reports mild nausea after lunch
segments.rationale: Mild nausea is a common chemotherapy effect.

questions.takeaway: In a neutropenic patient with infection, hypotension, new confusion and low urine output signal progression to sepsis. Sepsis can progress fast in neutropenia.
questions.strategy: Fever only says there is an infection. Sepsis shows up as organ perfusion failing: pressure, mind and kidneys.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Fever is infection.
Blood pressure, mental status, urine output.

elimination.verdict: The blood pressure drop, new confusion and low urine output.

questions.objective: Recognize oncologic emergencies and prioritize the initial nursing response

questions.stem: A patient with leukemia has blood oozing from the IV site, gums and nose and new blood in the urine. Which explanation is most likely?

options.text: Clotting factors are being used up by widespread clotting
options.rationale: In disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), clotting is triggered throughout the body, using up platelets and clotting factors, so the patient bleeds from many sites at once.

options.text: The IV catheter has punctured through the vein
options.rationale: A misplaced catheter explains bleeding at one site, not the gums, nose and urine.

options.text: The patient is brushing the teeth too firmly
options.rationale: Firm brushing could explain gum bleeding but not bleeding from the nose, urine and IV site.

options.text: High white cell counts are blocking the blood vessels
options.rationale: Leukostasis causes clogging problems, not oozing from many sites.

questions.takeaway: Bleeding from multiple sites at once in a patient with cancer suggests DIC, in which widespread clotting consumes platelets and clotting factors.
questions.strategy: Count the sites. A single cause at one site cannot explain bleeding everywhere at once.

strategies: Global or umbrella option

steps.detail: IV site, gums, nose, urine.

steps.action: Find the cause that explains all
steps.detail: Consumption of clotting factors in DIC.

elimination.verdict: Clotting factors used up by widespread clotting.

questions.objective: Recognize oncologic emergencies and prioritize the initial nursing response

questions.stem: A patient with breast cancer that has spread to bone reports new constipation, increased thirst and feeling tired. Which laboratory result does the nurse check first?

options.text: Serum calcium
options.rationale: Bone metastases release calcium. Constipation, thirst and fatigue are early, subtle signs of hypercalcemia.

options.text: Serum sodium
options.rationale: Low sodium causes confusion and headache, not constipation and thirst together.

options.text: Platelet count
options.rationale: Platelets relate to bleeding risk, which these findings do not suggest.

options.text: Serum potassium
options.rationale: Potassium changes cause muscle and heart rhythm problems, not this pattern.

questions.takeaway: Constipation, thirst and fatigue in a patient with bone metastases are early signs of hypercalcemia; check the calcium before it progresses to confusion and dysrhythmias.
questions.strategy: Link the history to the lab: bone metastases release calcium. Then check that the symptoms fit high calcium.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Bone spread releases calcium.
Constipation, thirst and fatigue fit hypercalcemia.

elimination.verdict: Serum calcium.

questions.objective: Recognize oncologic emergencies and prioritize the initial nursing response

questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting the condition the patient is most likely experiencing, two actions the nurse should take, and two parameters to monitor.
questions.scenario: A patient with lung cancer reports that shirt collars feel tight. The face and neck are swollen, neck veins are distended, and the patient now has a high pitched sound with each breath.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed
options.rationale: Elevation lets blood drain from the head and eases breathing.

options.text: Encourage a large glass of water
options.rationale: Swallowing is unsafe with a narrowing airway.

options.text: Call the rapid response team
options.rationale: Stridor means the airway is narrowing, which is an emergency.

options.text: Place the patient flat with legs raised
options.rationale: Lying flat worsens swelling in the head and neck.

options.text: Start an IV in the right arm
options.rationale: Arm veins above the blockage drain poorly; IV access goes in the lower body if possible.

options.text: Tumor lysis syndrome
options.rationale: Tumor lysis causes electrolyte changes after treatment, not swelling of the face.

options.text: Superior vena cava syndrome
options.rationale: A lung tumor compressing the superior vena cava blocks blood return from the head, neck and arms.

options.text: Hypercalcemia
options.rationale: Hypercalcemia causes constipation, thirst and confusion.

options.text: Spinal cord compression
options.rationale: Cord compression causes back pain and limb weakness, not facial swelling.

options.text: Airway sounds and respiratory effort
options.rationale: Stridor can progress to airway obstruction.

options.text: Deep tendon reflexes
options.rationale: Reflexes are monitored in calcium and magnesium problems, not here.

options.text: Bowel sounds
options.rationale: Bowel function is not affected by this problem.

options.text: Oxygen saturation
options.rationale: Saturation shows whether swelling is affecting gas exchange.

options.text: Urine specific gravity
options.rationale: Specific gravity relates to fluid balance, not to this obstruction.

questions.takeaway: Superior vena cava syndrome causes swelling of the face, neck and arms with distended neck veins. Stridor signals airway narrowing: raise the head of the bed, get help and watch the airway.
questions.strategy: Swelling above the heart with distended neck veins points to a blocked superior vena cava. Stridor makes the airway the priority.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Blocked superior vena cava.
Elevate and call for help.
Breathing and saturation.

elimination.verdict: Superior vena cava syndrome; raise the head of the bed and call the rapid response team; monitor airway and saturation.

questions.objective: Recognize oncologic emergencies and prioritize the initial nursing response

questions.stem: A patient treated with doxorubicin and chest radiation 4 years ago comes for a survivorship visit. Which report requires follow up?

options.text: Hair has grown back thinner than before
options.rationale: Changes in hair texture are common after chemotherapy and are not dangerous.

options.text: Short of breath when climbing one flight of stairs
options.rationale: Doxorubicin can damage the heart and chest radiation can cause lung fibrosis years later. New exertional shortness of breath needs evaluation.

options.text: Feels anxious before each yearly scan
options.rationale: Scan anxiety is common and is addressed, but it is not a sign of a late physical effect.

options.text: A scar that is lighter than the nearby skin
options.rationale: A pale, healed scar is expected.

questions.takeaway: Late effects of cancer treatment include heart and lung damage, fibrosis in a radiation field, neuropathy, fertility changes and second cancers. Survivors are monitored for years.
questions.strategy: Link the past treatment to the organ it can damage: doxorubicin harms the heart and chest radiation the lungs.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Heart from doxorubicin, lung fibrosis from radiation.
Shortness of breath on exertion.

elimination.verdict: Short of breath climbing stairs.

questions.objective: Plan patient and caregiver teaching for symptom management, follow up, and survivorship

questions.stem: After breast cancer surgery with axillary lymph node removal, which patient statement requires further teaching?

options.text: “I will wear gloves when I work in the garden.”
options.rationale: Protecting the arm from cuts lowers the risk of infection and lymphedema.

options.text: “I will report any new swelling or feeling of heaviness in that arm.”
options.rationale: Early report of swelling lets lymphedema be treated sooner.

options.text: “I will use my electric razor for my underarm.”
options.rationale: An electric razor reduces nicks on the affected side.

options.text: “I will carry heavy grocery bags with that arm right away.”
options.rationale: Heavy lifting soon after surgery strains the arm and can trigger lymphedema. Activity is increased gradually as advised.

questions.takeaway: After axillary node removal, protect the arm from injury, report new swelling or heaviness, and increase lifting gradually to lower the risk of lymphedema.
questions.strategy: This asks for the wrong statement. Find the one that overloads or injures the arm.

strategies: Negative polarity

steps.action: Read the question as a negative
steps.detail: Find the unsafe plan.
Heavy bags right away.

elimination.verdict: Carrying heavy bags right away.

questions.objective: Plan patient and caregiver teaching for symptom management, follow up, and survivorship

questions.stem: A patient with lung cancer that has spread to the spine starts radiation to relieve back pain. Which statement indicates understanding of the treatment goal?

options.text: “This radiation should cure my cancer.”
options.rationale: Radiation to one site cannot cure cancer that has already spread. The goal here is comfort.

options.text: “After this, I can stop my pain medicine.”
options.rationale: Radiation takes days to weeks to ease pain, so pain medicine continues.

options.text: “The goal is to shrink the tumor so my back hurts less.”
options.rationale: This is palliative radiation: it shrinks the tumor pressing on the spine to relieve pain and improve quality of life.

options.text: “Radiation to my spine will stop the cancer from spreading any further in my body.”
options.rationale: Radiation to one site does not stop spread elsewhere in the body.

questions.takeaway: Treatment aimed at symptoms in spread cancer is palliative: it relieves pain or pressure but does not cure.
questions.strategy: Name the goal first. Spread cancer plus a symptom target means palliative.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Relieve pain from a spinal tumor.
Local treatment, spread disease.

elimination.verdict: Shrink the tumor so the back hurts less.

questions.objective: Compare the goals and common types of cancer treatment

skills.title: Enteral Nutrition
skills.subtitle: Enteral vs parenteral nutrition, undernutrition, feeding tubes and routes, assessment before feeding, tube placement, aspiration prevention, feeding methods, formula, flushes and medications

questions.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts enteral and parenteral nutrition?

options.text: Enteral is given by IV; parenteral uses a feeding tube
options.rationale: This reverses the two. “Enteral” means through the intestine.

options.text: Enteral uses the GI tract; parenteral is given by IV
options.rationale: Enteral nutrition delivers formula into a working GI tract through a tube. Parenteral nutrition bypasses the GI tract and goes into a vein.

options.text: Both require a working GI tract to absorb nutrients
options.rationale: Parenteral nutrition is used precisely when the GI tract cannot be used.

options.text: Parenteral is preferred whenever the patient cannot eat
options.rationale: When the gut works, enteral feeding is preferred; parenteral is for a gut that cannot be used.

questions.takeaway: Enteral nutrition goes into a working GI tract (NG or PEG tube); parenteral nutrition goes into a vein when the GI tract cannot be used.
questions.strategy: Anchor on the word root: enteral means intestine. Then ask whether the gut is working.

strategies: Opposite pair, look closely

steps.detail: Into the GI tract.
By IV, bypassing the gut.

elimination.verdict: Enteral uses the GI tract; parenteral is IV.

questions.objective: Compare enteral and parenteral nutrition

questions.stem: A patient has a bowel obstruction and cannot be fed through the GI tract for at least 2 weeks. Which nutrition does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Nasogastric tube feeding
options.rationale: An obstructed bowel cannot be used, so formula into the stomach is unsafe.

options.text: Gastrostomy tube feeding
options.rationale: A gastrostomy still delivers formula into the blocked GI tract.

options.text: Total parenteral nutrition (TPN)
options.rationale: When the GI tract cannot be used, nutrition is given by IV. TPN is the complete form; peripheral parenteral nutrition (PPN) is a shorter term, less concentrated option.

options.text: Nasojejunal tube feeding past the stomach
options.rationale: Feeding past the stomach still requires a working bowel below it.

questions.takeaway: Parenteral nutrition (PPN or TPN) is used when the GI tract cannot be used; any tube feeding needs a working gut.
questions.strategy: Three options put formula into the gut. Only one bypasses it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Obstruction: it cannot be used.

steps.action: Find the route that bypasses it
steps.detail: IV nutrition.

elimination.verdict: Total parenteral nutrition.

questions.objective: Compare enteral and parenteral nutrition

questions.stem: Which patients are candidates for enteral nutrition? Select all that apply.

options.text: A patient after a stroke who coughs and chokes on thin liquids
options.rationale: The GI tract works, but swallowing is unsafe, a classic reason for tube feeding.

options.text: A patient with severe burns whose needs exceed what can be eaten
options.rationale: Needs that oral intake cannot meet are a reason for enteral feeding when the gut works.

options.text: A patient with a complete bowel obstruction
options.rationale: A gut that cannot be used calls for parenteral nutrition, not tube feeding.

options.text: A patient with head and neck cancer who cannot chew
options.rationale: Inability to chew with a working gut is an indication for enteral feeding.

options.text: A patient with an ileus and absent bowel sounds
options.rationale: A nonfunctioning bowel cannot accept formula.

options.text: A patient on a ventilator who cannot eat by mouth
options.rationale: A patient who cannot eat safely by mouth but has a working gut receives enteral feeding.

questions.takeaway: Enteral nutrition is for patients with a working GI tract who cannot eat safely by mouth or cannot eat enough: trouble chewing or swallowing, aspiration risk, or high needs.
questions.strategy: Ask two questions of each patient: does the gut work, and can the patient eat safely and enough by mouth?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Obstruction and ileus rule it out.
Unsafe or not enough means a tube.

elimination.verdict: Stroke with choking, burns, head and neck cancer, ventilator.

questions.objective: Identify patients who need enteral nutrition

questions.stem: Besides the medical indication, what else guides the decision to start enteral nutrition?

options.text: The cost of formula compared with regular food
options.rationale: Cost is not what guides the decision; the patient's goals are.

options.text: Whether the family prefers the patient eat by mouth
options.rationale: Family input matters, but the patient's own goals and preferences come first.

options.text: The nurse's judgment of the patient's quality of life
options.rationale: The nurse does not decide on quality of life for the patient.

options.text: The patient's treatment goals and preferences
options.rationale: Tube feeding is a treatment the patient can accept or decline. Goals of care and preferences are part of the decision.

questions.takeaway: Starting enteral nutrition considers the patient's treatment goals and preferences, not only the medical indication.
questions.strategy: Choose the option that keeps the patient at the center of the decision.

strategies: Patient centered option

steps.detail: Indication plus goals and preferences.

elimination.verdict: The patient's goals and preferences.

questions.objective: Identify patients who need enteral nutrition

questions.stem: Which statement best defines undernutrition?

options.text: A body weight below the ideal for height
options.rationale: Low weight can be a sign, but undernutrition is defined by intake or absorption, and a person of normal weight can be undernourished.

options.text: Inadequate intake or absorption of nutrients
options.rationale: Undernutrition can come from not eating enough or from not absorbing what is eaten.

options.text: Eating only one or two meals a day
options.rationale: Meal number does not define undernutrition; total intake and absorption do.

options.text: A lack of protein in the diet only
options.rationale: Undernutrition includes inadequate calories and other nutrients, not protein alone.

questions.takeaway: Undernutrition is inadequate intake or absorption of nutrients.
questions.strategy: Pick the broadest accurate definition; the others describe one sign or one part.

strategies: Global or umbrella option

steps.detail: Intake or absorption.

elimination.verdict: Inadequate intake or absorption.

questions.objective: Identify patients who need enteral nutrition

questions.stem: Which findings are signs of undernutrition? Select all that apply.

options.text: Weight gain from extra fluid
options.rationale: Fluid weight gain is not a sign of undernutrition, though edema can hide weight loss.

options.text: Unintentional weight loss
options.rationale: Losing weight without trying is a key sign.

options.text: Weakness
options.rationale: Muscle loss from poor intake causes weakness.

options.text: Fatigue
options.rationale: Too little energy intake leads to fatigue.

options.text: Poor wound healing
options.rationale: Healing needs protein, calories and micronutrients.

questions.takeaway: Signs of undernutrition: unintentional weight loss, weakness, fatigue and poor wound healing.
questions.strategy: Each sign follows from too little fuel and building material for the body.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Weight loss, weakness, fatigue, poor healing.

elimination.verdict: Weight loss, weakness, fatigue, poor wound healing.

questions.objective: Identify patients who need enteral nutrition

questions.stem: Which factors place a patient at risk for undernutrition? Select all that apply.

options.text: Poor appetite
options.rationale: Low appetite reduces intake.

options.text: Dysphagia
options.rationale: Trouble swallowing limits what can be eaten safely.

options.text: A daily walking routine
options.rationale: Activity is not a risk factor.

options.text: Chronic illness
options.rationale: Chronic disease raises needs and lowers appetite or absorption.

options.text: Limited access to food
options.rationale: Food insecurity directly limits intake.

questions.takeaway: Risk factors for undernutrition: poor appetite, dysphagia, chronic illness and limited food access. The nursing priority is to find deficits early and monitor the response to feeding.
questions.strategy: Each risk factor either lowers intake or raises needs.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Appetite, swallowing, food access.
Chronic illness.

elimination.verdict: Poor appetite, dysphagia, chronic illness, limited food access.

questions.objective: Identify patients who need enteral nutrition

questions.stem: For each tube, indicate whether it is a short term or long term feeding route.
questions.scenario: The nurse reviews the feeding tubes of six patients.

rows.text: Nasogastric tube
rows.rationale: A tube through the nose into the stomach is a nasoenteric, short term route.

rows.text: Percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG)
rows.rationale: A PEG goes through the abdominal wall into the stomach and is used long term.

rows.text: Gastrostomy tube
rows.rationale: A gastrostomy opens directly into the stomach for long term feeding.

rows.text: Nasoduodenal tube
rows.rationale: Through the nose into the duodenum: short term.

rows.text: Direct percutaneous endoscopic jejunostomy (DPEJ)
rows.rationale: A tube placed directly into the jejunum through the abdominal wall is long term.

rows.text: Nasojejunal tube
rows.rationale: Through the nose into the jejunum: short term, and used less often.

questions.takeaway: Nasoenteric tubes (NG, nasoduodenal, nasojejunal) are short term; enterostomal tubes (gastrostomy, PEG, PEG with a jejunal extension, DPEJ) are long term.
questions.strategy: Look at the entry point: “naso” means through the nose and short term; a tube through the abdominal wall is long term.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: naso = short term.
stomy = an opening in the abdomen, long term.

elimination.verdict: NG, nasoduodenal and nasojejunal are short term; gastrostomy, PEG and DPEJ are long term.

questions.objective: Compare types of feeding tubes and routes

questions.stem: For each feature, indicate the tube it describes.
questions.scenario: The nurse compares large bore and small bore nasogastric tubes.

rows.text: 8 to 12 Fr
rows.rationale: Small bore tubes are 8 to 12 Fr.

rows.text: Used for decompression and lavage
rows.rationale: Only a large bore tube can suction stomach contents or wash out the stomach.

rows.text: Double lumen
rows.rationale: The Salem sump has a second lumen, the air vent.

rows.text: Single lumen
rows.rationale: Small bore tubes have one lumen.

rows.text: Used only for feeding and medications
rows.rationale: A small bore tube is too narrow for suction; it is for feeding and medications.

rows.text: 14 to 18 Fr
rows.rationale: Large bore tubes are 14 to 18 Fr.

questions.takeaway: Large bore NG tubes (14 to 18 Fr, double lumen, such as a Salem sump) are for decompression, lavage and medications; small bore tubes (8 to 12 Fr, single lumen, such as a Dobhoff) are only for feeding and medications.
questions.strategy: Bigger tube, bigger jobs: only the large bore can suction or wash out the stomach.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 14 to 18 Fr large; 8 to 12 Fr small.
Suction needs the large bore.

elimination.verdict: Large bore: 14 to 18 Fr, double lumen, decompression and lavage. Small bore: 8 to 12 Fr, single lumen, feeding and medications only.

questions.objective: Compare types of feeding tubes and routes

questions.stem: Which factors guide the choice of feeding route? Select all that apply.

options.text: The color of the formula
options.rationale: Formula color has no bearing on the route.

options.text: How long the patient will need tube feeding
options.rationale: Nasal tubes are used for short periods; gastrostomy or jejunostomy tubes for long periods.

options.text: The patient's GI anatomy
options.rationale: Surgery or disease of the GI tract affects where a tube can go.

options.text: How well the stomach empties
options.rationale: Poor gastric emptying may favor feeding into the small intestine.

options.text: Which nostril the patient prefers
options.rationale: Nostril choice affects insertion, not the choice between routes.

questions.takeaway: Route depends on how long feeding is needed (nasal for short, G or J tube for long), GI anatomy and gastric emptying. Feeding into the small intestine may lower aspiration risk.
questions.strategy: Each correct factor changes where the formula can safely go.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Short or long.
Where formula can go and stay.

elimination.verdict: Duration, GI anatomy, gastric emptying.

questions.stem: Which step comes first before the nurse starts any tube feeding?

options.text: Flush the tube with 30 mL of water
options.rationale: Flushing comes after placement is confirmed.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed to 30 degrees
options.rationale: Positioning is needed, but verifying the order and patient comes first.

options.text: Verify the order and identify the patient
options.rationale: Every feeding starts with verifying the prescription and the right patient.

options.text: Prime the tubing with formula
options.rationale: Priming prepares equipment; it does not come before verifying the order and patient.

questions.takeaway: Before feeding, verify the order and the patient, then assess, confirm placement and position.
questions.strategy: Safety checks on the order and identity come before any hands on step.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: Right order, right patient.

questions.objective: Assess the patient before feeding

questions.stem: Which assessments does the nurse complete before starting enteral feeding? Select all that apply.

options.text: Abdominal assessment and bowel pattern
options.rationale: Distention, pain or absent bowel function can signal intolerance.

options.text: Level of consciousness and airway protection
options.rationale: A patient who cannot protect the airway has a higher aspiration risk.

options.text: Weight, hydration and intake and output
options.rationale: These set the baseline to judge the response to feeding.

options.text: Baseline respiratory status
options.rationale: A baseline lets the nurse detect aspiration later.

options.text: Nausea, vomiting and swallowing
options.rationale: These show tolerance and aspiration risk.

options.text: Recent laboratory results
options.rationale: Labs show nutrition and electrolyte status before feeding starts.

questions.takeaway: Before feeding, assess weight, hydration, intake and output, labs, abdomen, nausea and vomiting, bowel pattern, swallowing, level of consciousness, airway protection and baseline respiratory status.
questions.strategy: Every item either sets a baseline or shows aspiration or intolerance risk.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Weight, hydration, I&O, labs.
Abdomen, nausea, bowels.
Swallowing, consciousness, airway, breathing.

elimination.verdict: All of them.

questions.objective: Assess the patient before feeding

questions.stem: A small bore feeding tube was just inserted at the bedside. What confirms its placement before the first use?

options.text: Hearing a whoosh after injecting air
options.rationale: Auscultating an air bolus is not reliable; the sound can be heard with the tube in the lung or esophagus.

options.text: Aspirate with a pH of 4
options.rationale: pH supports placement but does not prove it, especially at first placement.

options.text: No coughing during insertion
options.rationale: Small bore tubes can enter the airway without coughing, especially in sedated patients.

options.text: An x ray
options.rationale: An x ray is required before using any blindly inserted tube. It is the only reliable way to confirm initial placement.

questions.takeaway: Initial placement of a blindly inserted tube is confirmed by x ray before formula, water or medications. Air bolus auscultation is not reliable.
questions.strategy: Only one option can show where the tube tip actually is.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: X ray.
Air bolus is unreliable.

elimination.verdict: An x ray.

questions.objective: Verify feeding tube placement

questions.stem: After x ray confirms a new feeding tube's placement, which action does the nurse take next?

options.text: Mark and document the tube length at the exit site
options.rationale: The mark sets the baseline for every later check: a change in the external length suggests the tube moved.

options.text: Inject air and listen over the stomach
options.rationale: Air bolus auscultation is unreliable and adds nothing after an x ray.

options.text: Order a repeat x ray before every feeding and every medication dose
options.rationale: Repeat imaging is for doubtful placement, not routine before every feeding.

options.text: Remove the tape so the tube can move freely
options.rationale: The tube must stay secured to prevent migration.

questions.takeaway: Once placement is confirmed, mark and document the external length at the exit site; it is the baseline for ongoing checks.
questions.strategy: Think about what later checks will compare against.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: External length at the exit site.

elimination.verdict: Mark and document the length.

questions.objective: Verify feeding tube placement

questions.stem: Which actions are part of ongoing tube placement checks? Select all that apply.

options.text: Check placement before each feeding and medication
options.rationale: Placement is checked before every use.

options.text: Compare the external length with the documented baseline
options.rationale: A longer or shorter external length suggests movement.

options.text: Listen for a whoosh after injecting air
options.rationale: Air bolus auscultation is not reliable.

options.text: Check that the tube is secured
options.rationale: Loose securement lets the tube migrate.

options.text: Hold tube use and verify if placement is uncertain
options.rationale: When in doubt, nothing goes down the tube until placement is verified.

options.text: Test aspirate and pH per facility policy
options.rationale: Aspirate and pH are used as supporting checks per policy.

questions.takeaway: Ongoing checks: before feedings and medications (and per policy during continuous feeding), compare external length with baseline, check securement, use aspirate and pH per policy, and hold the tube if unsure.
questions.strategy: Keep every check except the one shown to be unreliable.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Keep the length and securement checks
steps.detail: Baseline comparison.
Air bolus.

questions.objective: Verify feeding tube placement

questions.stem: Which pH value of aspirate from a gastric feeding tube is most consistent with gastric placement?

options.text: PH 7.8
options.rationale: A pH above 7 suggests intestinal or respiratory fluid, not stomach.

options.text: PH 4
options.rationale: Gastric aspirate is usually pH 5 or less because of stomach acid.

options.text: PH 6.5
options.rationale: A pH above 5 is not typical of gastric fluid, though acid suppressants can raise it.

options.text: PH 7
options.rationale: Neutral pH does not fit stomach contents.

questions.takeaway: Gastric aspirate is usually pH 5 or less. Acid suppressants and formula can raise the pH, and pH alone does not prove placement.
questions.strategy: Stomach means acid: pick the lowest value.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 5 or less.

elimination.verdict: pH 4.

questions.objective: Verify feeding tube placement

questions.stem: A patient taking pantoprazole has gastric aspirate with a pH of 6. Which statement explains this finding?

options.text: The tube must be in the lung
options.rationale: A pH of 6 does not point to the lung; it is not a reliable sign of either location.

options.text: A pH of 6 proves the tube is in the stomach
options.rationale: pH alone never proves placement.

options.text: Acid suppressants can raise gastric pH
options.rationale: Proton pump inhibitors reduce stomach acid, so gastric aspirate can test above 5. Formula can also skew the result.

options.text: The pH test strip must be expired
options.rationale: This assumes an equipment error; the medicine is a known cause.

questions.takeaway: Acid suppressants and formula can raise gastric pH, so pH or aspirate appearance alone does not prove placement.
questions.strategy: Look for what in the stem changes stomach acid: the medication.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pantoprazole lowers acid.
pH alone never proves placement.

elimination.verdict: Acid suppressants raise gastric pH.

questions.objective: Verify feeding tube placement

questions.stem: What position does the nurse maintain during a continuous tube feeding?

options.text: Flat with the head turned to the side
options.rationale: Lying flat increases reflux and aspiration risk.

options.text: Head of the bed raised to 15 degrees during the feeding
options.rationale: Fifteen degrees is too low to reduce aspiration risk.

options.text: Trendelenburg with the feet raised
options.rationale: Head down positioning promotes reflux.

options.text: Head of the bed at 30 to 45 degrees
options.rationale: Elevating the head of the bed lets gravity keep formula moving down and reduces reflux and aspiration.

questions.takeaway: Keep the head of the bed at 30 to 45 degrees during feeding and keep the patient upright after intermittent feedings.
questions.strategy: Gravity is the safeguard: choose the highest elevation offered in the right range.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

questions.objective: Prevent aspiration during tube feeding

questions.stem: A patient receives feedings through a nasojejunal tube. Which statement about aspiration risk is accurate?

options.text: Small intestine feeding removes the risk of aspiration
options.rationale: Feeding into the small intestine may lower the risk but does not eliminate it.

options.text: Aspiration risk is lower, but precautions still apply
options.rationale: Formula past the stomach may lower aspiration risk, but reflux and aspiration can still happen.

options.rationale: Small intestine feeding may lower, not raise, the risk.

strategies: Eliminate absolutes

Does not eliminate it.

questions.stem: During tube feeding, which findings does the nurse watch for that suggest intolerance or aspiration risk? Select all that apply.

options.text: Vomiting
options.rationale: Vomiting puts formula in the airway's path.

options.text: Reflux of formula into the mouth
options.rationale: Reflux is a direct route to aspiration.

options.text: Abdominal distention
options.rationale: Distention shows the feeding is not moving through, a sign of intolerance.

Distention.

questions.stem: For each order, indicate the feeding method.
questions.scenario: The nurse reviews the feeding orders of five patients.

rows.text: 50 mL/hr by pump around the clock
rows.rationale: A steady hourly rate on a pump is continuous feeding.

rows.text: 240 mL given over 10 minutes by syringe
rows.rationale: A large volume given quickly is a bolus.

rows.text: 80 mL/hr by pump from 1900 to 0700
rows.rationale: Pump feeding over a set period, such as overnight, is cyclic.

rows.text: 300 mL over 45 minutes at 0800, 1200, 1600 and 2000
rows.rationale: Feedings at scheduled times are intermittent.

rows.text: Rate increased by 10 mL/hr every 8 hours to a goal of 60 mL/hr
rows.rationale: This is a continuous feeding being advanced, only as ordered.

questions.stem: Before hanging a new container of formula, which actions are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Warm the formula in a microwave
options.rationale: Microwaving heats unevenly and is not done; formula is given at room temperature.

options.text: Check the expiration date

questions.stem: When does the nurse flush a feeding tube with water? Select all that apply.

options.text: Before and after an intermittent feeding

options.text: At intervals during continuous feeding
options.rationale: Scheduled flushes prevent clogging during continuous feeding.

options.rationale: A final flush clears the tube and delivers the full dose.

options.rationale: Flushing only after a clog is too late; routine flushes prevent clogs.

questions.takeaway: Flush with 30 mL of water (or as ordered) before and after intermittent feeds, at intervals during continuous feeds, and before, between and after medications.
questions.strategy: Routine flushes prevent clogs; waiting for an alarm does not.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

Before, between, after.

options.text: Count them as 120 mL of intake
options.rationale: Water flushes are part of the patient's total intake and are added to intake and output.

options.text: Count them only if the patient is on fluid restriction
options.rationale: Flushes always count toward intake.

options.rationale: Water given is intake, not output.

questions.stem: Before giving a medication through a feeding tube, what does the nurse confirm?

options.text: The feeding has been stopped for 24 hours
options.rationale: Feedings are not routinely stopped for a day for medications.

options.text: All medications can be mixed together
options.rationale: Medications are given separately with flushes between them.

options.text: The medication is appropriate for the tube
options.rationale: Some medications, such as extended release or enteric coated forms, cannot be crushed or given by tube. Each one is checked.

options.text: The tube is large bore
options.rationale: Medications can go through small bore tubes too.

questions.takeaway: Confirm that each medication is right for the tube; give each one separately with flushes before, between and after.
questions.strategy: Check the drug against the route first.

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing to start an intermittent feeding through a nasogastric tube. Place the steps in order.

options.text: Verify the order and identify the patient
options.rationale: Every feeding starts with the right order for the right patient.

options.text: Flush the tube with 30 mL of water
options.rationale: The flush checks patency and clears the tube.

options.text: Confirm placement by external length and aspirate pH per policy
options.rationale: Placement is confirmed before water, formula or medications.

options.text: Assess the abdomen, breathing and level of consciousness
options.rationale: Assessment shows whether the patient can safely be fed.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed to 30 to 45 degrees
options.rationale: Elevation is in place before anything enters the tube.

options.text: Give the feeding as ordered
options.rationale: The feeding goes in only after all checks.

questions.takeaway: Order: verify, assess, position, confirm placement, flush, feed.
questions.strategy: Safety checks come before hands on steps, and placement is confirmed before anything, even water, goes down the tube.

Then confirm placement.
Flush, then feed.

questions.objective: Assess the patient before feeding

questions.stem: The nurse checks the aspirate of a patient's nasogastric feeding tube. Complete the sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence: Gastric aspirate is usually pH [[1]], but [[2]] can raise the pH, so pH alone [[3]] placement.

options.text: between 6 and 7
options.rationale: This range is not typical of gastric fluid.

options.text: exactly 7.4
options.rationale: That is blood pH, not gastric pH.

options.text: 5 or less
options.rationale: Stomach acid keeps gastric aspirate at pH 5 or less.

options.text: 7 or more
options.rationale: A pH of 7 or more suggests intestinal or respiratory fluid.

options.text: water flushes given yesterday
options.rationale: Earlier flushes do not change the pH of today's aspirate.

options.text: acid suppressants and formula
options.rationale: Both can raise the pH of stomach contents.

options.text: an x ray of the chest
options.rationale: Imaging does not affect pH.

options.text: raising the head of the bed
options.rationale: Position does not change gastric pH.

options.text: replaces the x ray for
options.rationale: An x ray is still required before first use of a blindly inserted tube.

options.text: always confirms
options.rationale: Bedside test always confirms placement; x ray confirms initial placement.

options.text: is the only check for
options.rationale: pH is one of several ongoing checks, with external length and securement.

options.text: does not prove
options.rationale: pH and aspirate appearance support but do not prove placement.

questions.takeaway: Gastric pH is usually 5 or less; acid suppressants and formula can raise it, so pH alone does not prove placement.
questions.strategy: Recall the number, the two things that skew it, and the limit of the test.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 5 or less.
Acid suppressants, formula.
Does not prove placement.

elimination.verdict: 5 or less; acid suppressants and formula; does not prove.

questions.objective: Verify feeding tube placement

questions.stem: A medication is due through a small bore nasogastric tube. The external mark is 6 cm farther out than documented. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Give the medication, then report the change
options.rationale: Using a tube that may have moved risks putting the drug into the esophagus or lungs.

options.text: Push the tube back to the original mark
options.rationale: Pushing a small bore tube back can place it in the airway. Placement must be verified, not guessed.

options.text: Inject air and listen over the stomach
options.rationale: Air bolus auscultation is not reliable for checking placement.

options.text: Hold the medication and verify placement
options.rationale: A changed external length suggests the tube moved. When placement is uncertain, nothing goes down the tube until it is verified.

questions.takeaway: If the external length changes or placement is uncertain, hold tube use and verify placement before giving anything.
questions.strategy: The changed mark is the cue. Any option that uses or moves the tube before verifying is unsafe.

strategies: Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: Mark moved 6 cm.
Nothing goes in until verified.

elimination.verdict: Hold and verify placement.

questions.objective: Verify feeding tube placement

questions.stem: Thirty minutes after a bolus feeding, a patient asks to lie flat for a nap. Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: “You can lie flat now since the feeding is done.”
options.rationale: Formula is still in the stomach; lying flat soon after a feeding raises aspiration risk.

options.text: “I will keep the head of the bed up while you rest.”
options.rationale: The patient stays upright for a period after intermittent feedings. The patient can nap with the head of the bed raised.

options.text: “You can lie on your left side instead of flat.”
options.rationale: Side lying does not replace head elevation after a feeding.

options.text: “You need to sit in the chair for the next 4 hours.”
options.rationale: The patient can rest in bed with the head raised; 4 hours in a chair is not required.

questions.takeaway: Keep the patient upright after intermittent feedings to prevent reflux and aspiration.
questions.strategy: Meet the patient's wish to rest while keeping the safeguard: head elevation.

strategies: Patient centered option

steps.detail: Upright after intermittent feeds.
Rest with the head raised.

elimination.verdict: Rest with the head of the bed raised.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the note of a patient receiving continuous nasogastric feeding at 55 mL/hr. Highlight the findings that require follow up.
questions.nursesNote: Head of bed at 15 degrees. External tube mark at 62 cm, documented baseline 62 cm. Coughing after each sip of water. Bowel sounds active in all 4 quadrants. Abdomen distended and firm compared with this morning. Formula container labeled with date, time and initials. Respiratory rate 26/min, up from 18/min.

segments.text: Head of bed at 15 degrees
segments.rationale: The head of the bed must be at 30 to 45 degrees during feeding.

segments.text: External tube mark at 62 cm, documented baseline 62 cm
segments.rationale: The external length matches the baseline.

segments.text: Coughing after each sip of water
segments.rationale: Coughing with liquids suggests unsafe swallowing and aspiration risk.

segments.text: Bowel sounds active in all 4 quadrants
segments.rationale: Active bowel sounds are expected.

segments.text: Abdomen distended and firm compared with this morning
segments.rationale: New distention signals feeding intolerance.

segments.text: Formula container labeled with date, time and initials
segments.rationale: Labeling is correct practice.

segments.text: Respiratory rate 26/min, up from 18/min
segments.rationale: A rising respiratory rate compared with baseline can be an early sign of aspiration.

questions.takeaway: During feeding, act on a low head of bed, signs of intolerance (distention) and signs of aspiration (coughing, rising respiratory rate). Compare with the baseline.
questions.strategy: Compare each finding with its baseline or standard: the bed angle, the abdomen and the breathing all changed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 15 degrees is too low.
New distention.
Coughing, rising rate.

elimination.verdict: Head of bed, coughing, distention, respiratory rate.

questions.stem: Before an intermittent feeding, the nurse aspirates clear fluid with a pH of 7 from a nasogastric tube in a patient taking no acid suppressants. Which action is appropriate?

options.text: Give the feeding since fluid was aspirated
options.rationale: Getting fluid back does not prove gastric placement; the pH does not fit the stomach.

options.text: Flush with 30 mL of water and recheck the pH
options.rationale: Putting water down a tube of uncertain placement is unsafe.

options.text: Hold the feeding and follow policy to verify placement
options.rationale: A pH above 5 without an acid suppressant suggests the tube may not be in the stomach. Hold use and verify.

options.text: Advance the tube 5 cm and give the feeding
options.rationale: Moving the tube blindly does not confirm placement.

questions.takeaway: Gastric aspirate is usually pH 5 or less. An unexpected pH with no acid suppressant means hold the tube and verify placement.

steps.detail: 7 is above 5.
No acid suppressant.
Hold and verify.

questions.stem: An older adult living alone has unintentionally lost 5 kg in 2 months and has a slow healing wound. Which action is the nursing priority?

options.text: Teach the patient to eat three large meals a day
options.rationale: Teaching before assessing the cause skips the first step, and large meals may not be realistic.

options.text: Request an order for a feeding tube
options.rationale: A tube may never be needed; assessment comes first.

options.text: Encourage the patient to rest more to heal the wound
options.rationale: Rest does not address the nutrition deficit behind the poor healing.

options.text: Assess intake and nutritional risk and report the findings
options.rationale: Weight loss and poor healing are signs of undernutrition. The priority is to identify the deficit early so feeding can be planned and monitored.

Intake and risk.

questions.stem: The nurse finds a feeding set connector that will not fit the patient's ENFit feeding tube port. A Luer IV adapter is in the drawer. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Use the adapter to connect the set
options.rationale: Adapting connectors defeats the safety design and risks connecting enteral and IV systems.

options.text: Get an ENFit compatible feeding set
options.rationale: ENFit connectors fit only enteral devices to prevent wrong route errors, so the nurse gets matching equipment.

options.text: Tape the connector to the port securely
options.rationale: Taping does not make an incompatible connection safe.

options.text: Give the feeding by syringe through the IV adapter
options.rationale: This still uses an IV style connection on an enteral tube.

questions.takeaway: Never force or adapt connections between enteral and IV equipment; use ENFit compatible supplies.
questions.strategy: Any workaround that joins mismatched connectors creates a wrong route risk.

Adapters and tape.

questions.stem: A patient will need tube feeding for several months after head and neck cancer surgery. Which tube does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Nasogastric tube
options.rationale: Nasal tubes are for short feeding periods; months of use risk nasal injury and dislodgement.

options.rationale: This is also a short term nasal route.

questions.stem: A patient receiving continuous feeding at 60 mL/hr also receives 30 mL water flushes every 4 hours. What is the total enteral intake for an 8 hour shift?

options.text: 480 mL
options.rationale: This counts the formula only (60 × 8) and leaves out the two flushes.

options.rationale: This counts only one flush; every 4 hours in an 8 hour shift is two.

options.text: 600 mL

questions.stem: A patient who receives cyclic feedings overnight asks why the feeding stops in the morning. Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: “It runs during set hours so you are free during the day.”
options.rationale: Cyclic feeding runs by pump over a set period, often overnight, which leaves daytime free for activity and eating if allowed.

options.rationale: Many patients receive continuous feeding while awake; cyclic is chosen, not required.

options.rationale: Bag changes do not explain the schedule.
